name: Between Sand and Sea

neighbours.name: The Great Hunger
neighbours.summary:
The spirit at the centre of the Great Desert, whose strength even gods respect: the desert's heat and scouring wind given one will, which would leave the world dust. The Romans called it the Fames Magna, the Berbers Lazz, the Arabs Al-Ju'; along the Nile it is the Red.

Hostile creatures, spirits, faeries and jinn serve it, and some people do too: the settuten trace their line to the Yemma-t n Dunnit, perhaps its foremost servant.

neighbours.name: The Hope
neighbours.summary: The spirit of the Nile and the fertile black earth, called the Black, which holds back the Hunger. It favours people only by accident, being too vast to notice them. The lector priests who were magicians to the pharaohs served it, and so does Wesir, whom the Greeks called Osiris.

neighbours.name: The Pact of 1225
neighbours.summary: When most of the Cordovan sahirs joined the Order of Hermes in 925, one condition was that no covenant be founded in Africa for three centuries. Nobody now agrees why: to hide them from jinn they had betrayed, or to keep the settuten from becoming the Order's enemies. It expires in 1225, and some magi are eager to go.

stages.title: The pact expires
stages.ignored: Magi are free to found covenants in Africa.

neighbours.name: Mythic Africa
neighbours.summary:
The third of the world's three continents, lying between the Mediterranean and the Great Ocean, with the Nile on its east and the Atlantic on its west. It takes its name from the Roman province, which the Arabs still call Ifriqiyeh; Arab writers call the land Bilad al-Barbar or al-Maghrib, 'the West', and Europeans still draw Gaetula at its heart and Ethiopia beyond. The strip between desert and sea looks barely fit to live in, yet some of the widest-ruling dynasties the world has known began here.

To a European it is a land of wonder: in the markets of Marrakesh spices lie in open heaps beside cloth of impossible colour, blemmyae trade raw gold from camels guarded by huge black-furred dog-heads, and at the desert's edge the heat is a smith's forge. Small raiders ride ostriches, Tuareg ride out of a mirage and are gone, and in the deep sands travellers tell of ancient cities, the congresses of demons and talk with angels. It is also a land of hunger: the spirit at the desert's centre would dry every oasis and grind the mountains to dust, and only what has been raised against it has stopped it. Egypt called on the black earth, Carthage paid its gods for protection, and some think the Hunger moved Rome to destroy them and left it needing a protector of its own. Today the Dominion, Christian and then Muslim, makes a thin firm wall. Those who live here hardly notice either theme; a stranger notices both.

The time of legends gave the land the giant Antaios (Antaeus to the Romans, Anti to the Berbers), who raised a temple to his father Poseidon out of the skulls of those he beat at wrestling and drew his strength from his mother the earth, until Herakles, on the way to the Apples of the Hesperides, held him off the ground and crushed his ribs. By Antaios's wife Tinjis, Herakles fathered Sufax, mythic ancestor of the Berbers, who built Tangier in his mother's name and took up the giant's guardianship of the country.

Dido the Phoenician founded Carthage in 814 BC, and at its height its trade ran from the Gulf of Sidra to the Atlantic with colonies in Spain, Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica, while Greeks held the coast of Cyrenaica and Tripolitania and Berber kingdoms, Numidia and Mauritania the greatest, traded with it. In the Second Punic War the Numidian kings took opposite sides: Suphax of the western Masaesyli for Rome and Gala of the eastern Massylii for Carthage, until Gala's heir Massinissa, seeing who was winning, went over to Rome and Suphax allied with Hasdrubal, Hannibal's brother. Rome razed Carthage in 146 BC, salted its fields and made the Province of Africa; Massinissa received Numidia. His grandson Jugurtha fought Rome from 112 BC until Mauritania helped capture him in 104 BC. Claudius split Mauritania into Caesariensis and Tingitana.

The Roman provinces grew rich and Latin-speaking, and Christianity gave them Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, then, as Rome faded, Arianism, Pelagianism, Donatism and Montanism. The tribes of the interior paid tribute, sent auxiliaries and otherwise lived as before. The Vandals raided Tingitana in 422; invited in under Gaiseric by the Comes Africae to be penned there, they refused all control and the provinces were lost until Belisarius retook Africa for Byzantium in 522. Byzantium held only the coastal towns, playing chiefs against each other, while the Luwata in the east, the Sanhaja in the west and centre and the Zenata in the south and south-west held the rest.

Umayyad raiders reached Cyrenaica in 642 and were bribed away. 'Uqbah ibn Nafi returned in 670, founded al-Qayrawan and carried Arab rule across the Maghreb until the chief Kusayla slew him in 683. Under Kusayla and then the Kahina the Berbers held twenty years, and Umayyad wizards found their spirits deserting them before Berber magic. The Arabs won at last by buying tribes with land and reward, finishing the resistance in 711, and the mostly Berber army of Tariq ibn Ziyad went on to take Visigothic Hispania. By 720 the wazirs were fighting a magical war in Africa against their own rebellious jinn, whom Berber magic had goaded, and were driven back east. Umayyad governors enforced Arab rule by discrimination and slavery; in 739 the Berbers rose, united under Kharijite Islam, and with a revolt in Egypt and the caliph's death the Umayyad dynasty fell.

Most of the north now belongs to the Almohad confederation. Africa is not a land of feudal states with fixed borders: each village belongs to a tribe, and tribal leaders form confederations that raise or uphold a dynasty. Monstrous races such as the headless blemmyae, dog-faced cynocephali and child-sized tripithami mostly keep apart from people, save in the great cities, but meeting them is not rare. The Latin Church has almost no presence: no abbeys, most Christians in Tunis and a very small enclave at Kairouan, while mosques are everywhere and the call to prayer marks how far a Divine aura runs. The Genoese guard a busy trade with ports on both sides of the Pillars of Hercules. Sicily's west is still held by a Muslim warlord in 1220, and if history holds Frederick II begins his campaigns against him in 1221.
neighbours.secrets:
Why no covenants (pp. 8-11). Any of these may be true in a saga: the pact of 925, which questionable covenants may have broken; the early Order's heart being the Black Forest and not Rome, so young magi found sites nearer home; Muslim Sicily and Castille having once stood between the core Tribunals and the Maghreb; the desert uprisings of uncompromising nomad Muslims, unbribable and seemingly Divinely protected, who wreck irrigation and ruin agrarian lands. The book details no failed covenants, but a troupe may add them.

What Africa offers magi: rival-free vis and resources, troubled only by Moorish or Berber settlements and local sorcerers; no vote, no Tribunal approval, no Peripheral Code on vis sites, and little fear of a charge of mundane interference, though acts that spill over the Mediterranean can still bring charges in Europe. Against that: isolation from news and help, native distrust of foreigners, and no safe assumption that magic is superior, since a campaign of conquest may unite sahirs, murabitin, the Tuareg and the Wind Spirits. Weak Divine reach and thin population make Magic sites easy to find, and nothing stops magi evicting a weaker sorcerer, genius loci or faerie. Muslim magi avoid the strife of the Iberian or Levant Tribunals. Exiles from the Order may hide here, near enough to keep ties that may also betray them.

Logistics (pp. 11-12): a magus must belong to one Tribunal, and one may refuse an African covenant, or several may fight to claim it; Houses Mercere and Guernicus may object to the journeys, and a covenant may need an enchantment for redcaps or even a Mercere Portal. Hermetic settlement is left undefined, and later books assume none. Options for any city: a Mercere trading house with wharf and warehouse, keeping magic quiet; Jerbiton scholars at the madrasas, a loose network anxious about coming civil war; Criamon's small Sufi membership, welcoming to those learning Enigmatic Wisdom; or Tremere spies, African-looking magi raised from Gifted children Mercere gathered at the Primus's request a few decades ago.

Languages (pp. 18-19). Living: Arabic (Andalusi, Classical, Derija; Derija is the common speech, Classical the tongue of scholarship and the Qur'an, and reading the Qur'an needs Artes Liberales 1 and Arabic (Classical) 3; dhimmis from Iberia often speak Andalusi); Tamazight (Tarifit in the Maghreb and Rif, Kabyle, Tashelhiyt in the central highlands, Zenaga in south-west Mauritania, Tamahak among the Tuareg, Siwi at Siwah alone); Lingua Franca or Sabir (Western, Eastern), the commonest tongue of visiting Europeans; Punic (Khalidan). Dead: East German (Gothic, Vandalic), Greek (Classical), Latin (Classical), Libyan, Punic (Carthaginian, Phoenician). Scholars and travellers often lose their dialect for a standard specialty. Northern Arabic and Tamazight use Arabic script, the Tuareg and southern Berbers Tifinagh, Khalidan a Phoenician variant, the Germans Gothic. Penalties to both speakers: dialects of one language -1; northern Tamazight with Tamahak -2; any Tamazight with Punic (Khalidan) -3; Punic with Libyan -2. Others are mutually unintelligible. Almoravid and Almohad warriors and clerics often have only Arabic (Classical) 3.

Pronunciation and Tamazight plurals are on p. 19; Arabic pronunciation is in Realms of Power: The Divine p. 107. Art & Academe p. 28 discusses the shape of the world.

neighbours.name: Mauritania (Al-Maghrib al-Aqsa)
neighbours.summary: The Farthest West, on the Atlantic: mostly coastal desert whose plants drink the fogs off the cool sea, which lets people live south of the Tropic of Cancer. The Adrar highlands wall it from the furnace of the inland desert.

neighbours.name: Ifriqiyeh
neighbours.summary: The old Roman Province of Africa, among the Aures Mountains, ruled for the Almohads by Hafsid governors.

neighbours.name: Badja
neighbours.summary: A town near Tunis with a stone engraving of the seven Dii Mauri on a bench above the Latin words salutares, immortales and augusti: Bonchar at the centre with his staff, their lord; on his right Vihina of home and childbirth with an infant at her feet, then Macurgum of health with scroll and serpent staff; on his left Varsissima of secrets, then Matilam presiding over a boar's sacrifice; and at the ends Macurtan of the waters with a bucket and Iunam of the moon.

neighbours.name: The Grand Erg
neighbours.summary: The sand sea south of the Atlas Mountains.

neighbours.name: Erg Chech and El Djouf
neighbours.summary: The vast sand seas east of Mauritania.

neighbours.name: The Tademait Plateau
neighbours.summary: A hamada south of the Grand Erg, flat beyond compare and truly empty: no hills, villages or beasts, not even pebbles, only dust and the odd bush that eyes are glad to see. It ends at mountains to the south-west and Tuat to the south-east. It is known as a haunt of jnun, and its emptiness has driven men mad.

neighbours.name: The Libyan Desert
neighbours.summary: South and east of Cyrenaica, largely filled by the Great Sand Sea, with the Ubari and Murzuq ergs at its south-west.

neighbours.name: The Tibesti Mountains
neighbours.summary: The highest mountains of the desert, beyond the Great Sand Sea on the border of the torrid zone; Emi Koussi tops eleven thousand feet. In the local dialect the name means the Mountains of Hunger.

neighbours.name: The Torrid Zone
neighbours.summary:
The belt about the equator where the sun comes closest and burns the land, and at whose heart the Great Ocean must lie, known by logic and not by sight. Christian and Arab scholars agree it is impassable and lifeless and that Africa ends north of it; how far north it reaches is argued, though most say no further than the Tropic of Cancer. Some speak of a 'ring of fire', but it mostly comes on as a worsening of the desert, with no known water at all. Those who have returned from its fringes tell of fabulous lands. Logic also requires a twin habitable zone beyond the equator, for ever out of reach, which some think the place of the Magic Realm.

Beyond the desert the maps set Aethiopia on the equatorial ocean: Aethiopia Orientalis south of Egypt and Aethiopia Occidentalis south of Mauritania. Most of the black-skinned people known to the north are Ethiopians of the zone's fringes.
neighbours.secrets:
Deprivation rolls for thirst come every two hours (see Hazards of the Great Desert), and sun on bare skin does +5 non-combat damage as often. Patches that give life may lie in Magic or Faerie auras or regiones joined to the desert's regio network; desert dwellers are likely to know them. A storyguide may keep the south beyond the desert habitable, or in regiones.

If the troupe wants it impassable, it can be a Divine edict: the heat, coming from the superlunar sun, lies past Hermetic magic, grows until it beats any defence, foils magic spectacularly and may be patrolled by angels. Research on the Limit of the Lunar Sphere may profit here. Ideas for what lies within: a city of refugees from Carthage under a college of priestesses; Prester John's peaceful empire; grasslands and jungles whose nomads herd for sphinxes; a river of gems and vis through black ravines that trap the ghosts of those who die there; the true home of the Sudanese in Aethiopia Occidentalis. Whether Aethiopia is the torrid zone is for the saga.

neighbours.name: Almohad Caliph
neighbours.summary:
Yusuf al-Mustansir, also called Yusef II, Caliph of Morocco, was ten when his father died in 1213 and is seventeen now; the regency council set up then still largely rules for him. The Almohads, al-Muwahhidun or 'the monotheists', are Berbers of Masmuda leadership and hold the confederation to which most of the north belongs, in Africa and al-Andalus.

Ibn Tumart of the Masmuda studied in Granada and Baghdad and taught the strict unity of God, denying that God's attributes exist apart from Him. He came home in 1117, agitated against the Almoravids, built a fortress at Tinmel in the High Atlas and raided the Marrakesh road to Sijilmasa for eight years. His first true battle, the siege of Marrakesh in 1130, was a disaster, and he died months later, which only heartened his followers. Abd al-Mu'min drove out the Almoravids, reached Egypt's border by 1147, and took al-Andalus between 1147 and 1173.

Early in 1220 he took the advice of his sahir vizier and beheaded most of the Franciscan friars sent to preach on this coast. The Marinids beat his armies in the Rif in 1217 and have not been dislodged, and he has fortified his Iberian cities against them. If history holds, the last synagogue in Marrakesh closes in 1224.

links.note: Nomads of Cyrenaica and Tripolitania, which the Ayyubids control (p. 19)

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Sultan of Egypt
neighbours.summary:
Al-Kamil, sultan in Cairo since 1218, the head of Salah al-Din's family, the Ayyubids, whose princes rule Egypt, Syria, the Jazira and Yemen and spend much of their time plotting against one another. The Hijaz, Mecca and Medina are his in name; his kinsman al-Mas'ud Yusuf holds Yemen and 'Asir more closely.

In 1220 the Fifth Crusade sits in Damietta, taken in 1219 after he offered, and was refused, all the old Latin lands west of the Jordan for the Crusade's leaving Egypt and a thirty-year truce. He camps at al-Mansura. If history holds he reigns until 1238.

neighbours.name: Ayyubid Rulers of Cyrenaica
neighbours.summary: The Kurdish rulers the Ayyubid sultanate, founded by Saladin, sets over the cities of Cyrenaica, upheld by Bedouin and Turkish troops. The sultanate holds Egypt, Cyrenaica, Tripolitania and much of Arabia, and governs this region from Tripoli.

neighbours.name: The Rustamids
neighbours.summary: A Kharijite dynasty of Tahart, risen from the Banu Ifran under the Kahina. Abdul-Rustam ibn Rustam, of Persian descent, set up a theocracy of elected imams over Ibadite Berber tribes, honest, pious, friends of astronomy, mathematics and theology. They kept no reliable army, and the Fatimids' champion Abu 'Abdulla crushed them.

neighbours.name: The Banu Midrar
neighbours.summary: The Kharijite rulers of Sijilmasa, a cosmopolitan city of Sanhaja, Jews, Andalusians, Berbers and Arabs, with coal-black men, dog-heads and other wonders. Tolerant and peaceable to all save the Idrisids to the north, they fell to Abu 'Abdulla.

neighbours.name: The Idrisids
neighbours.summary: The Sunni Arab dynasty of Fes, which had fought beside the Shi'ites against the Abbasids. Having little Berber support, they made the north-west mostly Arab, to this day. They never conquered the Barghawata.

neighbours.name: The Barghawata Confederation
neighbours.summary: An Atlantic Berber confederation whose early ruler claimed to be a prophet, wrote a holy book in Berber and converted his people to his own faith. The Almoravids stamped out the heresy.

neighbours.name: The Aghlabids
neighbours.summary: The caliph's embassy at Qayrawan under Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab, which came to rule as a dynasty. Abu 'Abdulla beat them again and again from 903 to 909.

neighbours.name: The Fatimids
neighbours.summary: Abu 'Abdulla, a Yemeni Isma'ili missionary, won over the Kutuma and conquered Kairouan, Ifriqiyeh, Tahart and Sijilmasa. In 909 the Isma'ili leader 'Ubaydalla Sa'id came and took the dynasty from him, and within two years had him and his family murdered. They persuaded the Kutuma settuten to turn on Abbasid sahirs, whom they drove from Africa by disrupting magic, banishing spirits and stirring rebellion among bound jinn: Africa is still hostile to the Order of Suleiman. They took Egypt by 969, founded Cairo and left the Maghreb. Caliph al-Mustansir then loosed the Bani Hilal on the rebellious Zirids.

neighbours.name: The Zirids
neighbours.summary: The family of Buluggin ibn Ziri, a Sanhaja Berber made governor of the Maghreb by the Fatimids, whose rule became a dynasty. When they rebelled, the Bani Hilal overran them and the emir fell back from Qayrawan to Mahdia on the coast.

neighbours.name: The Hammadids
neighbours.summary: A Sanhaja dynasty, badly weakened by the coming of the Banu Hilal.

neighbours.name: The Almoravids
neighbours.summary: Al-Murabitun, from the zealot Abdallah ibn Yasin of the Gazzula, whose orthodoxy failed among his own people. Yahya ibn Umar of the Lamtuna invited him to preach, wanting the Sanhaja reunited, and together from the early 1050s they took the Maghreb: Sijilmasa in 1054, and by 1062 Yusuf ibn Tashfin had founded Marrakesh and spread over the Atlas. Invited to al-Andalus in 1086 against the king of Leon and Castile, he saw the princes' disunity, returned, and by 1094 held all Muslim Iberia but Zaragoza. His son Ali ibn Yusuf, raised in luxury, lost ground to Christians and Almohads; four years after Ali's death in 1143 Marrakesh fell and the dynasty ended.

neighbours.name: The Berbers (Imazighen)
neighbours.summary:
The first people of Africa, who call themselves Imazighen (one Amazigh), 'free men'; the Romans said Mazices or Mauri, whence Europe's 'Moor' for Berber and Arab alike. Phoenicians, Romans, Visigoths, Greeks and Arabs have all come, and Berbers remain the dominant culture, a Berber dynasty ruling most of the Maghreb. They are a Mediterranean folk with olive skin weathered by desert wind, dark-haired, sometimes auburn or blond. Men wear the hooded wool tajellabiyt, with an asilham cloak at night or in the mountains. Women wear the white haik and tahruyt headscarf, drawn across the face before strange men so that only the right eye shows, with an indigo set embroidered for ceremony.

Women's tattoos are thought to add beauty, and pass from mother to daughter, allowed by local custom despite the Hadith. Green siyala mark the face, neck and chest: a line from lip to chin at marriage that grows crosses and palm fronds for children and family events, and dotted 'ant-tracks' round the eyes. Ahadjam on the body, worn by both sexes, ward infertility on the back, wake the senses on the breast, turn the evil eye at wrist and ankle and keep off jnun at hand and foot. A neggafa paints festive tawzayt in henna, saffron or black harquus, and some ngagef put power in them.

Their society is in name leaderless, joined by resistance to central rule. Houses are of equal size, milk is shameful to buy and surplus is given and not sold. Men have everything outdoors: herding sheep and goats, metalwork, butchery, market and the grain store, where no woman should be seen. The wife or mother of the eldest male rules the house, and women hold weaving, dyeing, pottery, baskets, food and even carpentry, and teach each other letters at the loom, so a wife is likelier literate than her husband. Monogamy is the norm. They are freer with women than Arabs are, yet the fountain is as forbidden to men as the grain store to women.

A village or thaddart climbs a hilltop in steps to the minaret, or is dug into caves in the Atlas; old families live on top, new arrivals below, from 50 houses to 1500 near trade roads. In towns men hold the vaulted streets and women the roofs above, crossing gaps by leap, ladder and bridge. Houses of two or three storeys keep beasts below, windows only high up and a roof terrace; three or four share a courtyard, and these make a ward or thakherroubt with its own cemetery, threshing room and grain store. Outsiders live at the edge. Each ward's tajmait, chaired by an elected amin, judges public matters and fines men who fail to attend; its worst sentence is that nobody speak to the offender. The ward's most learned women form the tala at the fountain: they tend the dead, act on anonymous denunciations over private conduct, and enforce penance through their sons and husbands.

Two to eight or more villages make a tribe or 'arsh. Trees and irrigated plots are private, rain-fed plough land the village's, pasture the tribe's, which also terraces land and digs channels together. Members trade among themselves; Berbers hold no markets, though men go to those outside and peddlers are borne. Tribes may join a thaqbilt, and the three such great confederations are the Zenata, Masmuda and Sanhaja.

Coastal Arabs think them superstitious. Most are in name Ibadi Muslims, little given to persecuting anyone, and much pagan custom lingers, above all inland; Christians survive on the coast of the Tell. Villages hold one faith or another, the settuten, pagan nearly always, being tolerated for their service up to a point. Pagans honour Tafuyt the harsh sun, Ayyur the moon and sacrifices, bull-headed Gurzil of war, Anzar of rain, Dunnit of fertility and death (Tanit at Carthage, Neith in Egypt), and local gods such as Baccax of caves and Lilleu of a river. Their dead are gods too: they swear with a hand on a tomb and sleep in it for dreams. Householders lead the village's rites and chief women the family's. Remote villages still leave small gifts in cave shrines for the Dii Mauri, more to placate them than to worship.

In the beginning a man and a woman lived in the dark Netherworld, and she was the Yemma-t n Dunnit, the First Mother of the World, a great witch whose hundred children climbed to the light. She made sun, moon, stars, beasts and plants, and having no more to make, made destruction: eclipses, discord, death, gossip and lies. The porcupine bears the splinters of her spindle and the tortoise was a calf crushed in her millstones. Ayyur the moon is her son and Tafuyt the sun her daughter. Against her stands Awettuf the ant, husband of Tafuyt, who taught people to use what she made, to grow grain and bake, to sacrifice, and got the wild bulls to serve.

The Kahina (al-Kahinat, 'the seeress'), born Dihya, took up the resistance in the 680s, drove the Arabs from Ifriqiyeh and kept them besieged in Cyrenaica for five years while she wasted the land, losing the oasis folk's love. Her adopted son betrayed her, and she died sword in hand in 703, aged 127, having foreseen enough to save her line: her sons turned Muslim and led the Berber army into Iberia. An idol of Gurzil from Jugurtha's day went into every battle with her, and some think her a settut.

details.decides: Each ward's tajmait, under its amin; confederations meet in need
details.rules: Kharijism (p. 29): the earliest sect, who left Ali over arbitration, hold that major sin ends one's Islam, that any irreproachable believer may be caliph and any bad one deposed, that jihad is a sixth pillar, and that all believers are equal. It is extinct here but lives on in the gentler Ibadis, who reject violent rebellion: their Mashayekh elect and may remove an absolute Imam, and the 'Azzaba lead religious orders. Ibadism opposes Sufism but accepts the baraka of great leaders.

neighbours.secrets:
Most Berber gods belong to the Faerie Realm. Whether the Dii Mauri still hear, or lie smothered by the Divine, is left open. The settuten, dedicated to the god of sacrifices, are the nearest thing to a priesthood (ch. 4). Traditional ahadjam forms are in the Tattoo Magicians section, pp. 93-95.

Names (p. 21): most Berbers follow the Muslim pattern with Berber isms; traditional men are 'name ag name', women go by one name or a Tamazight laqab. Lists of men's and women's isms are on p. 21.

neighbours.name: The Netherworld
neighbours.summary:
The invisible shadow world under ours, its mirror: mountains are pits, ravines are cliffs and rivers run across the sky. Black sheep eat coal and black goats give black milk. When it is night above it is day below, for Tafuyt retreats there, and a moonless sky means Ayyur is visiting his mother. It holds the dead, hideous giants such as the teryelen ogresses, and dwarfs who swarm like their ant kin.

Pagans say people were born there, climbed out by a hole and go back at death, not quite cut off. Tombs, wells, caves and iron gates built by jnun join the two worlds, and snakes carry messages, so one treats them with respect lest they speak ill of one to one's ancestors.
neighbours.secrets: It is part of the Faerie Realm, and parts of it lie in Faerie regiones, which are easier to visit.

neighbours.name: The Masmuda
neighbours.summary: Berber confederation about Fes and Rabat, the western Atlas and Sijilmasa. Ibn Tumart was one, and they dominate the Almohad hierarchy.

neighbours.name: The Sanhaja
neighbours.summary: Berber confederation in two parts: the east on the Tademait and Ahaggar, and the west in Mauritania, from the Anti-Atlas down to the edge of the torrid zone. The Almoravids, Zirids and Hammadids grew from them. Allies of the Fatimids of old, and rivals of the Zenata.

neighbours.name: The Zenata
neighbours.summary: Berber confederation through the Tell and northern Numidia, once allied to the Caliphate of Cordoba, and rivals of the Sanhaja.

neighbours.name: The Marinids
neighbours.summary: The Ayt Mrin (Arabic Banu Marin), a Zenata dynasty at war with the Almohads from the start. In 1217 they won a decisive victory in the Rif, though it cost them their leader Abd al-Haqq. His son holds Er-Rif and looks to spread further, and Almohad counterattacks have failed.

neighbours.name: The Banu Zayan
neighbours.summary: The Abd al-Wadids, a Zenata tribe gathering power in Tlemcen.

neighbours.name: The Hafsids
neighbours.summary: A Masmuda dynasty whose governors hold Ifriqiyeh for the Almohads. If history holds, the governor of Tunisia seizes the city in 1228 and takes the title of emir (p. 134).

neighbours.name: The Barghwata
neighbours.summary: A Masmuda subtribe.

neighbours.name: The Ghomara
neighbours.summary: A Masmuda subtribe.

neighbours.name: The Doukkala
neighbours.summary: A Masmuda subtribe.

neighbours.name: The Hintata
neighbours.summary: A Masmuda subtribe.

neighbours.name: The Kutama
neighbours.summary: An eastern Sanhaja tribe (also Kutuma), the Fatimids' first allies.

neighbours.name: The Gazzula
neighbours.summary: Western Sanhaja of the Anti-Atlas.

neighbours.name: The Lamta
neighbours.summary: Western Sanhaja of the Anti-Atlas.

neighbours.name: The Massufa
neighbours.summary: Western Sanhaja south of the Anti-Atlas.

neighbours.name: The Lamtuna
neighbours.summary: Western Sanhaja south of the Anti-Atlas, whose chief raised the Almoravids.

neighbours.name: The Banu Warith
neighbours.summary: Western Sanhaja south of the Anti-Atlas.

neighbours.name: The Gudala
neighbours.summary: The southernmost Sanhaja, on the edge of the torrid zone.

neighbours.name: The Banu Hilal
neighbours.summary: Bedouin clans (Bani Hilal, 'children of the crescent moon'), grown in Egypt from other nomads and peasants fleeing debt into an anarchic quarter-million with 50,000 young warriors. Caliph al-Mustansir, advised to spend them on the rebel Zirids, offered them governorships, and in 1051 they moved west, some staying in Cyrenaica. Wanting grazing and not towns, leaderless and untaxable, they destroyed the town life of the interior at a stroke. The steppe and Atlas plateaus went from Tamazight farming to Arabic herding and Sunni Islam, and the north became a patchwork of Berber lords and Arab clan chiefs.

neighbours.name: The Maqil
neighbours.summary: Yemeni allies of the Banu Hilal, whose chief subtribe, the Banu Hassan, names the Hassaniya Arabic. They settled in the far west beyond the High Atlas; some stayed in Ifriqiyeh with their sahirs, now advisers to the Banu Hilal.

neighbours.name: The Banu Sulaym
neighbours.summary: Nomads from Nejd and Hejaz who followed the Banu Hilal west. The Banu Hebib settled in Cyrenaica; the 'Awf, Debbab and Zegb in Tripolitania and the Libyan Desert's fringes, where a century of feuding left the Debbab on top.

neighbours.name: The Maghrebi Arabs
neighbours.summary:
The most numerous people of the north. The first Arabs, Umayyads of the eighth century, built cities and made a town-dwelling upper class over rural Berbers on the coast; the Banu Hilal came in the eleventh, and the Almoravids put Berbers on top. Almost all are Muslim, and the further west and the poorer or more nomadic, the stricter, Marrakesh excepted. They make the five duties public: the profession of faith, prayer five times a day towards Mecca, above all Friday noon, alms, which none here think the poor don't deserve, the Ramadan fast, which spares children, the old, the pregnant, the ill and travellers, and pilgrimage. Pork, alcohol and garlic are shunned, some more strictly than others. A returning Hajj or Hajja may wear a green head covering; three pilgrimages to Kairouan count as one to Mecca for the poor.

Baraka here is fortune, set before birth and not earned: the fortunate are skilful, lucky and happy, and it rubs off on those near them. Thankful for it, many turn devout. Saints' fortune stays in their relics and in the tomb, also called a murabit, which each family visits yearly or expects spirits or faeries to torment it. Outsiders and strict Muslims fear these intercessors are demons.

Shame is public knowledge of a wrong, not the wrong: a sin with no witness brings none. So a Muslim here seeks to wipe out a bad name before his family repudiates him, and his neighbours accept this; the Hajj is the finest way. Speech is formal even among friends, using sidi or lella as courtesy, though in the street anybody may be jostled. One never asks outright, since refusal costs both sides face, and that covers questions; a reasonable request must be met. One says 'if God wills' of the future, and never boasts of coming luck, which invites the evil eye.

The educated and wealthy must command others and do no labour: not to employ people fails the community. Men wear loose trousers, a hooded robe and a head covering that shows origin, with slippers and a jacket; women cover body, arms and hair with a pinned cloth and scarf, and Berber women are brighter and bolder. Wealth shows in colour, embroidery and jewels, and pilgrims all wear plain white.

Life is lived in company to keep up one's network: washing, cooking and every task done with others, gifts unopened before the giver, and circumcisions, weddings and funerals held at home. Magi who shut themselves away must be holy, shameful or mad, and to live apart from family and unmarried seems tragic. Lunch is the big meal, of spiced shared dishes, dates, flatbread with aniseed and couscous, eaten with the right hand. In the Tell the fashion is for carousing on the diwan in bright robes and perfumed beards, with wine, date wine and slave-songstresses open to negotiation, which holy men dislike. Men meet at the Roman-style baths, and sport outside the walls: archery, fencing, racing, javelins, polo and a mallet game, hunting and falconry, the falconer cutting the prey's throat so that the law allows it to be eaten.

Public life is men's. High-born women are unreachable to unrelated men, so female agents hear what men cannot at the baths and on rooftops, and may pass as boys. A married woman travels more easily. A man may have four wives if he treats them equally; kings ignore the rule, concubines do not count, and some nobles marry and divorce by the minute, which most scholars condemn. Arab tales are full of jealous wives.

details.rules:
Reputations: a negative local Reputation is removed by building a rival one until it equals the first, then spending experience against the first (ArM5 p. 167). The Haj, as a series of scenes, erodes bad Reputations and gives Haji +1; shorter pilgrimages give less, which is what 'three pilgrimages equal one' means. For its religious side use The Church pp. 15-19. Shame removal is social, not supernatural.

The Gift breeds distrust, so magi easily gain shameful Reputations. Speaking of coming good fortune gives +3 to Hex rolls by those who envy the speaker. Fortune is no Virtue, and Hermetic magic cannot detect it; player characters who are wealthy, lucky or skilled have it. Maintaining the network is pushing up bond scores under the agency rules of Houses of Hermes: Societates pp. 140-144. A woman passing as a boy may take Dark Secret, or nothing if the troupe wants no stories from it.

Local saints may be of any Realm: a fortunate but unholy 'saint' is a Magic spirit of place or a faerie. Observing a sect's rites or the tomb's aura may show which, though Infernal murabits mask themselves. Murabitin rules are in ch. 4.

Muslim names (p. 20) join an ism, nasab (ibn, bint; Berber ag), kunya (abu, umm), laqab and nisba: Saladin's breaks down there. Lists of isms, laqabs and nisbas are on pp. 20-21.

neighbours.name: The Dhimmis
neighbours.summary:
Christians and Jews, suffered if they do their duties and provoke nobody, and treated worse the further west one goes. They pay a yearly tax, and may not hold office or army rank, preach, touch Muslim women, bear arms, plot, testify against Muslims, wear religious signs, pray or toll loudly or hold lavish funerals, build or repair places of worship unpermitted, eat pork or drink in public, hide any badge they must wear, ride horse or camel, or resent contempt. Jews fare particularly badly: the golden age of the last century is over here, with exceptions in some cities.

Christians work chiefly as guards and merchants. Lords hire younger sons of European houses, free of local obligations, cut off from home and bound by favour and sometimes conversion or concubinage; the ban on arms is waived for them. Merchants keep enclaves in coastal cities, may not trade through the Straits, and sell much to Sicily. Barred from much else, Christians take the jobs Jews take in Europe: moneylending, with the same contempt, and smuggling drink, mostly date wine, since every Christian knows someone who knows the priest's vintner.

details.rules: The Dhimmi Minor General Flaw reflects this; those not resident may use Outsider instead.

neighbours.name: The Tuareg
neighbours.summary:
Nomads who share the Berbers' origin and know the Great Desert better than anyone, centred on the Ahaggar and Air massifs (their Atakor and Ayar). Arabs say the name means 'abandoned by god' (one Targui); they call themselves Kel Tagelmoust, People of the Veil, or Kel Tamahak, and all speak Tamahak. An Arab proverb counts them with the scorpion as the desert's only enemies.

To them the word for 'he is free' also means 'he pillages'. A ghefara, or paid pardon, protects a merchant only as far as that band's land. Only camels, clothing, slaves and weapons have real worth; men show rank by layers of exotic cloth, however hot. They live on sheep's and camels' milk with foraged roots, and nobles demand mouna, or tribute, from any they think inferior, which is everyone not a noble Targui.

The drum group or tewsit gathers at the amghar's ettebel; tribes (tawsheten) form a Kel under an amenoukal, respected as judge and safely ignored. Raiding bands of one or two dozen ride camels with lance and takouba, some with a settut in disguise, and the best leaders vanish through hidden regiones. Women and children are left unharmed and provisioned; slaves and goods go.

The imajeghen (one amajegh) are nobles who lead raids. Below them the imghad (one amghid) fight and herd, and whole tribes such as the Kel Ulli, 'the goat people', are of this class. The ineslemen, descended from marabouts, mediate feuds. The eklan, black-skinned serfs like the Haratan of the north, farm the nobles' plots, and the true slaves are the abid. The inenden are pariah wandering craftsmen, thought to be of Jewish origin, with a magic of their own.

Women go unveiled, speak their minds, may hold chief places in counsel, and pass noble rank through the mother, for 'the stomach holds the child'. A wife may have male friends visit while her husband raids, though seldom more. They are tall, elegant, finely braceleted, carelessly dressed and better schooled, handing on Tifinagh, written in any direction, and singing to the anzad and tende.

Men take the tagelmoust (Arabic litham, also tamelghoust), an indigo veil of Sudanese cloth, at eighteen from an ineslemen, and by twenty-five never remove it, even to eat. Its hue marks kin, its folds rank, and small shifts mood; Arabs say it hides their ugliness. Those who have made the hajj alone go without. Indigo, known to the Romans as indicum, must come from far beyond the desert. Their dress, cross-marked gazelle shields and long swords lead some Arab writers to call them Nasara al-Sahra, Nazarenes of the Desert. Few men are lettered. In the eleventh century one inenden joined House Ex Miscellanea, his line later lost in a small Muslim lineage of House Verditius, and one Suleimani sahir claims part-Tuareg blood.

details.rules:
Rank: amajegh as Knight or Emir with a hunting and travel focus, bound by a code like Dutybound; amghar as Landed Noble or Muslim Muqta'; amenoukal as Great Noble (Lords of Men p. 31), the Kel Ahaggar's equal to a duke. Common noble traits: Fury, Obsession (appearance), Overconfident, Oversensitive, Piercing Gaze, Proud, Self-Confident, Social Handicap, Strong-Willed, Wrathful. Ineslemen is a Minor Social Status Virtue (p. 34) with free Noncombatant, and inenden have Outcast. Ineslemen lack Dream Interpretation and Create Vis, may take Purity, Adjuration or Wonders, and may hide other Realms behind false baraka.

The veil (p. 31) carries a hedge enchantment: ReAu 25, Duration Sun, 2 uses a day, against sandstorms, and once a day a Ward against Spirits of the Desert, Penetration 5 to 20 by rank. Wearers take Vow (constantly wear litham veil); hajis exchange it for Pious, and magicians who drop the veil for Judged Unfairly. It gives at least 2 Warping Points a year: from the eighth year Short Attention Span or Poor Concentration (Realms of Power: Magic p. 50), Warping 3 at forty and 5 at fifty, faster in strong auras. Warping 2 Short Attention Span or Poor Concentration; 3 Disfigured (deep indigo skin); 5 a Minor Supernatural Virtue (Desert Regio Network, Dowsing (water), Lesser Immunity: Thirst, Second Sight or Wilderness Sense); 6 Wanderlust; 7 Magical Air; 8 Blatant Magical Air. Most blame settut curses and buy stronger veils and amulets, which worsens it. Male asseher, imhergi, ineslemen and ineden avoid these effects but Warp faster.

Tuareg magic is mostly women's; settuten are rarer here than among other Berbers. See ch. 4.

neighbours.secrets: Elder men, driven apart by Warping, wander into the deep desert, where some bargain with the Hunger for release and become Spirit Votaries with Servant of the Desert, or Dessicated Men, undead Magic Humans with Might.

neighbours.name: The Banu Khalida
neighbours.summary:
The people of the Twelve Cities, on twelve oases in the far south of Mauritania, deeper into the torrid zone than anyone, with gold beyond counting, well-watered fields and mild air in the midst of the blast. These are the sinister Moors of the Song of Roland. They claim Khalid ibn Yazid, adopted son of the Kahina, an Arab who gave up Islam to live, feigned paganism, delivered his foster brothers to the invaders, and came back a Muslim leading Berbers into Iberia. His sons fled Roncevaux alive, held land as viceroys in al-Andalus and survived among the taifa princes by keeping them at odds. The Almoravids ended that game, and the whole people went back to the bled es-Siba, 'the land of dissidence', beyond their reach.

The ruling Hassane descend from Khalid. The clerical Zawiya serve and pay them; the Znaga labour, including mraguen fishermen, mallemin smiths and igawen poets, pay tribute and bear no arms. These three are the bidan, 'white', of mostly Zenata stock in the lower two. Below are the Haratan, freed slaves who fill the army and offices, and the 'Abid, slaves: every bidan household has one at least, and rich Hassane hundreds. Colour is no sure sign: recognised children of slaves are ebony-skinned bidan, and northern captives are pale slaves.

Their tongue, once a secret Punic of the taifa days, now mixed with Arabic and Tamazight, is written in a Phoenician variant; the Zawiya and many Hassane also learn Arabic, and Znaga traders some Tamazight. Their piety is private, their mosques plain, their practice nearest Khariji to the scholar's eye. Their emirs fight not for land or wealth but to spend their champions abroad on trade roads and nomads.
neighbours.secrets:
They worship the Unholy Trinity. The Zawiya and most Hassane know these are demons and believe, after five centuries, that they hold the upper hand; the Znaga and slaves mostly do not know. The upper ranks are goetic sorcerers, usually by pact, as the Gift is no commoner than in Europe. Hassane Summon and Ablate for life, healing and strength, so a duel goes to the greater demon. Zawiya Command demons to build roads and houses, and Bind Aerial Powers into stone pylons that cool the cities and bring rain. Almost yearly a demon breaks loose. Hell lets them be: with no Divine faith to reach, every one of them can fall, and the emirs play the Three against each other.

Characters: Hassane, Knight or Emir, or Landed Noble or Muqta', the great ones Diabolist Mythic Companions; Zawiya, Priest or 'Alim with Commanding and Binding; Znaga, any Free status; Haratan, the Freed Slave Flaw (p. 37) with Warrior or Educated; 'Abid, the 'Abid Flaw. See Realms of Power: The Infernal ch. 11 and Realms of Power: The Divine pp. 114-115. Names: Abisme, Alphaien, Burdel, Canabeus, Chernubles, Corsablix, Esperveres, Eudropin, Faldrun, Gemalfin, Guarlan, Jouna, Malduit, Marcule, Priamon, Timozel.

neighbours.name: The Unholy Trinity
neighbours.summary: The three gods Europeans think Muslims worship, Mahound, Termagant and Apollyon, a mistake born partly of early meetings with the Banu Khalida.
neighbours.secrets:
Demons of the Order of False Gods (Realms of Power: The Infernal p. 37) who sow hate between Christian and Muslim anywhere from Africa to the Middle East, in whatever form suits the listener, high in Hell and able to feign patience.

Mahound: a parody of a prophet in green silk and gold, leering, with immense ears. It seeks apostasy, sends missionaries north and watches visitors to the Cities.

Termagant: a wrinkled hag with bulging eyes, spitting venom and clawing at eyes with jagged nails. It wants blood, drives the Hassane to pointless violence, teaches contempt for slaves and seeks more of them.

Apollyon: a hunchbacked, ugly blond parody of Apollo in a dripping, acid, oversized gold cloak, whose lyre jangles the senses to stillness. It is greed: it brings gold, always stolen from elsewhere, to lure merchants and sends them home corrupted.

neighbours.name: The Twelve Cities
neighbours.summary:
Twelve oasis cities in a stony desert, a day apart on paved roads, each of sun-baked red clay about a central plaza, with millet, dates and forage in the fields. Each has three to six extended families each of Hassane and Zawiya, a dozen of Znaga, five hundred Haratan, a quarter to a half of them soldiers, and maybe two thousand 'Abid. One Hassane family dominates, and its head is the city's absolute emir.

The cities are named for the twelve peers of King Marsile.
neighbours.secrets: A council of twelve emirs and the senior Zawiyas balance the Three. The demon-bound pylons keep the climate.

neighbours.name: The Kahina's Legacy
neighbours.summary: Relics of the Kahina's war, her sword, veil or jewels, may lie in the Atlas caves, hidden from the conquerors. A magus who shows them and claims her descent would meet less opposition and might unite the quarrelsome tribes. Might her secrets open older magic?

neighbours.name: Muting the Muezzin
neighbours.summary: A town's call to prayer is eroding the covenant's Magic aura. An item that keeps the song inside the oasis would be a large enchantment, to be hidden inside the Divine aura. If the Divine retreats, what comes in its place? Perhaps something Infernal.

neighbours.name: Seizing the Sahir's Bounty
neighbours.summary: St. Francis sent friars to this coast in 1219, and in the first weeks of 1220 the caliph beheaded most of them on the word of his vizier. Princess Sancha of Alenquer rewards the return of their remains and suggests a great reward for proof of ibn Jam'i's death.

neighbours.name: Hunting the Hunted
neighbours.summary: Magi hunt a renegade to his stronghold in the Maghreb and find it a fine site, but the local tribes, genius loci and jinn all had bargains or grudges with him, and now take the magi for his heirs.

neighbours.name: Waging War
neighbours.summary: The covenant's work threatens to make an Order of Atlas against the Order of Hermes. Trianoma envoys urge it to stop, Hoplites work indirectly against its resources, House Flambeau is split over a second front to the Reconquista, Castra Solis may help or hinder, and native sorcerers gather for a clash that will reshape the Maghreb.

neighbours.name: Lost Sodales
neighbours.summary: The magi are sent to find what happened to an earlier covenant, funded by senior covenants for an important task. Tuareg, fouled water from Wind spirits, a pack of bouda within, or Infernal seduction? Survivors may be deep in the desert or on the streets of Marrakesh, and the trail runs from Rabat to Taghaza to Bilma to the ruins of Cyrene.

neighbours.name: The Lonely Lighthouse
neighbours.summary: An elder Verditius, a Hermetic Architect, keeps his sanctum in the lighthouse of half-buried Leptis Magna. The characters' seniors bought his work with five years of theirs, clearing sand and repairing his grounds under a list of tasks and rules. How do the neighbours take them, and what enemies did the old man make?

neighbours.name: Mysterious Sources
neighbours.summary: Magi of a Mystery Cult such as the Neo-Mercurians or Mithraists are chartered to find its relics and lost shrines in the Roman ruins, and must thrive to rise. A rival cult such as the Disciples of the Worm sets up nearby to plunder them.

neighbours.name: Seekers of Lost Magics
neighbours.summary: Seekers come to unbury Carthage's magic for House Bonisagus, and may also find Garamantian remains or Berber traditions, the settuten's among them, fit for Hermetic Theory.

neighbours.name: The Golden Idol of Gurzil
neighbours.summary: Khalid ibn Yazid stole the Kahina's idol before her last battle, and his descendants had to leave it in al-Andalus. A disreputable merchant sells its whereabouts to the characters and to a faction of the Banu Khalida. If they win the race, the Almohads may suffer.

neighbours.name: The Chameleon
neighbours.summary: A lady whose husband visits prostitutes offers a jewel for a dead chameleon, whose bones in his food will, by Tunisian folk magic, turn his desire home. It is nearly invisible and its bite is venomous. What might that venom do besides?

neighbours.name: The Christians of the Desert
neighbours.summary: Characters hear of the Nasara al-Sahra and seek them as Prester John's people. The Tuareg will rob and beat them unless paid in camels, slaves or clothing. Will they be stranded in the sand?

neighbours.name: The Deep Tuareg
neighbours.summary: Elder Tuareg, cast out by Warping, go deep into the desert and bargain with the Hunger to be free of it.

neighbours.name: Indigo Dye
neighbours.summary: Indigo is a treasure in the desert, and magi can make its colour easily: they may meddle in the dye trade from as far as Europe, or bring cloth to win Tuareg allies.

neighbours.name: A Lost Treasure Returns
neighbours.summary: A possession the characters lost years ago turns up with a local notable, honestly bought. The chain of trades leads to the Twelve Cities, where it was stolen by demonic wealth-summoning.

neighbours.name: Slave Revolt
neighbours.summary: An Ibadi imam from the north has been quietly teaching Islam to the 'Abid of several cities. An escaped slave asks the characters to free his kinsman.

neighbours.name: Invasion
neighbours.summary: Three emirs, urged on by Termagant, plan war on the Almohads and send sorcery-enhanced spies north to find weaknesses or make them.

neighbours.name: The Fourth Estate
neighbours.summary: The emir of Malprimis serves a fourth False God, Baal-Peor, Lord of Filth (Realms of Power: The Infernal pp. 50-51). The Three, through Zawiya go-betweens, steer outsiders into exposing him.

neighbours.name: Twice-Won Gold
neighbours.summary: To keep Hassane busy, Khalida sell gold to foreign merchants with Haratan guards under one scion, then send another as 'bandits' to win it back. Characters in the caravan may ruin the game.

neighbours.name: The Maghreb
neighbours.summary:
North Africa lies in four bands, each with its own way of travelling. Along the shore ships are quickest: the Atlantic cities of Mauritania to the west, old Cyrenaica on the Mediterranean to the east. The great cities stand in the fertile Tell, the country of carts. South of it the High Plateau climbs to the Atlas, the country of horses, and beyond lies the Great Desert and its camels.

The sea is the swiftest and the safest road, so much so that many Christian ports are nearer by ship than other African cities are by land. Open piracy is rare, since the rulers of the southern Iberian shore keep a strong fleet to protect the sea lanes; what piracy there is hides behind merchant houses and marginal men.

Punic colonies came first, on rocky headlands above deep harbours; Rome broke Carthage in three wars and took them over, settling its veterans along the coast. Vandals, Belisarius and the Arabs followed, and ruins now lie from Sala Colonia on the Atlantic to Cyrenaica. Two Roman roads begin at Tangier: the Northern Road runs by the mountains to Carthage and along the shore to Alexandria, with branches to every villa and fort; the Western Road runs south past Ad Mercuri and the ruins of Augustus Zilil, then forks for Rabat and for Walili. Looters want dressed stone, not roads, so the roads survive.

The Tarikh Ifriqiyya wal-Maghrib of Ibrahim ar-Raqiq, an 11th century Zirid courtier, is the respected history, kept in private libraries of merchants and nobles here and in al-Andalus: in Arabic, a summa on Area Lore: Maghreb (Level 4, Quality 10) with a tractatus on Area Lore: Great Desert (Quality 10). It reports the Fatimid caliph Isma'il al-Mansur's visit to the jedars of Jabal Lakhdar, and gives the true places of the thirteen great Berber tombs in the hills south of Tahert, though its interpreter's reading of their inscriptions is wrong (p. 42).
neighbours.secrets: A large pack of bouda has come up from the south to strip the ruins (p. 42).

neighbours.name: Mauretania Tingitana
neighbours.summary: The old Roman province of the far west. Many of its sites still have people in them, as Ceuta (the Roman military town of Septa) and Mlila on the coast, where the old buildings have mostly gone into new walls. Tangier and Walili are the largest survivors.

neighbours.name: Lixus
neighbours.summary: A Punic and Roman ruin, abandoned, its stone only partly robbed by the locals over the centuries and so still substantial.

neighbours.name: Iulia Valentia Banasa
neighbours.summary: An abandoned Roman town, partly scavenged, its ruins still substantial.

neighbours.name: Ceuta
neighbours.summary: A coastal city, once the Roman military town of Septa, its old stone recycled into later building.

neighbours.name: Mlila
neighbours.summary: A coastal city still lived in, on a Punic and Roman site.

neighbours.name: Mauretania Caesariensis
neighbours.summary: The temperate hills and valleys later called the Tell, thick with Roman colonies: some eighteen follow the two forks of the Northern Road. Sharshal, Saldae, Tlemcen, Algiers, Djemila and Tifesh are among them.

neighbours.name: Numidia
neighbours.summary:
The most thickly colonised land of the Phoenicians and Romans, mostly seized after Carthage fell and the rest annexed when its Berber client king died and civil war broke out. It covers the eastern Tell and Tunisia: Carthage, Constantine, Soussa, Bouna, Tbessa and the ruins of Lambaesis and Tamagudi.

The Middle West, the most thickly peopled land in Africa after Egypt, with a Mediterranean coast sheltered by the Atlas, which is not one range but several: the Tell Atlas by the sea, and the Anti-Atlas, High Atlas and Saharan Atlas to the south, with crops and pasture between.

neighbours.name: The Western Coast
neighbours.summary: A temperate Atlantic shore of fertile plains and hills, dotted with cities from Anfa and Asfi to the twins Rabat and Sale, now and then scoured by biting sand-laden winds from the dunes to the east.

neighbours.name: Anfa
neighbours.summary:
A walled city with a deep harbour, set in green farmland under the tall minaret of its great mosque. A Carthaginian colony and then a Roman town, it is mostly Berber. From the seventh century to 1068 it refused the Caliphate as the Kingdom of Anfa, until the Almoravids besieged it and took it.

Through all that time it has sheltered pirates who raid the Straits and the Mediterranean, yet it is a true port too, selling Saharan goods, grain and cloth to Seville, Genoa and other European cities. Foreigners find it cosmopolitan and tolerant, if not warm: some call it the secret door into the Maghreb, and the merchants who use it guard the secret.

neighbours.name: Asfi
neighbours.summary:
An old Punic colony famed for fine pottery and rich fishing, and a trusted partner of Marrakesh. Its deep harbour is busy with trawlers and with merchantmen bringing Iberian luxuries and taking away exotic goods from beyond the Great Desert. The Sufi Abu Mohammed Salih keeps his ribat here.

The town takes its name, it says, from early 11th century sailors of al-Andalus who strayed onto the Hesperides and took souvenirs; the islanders blindfolded them and set them adrift on a storm, cursed never to sail again from their next port. When they learned at Asfi how far they were from home, one cried out his regret, 'Wa asafi'. Al-Idrisi repeats the tale. Descendants of those sailors still own the relics and their accounts of the voyage, priceless to anyone seeking the way there.

neighbours.name: Island of Mogador
neighbours.summary: An uninhabited island, shunned for tales of a bloodthirsty monster. The Periplus of Hanno names it as the home of a sea snail whose crushed shell gives the rare dye of the purple stripe on senators' togas. Harvesters cross from Essaouira, and guard the foul-smelling secret of the dye.

levels.name: The Villa of the Dye
levels.enter: Through the ruined cellar door of the crumbling villa.
levels.notes: The villa as it stood at the height of the Empire, peopled by descendants of the craftsmen and overseers who made the dye for the Emperor. The book gives the regio no aura of its own; the 4 is the island's.

neighbours.secrets: A ruined cellar door in an overgrown Roman villa is the way into the regio.

neighbours.name: Essaouira
neighbours.summary: A town across the bay from Mogador, home of the people who harvest the island's shells and keep the secret of the dye.

neighbours.name: Rabat
neighbours.summary:
The town on the south side of the mouth of the Bou Regreg, grown from the Almohads' fortress of Rabatu l-Fath, the Stronghold of Victory, their staging point for Iberia. Caliph al-Mansur made it his capital in 1190, finished its great walls and built widely until his death in 1199. His heir al-Nasir turned to the Reconquista and died in 1213, and the absent caliph Yusuf al-Mustansir leaves the region to a bureaucrat whose eyes are on Sale.

The Kasbah, an enormous palace-fortress with its own mosque at the river mouth, has held only squatters since 1199, and no aura remains in that mosque.

neighbours.name: The Hassan Tower
neighbours.summary: Al-Mansur's unfinished mosque at Rabat, meant to be the world's largest and to hold 20,000. Work stopped at his death. The tower stands 50 paces high, with ramps inside wide enough for a rider, among a forest of 200 columns under a cedar roof, and the locals pray here all the same.

neighbours.name: Chellah
neighbours.summary: A walled royal necropolis near Rabat, made by al-Mansur from an abandoned Phoenician town that had become the Roman Sala Colonia. Few people live near, and its walls keep out the sound of prayer. Rome sent its searchers for the Hesperides out from here.
neighbours.secrets: Little Divine aura troubles the place. Those who speak Aramaic may talk to Punic ghosts as if they had Dead Language: Punic at their score less 3 (below zero, not at all). Defixiones may lie in the abandoned Roman quarter.

neighbours.name: Sale
neighbours.summary: Rabat's partner on the northern shore, walled and grown up over the last century with Rabat's rise. Rowboats ply the river at all hours, and a canal lets some boats sail straight into the Beb Mrisa souk. The region's administrator works from here.

neighbours.name: Pithecousa, the Island of Monkeys
neighbours.summary: A legendary land of monkeys off the African coast, not to be confused with Ischia near Naples. Some place it among the Balearics or beside Gibraltar, some through the Pillars in the Atlantic, some in the Nile Delta. All of them may be right. The way is through unexpected patches of fog at sea.

levels.name: The Island
levels.see: A cone of an island in the fog, its slopes lush.
levels.enter: Land on the beaches once the island is seen; EF 15.
levels.notes:
One steep mountain, five rivers cut deep ravines from plentiful rain, thick forest of strange flowers and fruit, bright birds, huge insects, lizards, frogs and fish. Hoofed and clawed beasts other than monkeys are tiny: goats, lions the size of house cats, elephants no bigger than pigs. None threatens the monkeys. There are no snakes, the monkeys' old enemies, hunted out long ago; any brought here meet fear and violence.

Court lies in a bowl of date palms round a rock throne. Lost or stolen goods tend to end up in the tribute pile before it.

neighbours.secrets:
It lies in a regio with several entrances, all at sea in fog. Seeing through the boundary takes Ease Factor 15 (ArM5 p. 189); at certain times of year particular headings lead straight through without any special ability.

The first enchantment, Penetration 0, turns every human and any other creature affected by Corpus who does not resist into a mundane monkey suited to its nature: warriors hamadryades, the clever callithrices, the agile cercopitheci. Intelligence, Virtues, Flaws and Abilities remain; clothes and gear do not change. A monkey character can talk with monkeys, and understand but not speak human tongues, so a magus casts only with quiet words (ArM5 p. 83). It lasts while on the island and causes Warping as a powerful mystical effect, and Flaws so gained are simian. Dispelling it is as a level 55 enchantment (about MuCo base 10, +1 Touch, +4 Until, +4 Boundary); a Bjornaer's Heartbeast Ability also ends it.

The second, Penetration 50, keeps out anything in human shape: one it overcomes cannot leave the beach landward or affect anything beyond it, and is driven to the nearest beach if it takes human shape inland, even partly once the shape is recognisable. It is as a level 85 enchantment (about ReCo base 15, +1 Touch, +4 Until, +4 Boundary, +25 for Penetration). Magi who want to explore must probably suppress their Magic Resistance and accept the change. Both effects come from the island, by no known magic; the guidelines are only for investigating and dispelling them.

neighbours.name: The Court of the King of Monkeys
neighbours.summary:
Monkey society parodies the human kind. Noble sphinxes rule peasant satyri, upheld by a warrior caste of hamadryades; callithrices play clerks and scholars, and cercopitheci are specialists, entertainers and criminals. Most have Cunning and not Intelligence, so it is all pantomime: the scribe's marks mean nothing, the smith makes nothing.

Visitors meet curiosity, except at the new moon, when the monkeys sink into gloom. They may also be set on by angry hamadryades, swept into a cercopithecus revel on fermented fruit, or tried by a court of sphinxes. All come in the end before the King, who has the satyrus's lack of tail, the sphinx's markings, the hamadryas's mane, the callithrix's beard and the cercopithecus's size.

At each half moon he takes tribute of fruit, shells and bright stones. At each equinox tribute joins the Ceremony of the King's Urination: before the full court he passes water seven times, and all watch closely. It may be a kind of divination.
neighbours.secrets: The King and his counsellors, drawn from all five kinds and more exotic ones, are Magic Animals. He and many of them have true Intelligence. He may have higher Might and further powers, as his storyguide chooses; the book prints no block for him.

neighbours.name: The Rif
neighbours.summary:
The one great exception to the bands of the Maghreb: a triangular spike of mountains rising to meet Europe at the strait of Gibraltar. The Marinids, a Berber tribe opposed to the Almohads of Marrakesh, hold it, raid Almohad lands from it, and make trade with Spain and rule of it harder.

Almohad loyalists paint the Marinids as barbarians, which may be unfair.

The mountains between the Middle Atlas and the Straits of Gibraltar, held by the Marinids.
neighbours.secrets:
The troupe chooses what the Marinids are: a rampaging horde like the Mongols, or, as in history, future conquerors of the western Maghreb who spare Fez and bring a new age of art and learning.

Their weakness: the dynasty holds together only while it raids and grows. When plunder or conquest stops, each warlord looks to swallow his cousins and their followers. Stalling their advance forces a civil war that leaves them united but far smaller (p. 49).

neighbours.name: Tangier
neighbours.summary:
A modest port under the Phoenicians and Romans, grown under the Caliphate into a rough, busy crossroads of Iberia, Europe, the Mediterranean and the desert caravans, with a navy of sixty ships. It sells wool, hides, fruit, honey and wax. St. Francis has called it a city of madness and illusions.

Its name is that of Tinjis, goddess or giantess, who married Heracles on his way to his labours and bore the first king, the giant Sophox. His barrow is still pointed out in the city, and many Berber chiefs claim descent from him. Giant Blood and Great Strength do turn up here, in a people who reward victors.

The Periplus of Hanno, in Classic Greek from the lost Punic, is a very rare book kept in private collections here and in Alexandria, Rome and Constantinople: a tractatus on Area Lore: Beyond the Pillars of Heracles (Quality 6) and one on Magic Lore (Quality 6). It follows Hanno's sixty ships out past the Pillars, west for 35 days and then south, into thirst, heat, great hairy men and fire running into the sea (p. 44).

neighbours.name: Tumulus of Antaeus
neighbours.summary:
South of Tangier, before the mountains, the lonely grave of Antaeus, titan or giant, rises five paces inside a ring of 175 lesser menhirs. He was once king here, and many local kings have claimed his blood. The Roman Quintus Sertorius is said to have dug it open and found huge bones, made offerings, sealed it again and paid for epics in its honour. Juba II, the learned client-king, traced his line to Heracles and Tinjis, Antaeus's consort. If the legends hold, Antaeus was the child of a Magical creature and a Faerie.

Lucan's Pharsalia, Book IV (Latin) tells of Heracles's victory through a Libyan's words to the Roman Curio: tractatus on Area Lore: Maghreb (Quality 6) and on Magic Lore (Quality 6), hard to find, in heirloom collections in Italy, Iberia and Constantinople (p. 50).

His descendants may have the Virtue Antaeus' Bloodline, Major or Minor (p. 50, Of Kings and Giants).

neighbours.name: Cave of Heracles
neighbours.summary: South of Tangier, the cave where the hero slept on his way to the Eleventh Labour, to kill the dragon and take the Apples of the Hesperides.

neighbours.name: Walili
neighbours.summary: Once Volubilis, a provincial capital amid fertile plains, and the capital claimed by the Berber king Juba II, where Latin lived on until the Caliphate came in 790. The best Roman stonework of the region survives here. When the aqueduct failed the people moved to a wadi nearby and the old city became their cemetery. Mosaics and statues stand yet, with the decumanus maximus, basilica, forum and Caracalla's arch.

neighbours.name: Ab Muammad Abd al-Wahid bin Yusef
neighbours.summary: Governor of Sijilmassa. He still accepts the Caliph's suzerainty, in an increasingly nominal way. No governor wants to be first to break away while the Almohads might have one good battle left, nor to spend his best men saving them. Whoever lets someone else exhaust himself destroying them may be free, or rule Marrakesh.

neighbours.name: Yusef ibn Ali
neighbours.summary: Governor of Tinmal. He still accepts the Caliph's suzerainty, in an increasingly nominal way. No governor wants to be first to break away while the Almohads might have one good battle left, nor to spend his best men saving them. Whoever lets someone else exhaust himself destroying them may be free, or rule Marrakesh.

neighbours.name: Abdul-Wahid
neighbours.summary: Viceroy of Ifriqiya. He still accepts the Caliph's suzerainty, in an increasingly nominal way. No governor wants to be first to break away while the Almohads might have one good battle left, nor to spend his best men saving them. Whoever lets someone else exhaust himself destroying them may be free, or rule Marrakesh.

neighbours.name: Abu Zayd bin Yujjan
neighbours.summary: Governor of Tlemcen, which rules Tahert. He still accepts the Caliph's suzerainty, in an increasingly nominal way. No governor wants to be first to break away while the Almohads might have one good battle left, nor to spend his best men saving them. Whoever lets someone else exhaust himself destroying them may be free, or rule Marrakesh.

neighbours.name: Abu Zakariya
neighbours.summary: Governor of Fez. He still accepts the Caliph's suzerainty, in an increasingly nominal way. No governor wants to be first to break away while the Almohads might have one good battle left, nor to spend his best men saving them. Whoever lets someone else exhaust himself destroying them may be free, or rule Marrakesh.

neighbours.name: The Tell
neighbours.summary:
The fertile strip of the north, called Massyli, Carthage, Africa, Ifriqiya, Tunis and now Tunisia as its lords changed, reaching from the far west to Tripoli. Here are grand Marrakesh, busy Fes, Tunis on the site of Carthage, holy Kairouan and lively Tripoli. Pirates work the coast from Mahdia, Sfax and the empty wharves of Girba.

Wheeled carts go by land here behind horses, donkeys, oxen or camels; donkeys and horses are quicker than oxen but haul less. In mountain and desert wheels are worse than useless.

The high plateau south of the Tell Atlas.

neighbours.name: Marrakesh
neighbours.summary:
The Red City, named for its ochre earth and pink stone, the largest in the region and capital of the Almohads, founded at the foot of the Atlas by the sultan Abu Bakr in 1062. Its heart is the great souk of the Djemaa El Fna: desert baubles, Christian and southern slaves, gold, salt, and a few faeries among the sellers, players and street urchins. The Kasbah overlooks it, ringed by a hospice, mosques, the palace, parade grounds and a garden. Nineteen gates admit the caravans.

Sufis shelter in the hillside caves and come in on Fridays for prayer. Since the 1180s, when al-Mansur began the Koutoubia Mosque and renewed the Kasbah, they have been welcome, and booksellers crowd round the mosque.

It is the richest city of the Maghreb, all gardens, running water and shade, and the one with the deepest shadows. The empire is crumbling; some settle scores, some enjoy what is left. Thieves here are skilled by birth, assassins by training. Its name, from 'to cross over' or 'to hide', honours a watchful fortress say the scholars, and say the locals, the horse thieves who raided the old camp.

The ruler is a boy of seventeen who cannot lead his nobles; his close kin rule what he still truly holds and feud without end, and distant governors own him less each year. The empire has been failing since Las Navas de Tolosa (Al-Uqab) in 1212, which cost over 100,000 men, mostly African loyalists, and the revenue of most of Iberia. Worse came nearer home, latest in 1217 outside Fes, where only ignorance of siege work kept the Marinids from the second city. The governors of al-Andalus and Majorca may have designs on the title of Caliph, and might carry power across the Strait.
neighbours.secrets: Thieves of Marrakesh take Virtues that suit them only if they use those Abilities often (pp. 52-53): Affinity, Cautious with or Puissant in Athletics, Awareness, Legerdemain or Stealth, Intuition, Keen Vision, Light Touch, Perfect Balance, Premonitions, Ways of the Town, and the catalog's All According to Plan, Falls Like a Cat, Indescribable Face, Just an Instant, Finding Hidden Loot, Rat Up a Drainpipe, Schooled in Crime, See in Darkness (the book's Sees in the Dark) and Skilled Smuggler. Childhoods raised by thieves (p. 53, each with Native Language 5): burglar, Awareness, Bargain, Stealth 2; grifter, Charm, Guile, Legerdemain 2; lookout, Awareness, Legerdemain, Stealth 2; runner, Area Lore, Athletics, Legerdemain 2.

neighbours.name: The Sons of Sasan
neighbours.summary:
The Banu Sasan of Arabic folklore: a hidden tribe of bandits, thieves, murderers and prostitutes, sprung from the evil retinue of a Persian prince who lost his kingdom. Each city is said to have a Beggar King, and they are said to share tainted blood, school one another's children and keep unhallowed places for dark rites.

Most criminals claim to belong. All in the Maghreb know the argot, the monogat Bani Sasan: Arabic full of Persian and Kurdish loans, which marks a speaker's class and carries basic private meanings, and which outsiders know at once for something odd.

details.rules: A character with a criminal background and Arabic 3 or more speaks the argot (p. 53). How close the family truly is varies by saga.

neighbours.name: Fes
neighbours.summary:
The empire's second city, for centuries its imperial capital, revived by refugees from Iberia. Even its labourers quote the Prophet to one another. Green is everywhere, with deep blue tiles set in geometry that shines as the sun crosses them.

For all its age it is fragile: nomads nearly took it three years ago, and the last nomads to raid North Africa pulled down every city and aqueduct. Its faith keeps it from the sordid fatalism of other towns. The Almohads have settled many Christians and some Jews here, and the new quarter of strange music, ideas and food is what the city's rich do instead of bars and brothels.

Outside the city a fig tree fruits out of season, some figs white, some black. The black raise tender horns on the eater's brow (Monstrous Appearance), which hurt terribly if struck; the white remove them. A leper is said to have won a Sultan of Fes's daughter so, tricking the ruler into the black figs and curing him in a foreign magician's dress. Hermetic listeners may wonder if he was a magus, and where he lies. The figs hold Muto vis (p. 54).

neighbours.name: Al-Kairouine Madrasa
neighbours.summary:
In the eighth century one of two heiress sisters from Kairouan built a mosque in Fes, and fellow emigrants endowed it so well that a school opened. It now draws students from the Arabic world and the small communities of the Christian Mediterranean. Theology and Islamic law are the core, with the Artes Liberales and practical subjects for many. The master sits in a chair and students gather round. Some say a few teachers are astrologers, or magical.

Subsidies have paid for students in good times; now they need work. All are literate and at home in mundane society, many have useful Area Lores, and some have a Realm Lore, usually Divine. Hermetic covenants could use them. Art and Academe's university hooks suit this place.

neighbours.name: Tunis
neighbours.summary:
The Maghreb's largest port, a centre of trade and naval power for the Almohads, whose fleet has weakened with the loss of al-Andalus. It stands strikingly white under the sun, its doors ultramarine, facing a lake and living by the sea. Round the central mosque lie the markets of perfume to the north, cloth to the west, wool to the south, and dried fruit and books to the east. Others ring outward, fouler with each circle.

Sailors, the navy and the water colour everything here. Nearly 100,000 people live in it, and merchants from across the Mediterranean come for the desert's gold and slaves. It needs wheat from Sicily and sells desert goods to Italy.
neighbours.ruler: The Hafsid family, for the Almohads

neighbours.name: Tripoli
neighbours.summary:
The gateway to the Great Desert, chief port of the gold and slave trade in the eastern Maghreb: Carthaginian Oea, which took in two neighbours and with them the name of three cities. It depends on dhimmi trade even for its bread, and is the friendliest port to dhimmis. Its navy is weak and its farmland poor.

It is laid out as a Roman would know it, two great roads crossing to make four quarters, with a mosque and fortress at the centre. Most of it is yellow sandstone, some pink, the fortress red.

Phoenicians, Greeks, Egyptians, Romans, Arabs, Normans and Berbers have each left a layer, and most western schools of magic had time to plant colonies, perhaps even druids and Odinites. Seekers find the remains of each mystical occupation, and people here have links to the ruins and relics of earlier rulers.

neighbours.name: Mahdia
neighbours.summary: A harbour of the Tell coast from which pirates operate.

neighbours.name: Sfax
neighbours.summary: A harbour of the Tell coast from which pirates operate.

neighbours.name: Sharshal
neighbours.summary: Roman Caesarea, a busy port joined to the old Northern Road by a branch, most of its Roman stone reused.

neighbours.name: En Nassria
neighbours.summary: Roman Saldae, a busy port joined to the Northern Road by a branch, most of its Roman stone reused.

neighbours.name: Algiers
neighbours.summary: Icosium, founded it is said by twenty companions of Heracles, Phoenician, then Roman, now the seat of a kasbah. White buildings run down to the shore behind a high wall built largely of old Imperial stone when the Arabs renewed the site in 942. Roman cemeteries lie in the sea-cliffs to the west.

neighbours.name: Qusantina
neighbours.summary: Constantine, which held off the Visigoths but fell to the Arabs in the seventh century: the City of Bridges, on a high plateau within the cave-riddled gorge of the Rhumel, crossed by several bridges and a treacherous natural arch. Its prosperous market deals with Pisa, Genoa and Venice.

neighbours.name: Soussa
neighbours.summary: Hadrumetum, founded by the Phoenicians in 1100 BC, an ally of Rome in the Third Punic War and one of its chief towns in Africa, until Oqba Ibn Nafi's army razed it. The rebuilt town hides the old one: mosaics of Virgil, strange beasts and Hellenistic gods survive, and Roman and Christian catacombs run beneath the streets.

neighbours.name: Bouna
neighbours.summary: Bouna Al Haditha, the new town the Arabs built a league north of old Hippo Regius in the ninth century.

neighbours.name: Tbessa
neighbours.summary: Roman Theveste, within a Byzantine wall of thirteen square towers, with an amphitheatre, a nearly whole Temple of Minerva and the remains of the basilica of St. Crispinus, with its chapels, baptism urns, catacombs and gardens.

neighbours.name: Tlemcen
neighbours.summary: Once the fort of Pomeria, now a rich end of the desert caravan routes, run by families such as the al Makkari. Nearly all its Roman stone has gone into its buildings and protective wall.

neighbours.name: Tahert
neighbours.summary: A thinly peopled end of the slave trade in a high central pass, better known for the ruined stone tombs called jedars to the south. Few remain of its Jewish community, and it never recovered from the Fatimid conquest of 933.

neighbours.name: Kairouan
neighbours.summary:
The fourth holy city of Islam, large parts of it closed to non-Muslims on pain of death. Its mosque, among the oldest and the largest in North Africa, is thought the model for all those of the region and draws pilgrims and students. No city of the Maghreb has a higher Dominion aura.

The sack of 1057 ended its fame for learning and as a court of the Jewish exilarchs; the Jews have mostly gone to Egypt and the scholars to Tunis, and rebuilding is unfinished. Libraries lost in the flight may lie in the ruins.
neighbours.secrets: The book gives no figure for its Divine aura (p. 56).

neighbours.name: Djemila
neighbours.summary: Spectacular ruins where two rivers meet: arches, half-standing basilicas, two fora, houses, temples and a fine amphitheatre. It could house a covenant.

neighbours.name: Tifesh
neighbours.summary: A forgotten mountain fortress with outer walls 3 paces thick and three crumbling basilicas. It could house a covenant.

neighbours.name: Tiddis
neighbours.summary: Hilltop ruins near Qusantina: an entry arch, paved streets, cisterns, a small forum and a Mithraeum with a Magic aura of 3. An excellent site for a starting covenant.

neighbours.name: Hippo Regius
neighbours.summary: A Phoenician colony of the 12th century BC near the mouth of the Ubus, called 'of the King' for the Numidian pyramid tombs there, and St. Augustine's bishopric in his later years.
