Synods here helped settle the books of the New Testament. Arabs took it in 698 and left it in the ninth century; Africa's largest theatre remains.

neighbours.name: Lambaesis
neighbours.summary: An empty legionary town on the military road south, with triumphal arches, undisturbed graves, dry aqueducts and the bones of temples to Aesculapius, Minerva, Jupiter and Juno, where the aura centres. No Christian inscription exists here. A column bears the whole of Hadrian's address to the Legio III Augusta.

neighbours.name: Tamagudi
neighbours.summary: Seven leagues west of Lambaesis, the best preserved ruins in Numidia, similar in kind. Hermetic wizards might make it habitable with some effort.

neighbours.name: Basilica of St. Augustine
neighbours.summary: The mostly destroyed church in the ruins of Hippo. Under the rubble of the altar lies a saint's relic of 3 Faith Points.

neighbours.name: The Catacombs of Soussa
neighbours.summary: Some reaches of the Roman and Christian catacombs under Soussa strangely keep a Magic aura of 4.
neighbours.secrets: A Virgilian cabal left texts and works here when the Arabs came, and never returned.

neighbours.name: Mouth of the Bagradas
neighbours.summary: A river mouth just over twenty miles north of Tunis, where a Roman general of the First Punic War fought a serpent for hours with all his men and engines. Its skin, sent to Rome, measured 120 feet.
neighbours.secrets: Magical creatures rest in auras larger than themselves, so a site of aura 3 or more, big enough for laboratories, must lie here (p. 55).

neighbours.name: Wadi of the Molting Beetles
neighbours.summary: A hidden canyon a day east of Marrakesh, where scarab beetles of Virtue gather to shed their skins in the sun. The sparkling indigo husks dye the brightest Tuareg veils, and the nomads who gather them prize them.
neighbours.secrets: Gathered in late summer after the sirocco, the husks give four pawns of Muto and Imaginem vis (p. 54). Taking the vis ruins them for dye, so a magus must come to terms with the tribe, which guides southbound caravans and keeps grudges for generations.

neighbours.name: Djerba
neighbours.summary:
A low, temperate island, one of the few off this coast, lived on since the Phoenicians, who called it Meninx, and briefly taken by Roger of Sicily in the early 12th century. Here lived the lotus-eaters of Odysseus's tale. Villages cover it, joined by good Roman roads; people weave, farm, press olives and make ceramics. Thorny lotus shrubs grow everywhere, with sweet berries eaten fresh or dried or made into liquor.

An enclave of Ibadi Muslims in Ajim, like those of Ghardaia, shun outsiders and pray in underground mosques.

South of Girba, in one of the villages, the mosque empties by dusk for fear of the capricious jinn who come at evening with their lovely wives.
neighbours.secrets:
The Lotophagi withdrew long ago into isolated regiones marked by clusters of lotus shrubs, avoid the islanders, and come out rarely to gather Lotus Fruit of Virtue on the Summer Solstice.

In a secluded gully on a nearly inaccessible shore grows an untended copse of Lotus of Virtue, the narcotic fruit that held Odysseus's crew. Berries picked on the morning of the summer solstice give three pawns of Herbam and three of Mentem vis. Three seeds exposed only to full moonlight for a year and then sealed in an amulet give the wearer Clear Thinker (p. 57).

neighbours.name: Girba
neighbours.summary: A ghost town on the north shore, its walls in good repair, visited only by pirates and pedlars who trade with Midoun's people.

neighbours.name: Midoun
neighbours.summary: A large village of Djerba that trades at empty Girba.

neighbours.name: El Kantara
neighbours.summary: Ancient Meninx Proper, at a southern corner of Djerba, with a Roman bridge to the mainland. A very few craftsmen here know the secret of the purple murex dye, found only here and on Mogador.

neighbours.name: Ajim
neighbours.summary: The Roman town of Tipasa, at Djerba's other southern corner.

neighbours.name: Hara Seghira
neighbours.summary: A village a league south of Girba where a large Jewish community has lived since before the fall of the Second Temple.

neighbours.name: The Ghriba Synagogue
neighbours.summary: The centre of Hara Seghira, built with stones from Temple Mount, and a pilgrimage for Kabbalists and those keeping Lag BaOmer.

neighbours.name: Malta
neighbours.summary:
Three islands now held by the Hohenstaufen of the Holy Roman Empire: largely a fortified garrison, given over to its own defence after being emptied and resettled by Arabs and joined to Sicily. Phoenicians, Romans, Vandals, Arabs and Normans have all held it. Dolmens and deep cart ruts in the stone recall the one-eyed, tusked cyclopskin giants, whose bones sometimes appear after a flood or earthquake.

Paul of Tarsus was wrecked here in 59 AD and in three months healed the sick and founded the Christian community.

neighbours.name: Mdina
neighbours.summary: The capital of Malta.

neighbours.name: Ir-Rabat
neighbours.summary: A village beside Mdina.

neighbours.name: Cathedral of Mdina
neighbours.summary: Dedicated to St. Paul, and much repaired after neglect under Muslim rule.

neighbours.name: Catacombs of Ir-Rabat
neighbours.summary: Where the early Christians held their secret Mass.

neighbours.name: Ghar Dalam
neighbours.summary: A cave of Malta running deep into the rock.

levels.name: Subterranean Vaults of the Cyclopskin
levels.enter: When the night of the winter solstice falls on a new moon, go deep without any light.

neighbours.secrets: The cyclopskin retreated to regiones here, and may be at war beneath the island.

neighbours.name: Caves of Comino
neighbours.summary: The smallest island, with a few farmers and shepherds, its sheer limestone cliffs riddled with caves where pirates sometimes hide before an ambush, until the sorcerer Kerrew routs them.

neighbours.name: Gozo
neighbours.summary: The second island, said to be the home of the nymph Calypso, daughter of Atlas, who kept Odysseus seven years and bore him Nausinous, Nausithous and a daughter. His blood still shows in Blessing of Venus or Great Presence among its women, and at least one magus from here claimed descent and could call up Aura of Rightful Authority.

neighbours.name: Ggantija
neighbours.summary: A huge clover-shaped stone complex within a boundary wall, with a stone circle nearby, built by a giantess of Calypso's titan kin. She has not been seen in living memory; some say she sleeps in a cave near by, waiting for her lover.

neighbours.name: Cyrenaica
neighbours.summary:
The eastern coast, settled by Greek refugees from Thera on the plains below the Jebel Akhdar: the Pentapolis, small city-states led at first by Cyrene. It borders the Libyan deserts and has few cities, but many forts and nearly 2000 fortified farms of the Legio III Augusta. The Limes Tripolitana lasted in some form until the Banu Hilal overran it in the 11th century, and within decades the sand had most of it.

After the Arabs came in 643 it became al-Maghrib al Adna, the Nearest West, and it is now a backwater. Though Muslim, its people keep the Greek settlers' stories, and its supernatural fauna and flora are nearer to Greece's than the Arabic or Berber desert's, so magi from Europe find it oddly familiar.

Outside every Tribunal and far from any great Islamic town, the hills would suit a Spring covenant of Theban magi, though the Children of Olympos (The Sundered Eagle pp. 125-127) lately tried and failed in mysterious circumstances.

Silphium, the herb of Cyrene's coins, was the region's fortune and is thought extinct since Nero ate the last stalk. Lesser asafoetida (tyib, devil's dung) stands in for it in the kitchen, and some magi think silphium merely its Virtuous form. A bag of the resin at the neck is a Traditional Ward for some lesser Faerie jinn; it can replace myrrh, with Shape and Material bonus: protect against evil spirits +3 (p. 62).

The Nearest West: Cyrenaica next to Egypt, and Tripolitania round the Gulf of Sidra north of the Libyan Desert. Few live here, mostly the nomad Banu Sulaym.
neighbours.secrets: Silphium of Virtue survives only in a few lost Magic regiones in the coastal mountains. Enriched by cutting the stem and sealing the faintly scented resin in a jar of pine nuts for a season, then eating one nut a day, it wards against poison as Greater Immunity for a year, with infertility as Lesser Malediction for as long. Unenriched, its heart-shaped seeds hold 2 pawns of extraordinary Corpus vis, or serve as a finite-use Lesser Enchantment, Silphium Seeds of Corpus Vis (PeCo 15; R: Touch, D: Mom, T: Unborn Child; Base 5, +1 Touch, +1 Part), which ends a pregnancy, with a Stamina stress roll against 6 after the first month or a Medium Wound. It derives from Black Anne's Kiss (Ancient Magic pp. 54-56), and study may give Insight into that magic (pp. 62-63).

neighbours.name: Barce
neighbours.summary: A small inland town, first capital of Barqah under the Fatimids, now ruled by the distant Ayyubid sultans of Egypt.

neighbours.name: Sidi Rafaa
neighbours.summary: A village port on the site of Greek Balagrae, named for the Prophet's Companion Ruwaifi bin Thabit al-Ansari, entombed here.

neighbours.name: Apollonia
neighbours.summary: Cyrene's port, 8 miles to the north and some 20 miles from Sidi Rafaa on the old coast road: renamed Sozusa for Apollon Soter, nominally Christian by the fifth century, with abandoned churches inside crumbling walls. The land has sunk and much is under water. Only a small village marks the stop on the road from Alexandria to Leptis Magna, but the Genoese have lately set up a small outpost and are building up trade. Of three islets, the largest held the Theran shipyards and the smallest ended the western mole.

neighbours.name: The Pharos of Apollonia
neighbours.summary: The ruin of an ancient lighthouse on the third islet just outside the harbour.
neighbours.secrets: Inside are a makeshift Hermetic laboratory, a shattered oversized glass lens, a freshly slain man and signs of a fight with a great sea creature.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Cyrene
neighbours.summary: Rome's metropolis and regional capital until Diocletian favoured Ptolemais late in the third century. People and governor moved to the coast, a garrison lingered in the forum-fort, and no civilians have been recorded here since the Arabs passed in the seventh century. A temple of the Faerie god Zeus lies by the ruined circus, and there are shrines of Demeter and Dionysos within the walls. The Olympian temples hold Faerie auras of 4.

neighbours.name: Sacred Spring of Kura
neighbours.summary: The spring near the Temple of Apollon, sacred to the water nymph Kura, once worshipped by Cyrene's citizens. Its rivulet joins the river that runs through the necropolis to the sea.

levels.name: Kura's Regio
levels.enter: Follow the rivulet from the sacred spring upstream from where it joins the river.
levels.notes: The book gives the regio no aura of its own; the 5 is the spring's grounds, which lead to it.

neighbours.secrets: Kura is an unfettered Magic spirit, a nereid and genius loci who remembers true silphium and the groves above the city. She cannot leave her precinct. Sacrifice or a restored shrine will win her help, and she may use Zeynab as intermediary through a Spiritual Pact, taking her as Spirit Votary (Realms of Power: Magic pp. 88-89). She might be patron of a Theban-style covenant (The Sundered Eagle pp. 30-31) but mistrusts Hermetics after hostile Berber and Arab wizards; her price includes veneration, perhaps a magus's Spiritual Pact and a promise to restore her public worship, which risks the Code.

neighbours.name: Myrtoessa, the Hill of Myrtles
neighbours.summary: The hill over Cyrene where Apollon seduced Kura. A grove of Myrtles of Virtue grows on its northern slopes.

neighbours.name: Leptis Magna
neighbours.summary: The finest ruins in Africa, raised by its son the Emperor Septimius Severus: nearly perfect arches, a largely whole basilica, a broad theatre and forum, a harbour guarded by a Byzantine wall and a lighthouse still looking out to sea. Many buildings lie half under the preserving sand, which ate the farmland, so only caravans camp here now.

neighbours.name: Temple of Serapis
neighbours.summary: A seaside temple in the ruins of Leptis Magna.

neighbours.name: The Jebel Akhdar
neighbours.summary: The Green Mountain, a forested coastal plateau riddled with wadis, rivers and springs, among the wettest lands of North Africa. Muslim villages lie scattered through it, but its groves hold nymphs and fauns more than the ghul and jnun of Libya's deserts. Myrtle and herbs abound, and Bees of Virtue, fed in the hills' many Magic auras, make honey of varied magical powers.

neighbours.name: The Altars of the Philaeni
neighbours.summary: Two heaps of broken stone on a hillock above the easternmost point of the Gulf of Syrtis, once the border of Carthage and the Greek colonies and later of the two halves of the Empire. Here two Philaenus brothers, Carthaginian runners accused of cheating in the race that was to fix the border, are said to have offered to be buried alive.

levels.name: The Twin Pillars
levels.enter: A Key to the Mystic Veil set in the northern pile of stone.
levels.notes: Twin pillars with blood-stained altars, turned from a Carthaginian to a Mercurian site after Carthage fell.

neighbours.secrets: The Philaeni are inseparable daimonic Heroes with pooled Magic Might 35, summoned only by a joint theurgic rite of two wizards using Wizard's Communion. Once they gave swiftness to legions on their stretch of road; they can also grant duplication of a recently cast spell, enforce truth, and curse oathbreakers. The contemporary Cult of Mercury (The Mysteries: Revised Edition pp. 114-117) sometimes holds initiations here.

neighbours.name: Siwa
neighbours.summary: A large oasis in a long depression at the north-west edge of the Great Sand Sea, the old border of Libya and Egypt. As Ammonium it held the oracle of Ammon, equated with Zeus and consulted by Hercules, Perseus and Alexander. Tracks run to the coast at Sallum and Matruh, north-east to Cairo, and south-west to the Tuareg outpost of Ghat.

neighbours.name: The Grand Plateau
neighbours.summary: Foothills and highlands along the Atlas, fertile enough in places for large towns, but mostly grazed by nomad flocks. Near as it is to the Tell, its roads are poor outside a few trade routes, and people have given up wheels; they keep clear tracks for riders and herds. This is the country for the sort of tale told of remote rural Europe.

neighbours.name: Sijilmasa
neighbours.summary:
The western gate of the desert trade, the last cosmopolitan stop before the oasis towns, and the home of the world's finest dates. Its stone-faced brick walls and all its grandeur are decaying, like a city that was vastly rich a century ago with nothing spent since. Nomads raid it in hard times, and its rulers plot rebellion in easy ones.

An Almohad army took it last century and a governor holds it, for the empire must have the desert's money, and the people loathe them for it. The Jewish community is gone, fled or killed in a pogrom driven by fanaticism or, more likely, money. Tall wheels lift water from the Ziz for gardens and for the bathhouse of the largest mosque, where Sufis talk philosophy. The Almohads watch for popular Sufis, and founded many madrasas. With its stone mosque, those give the city a Divine aura of 4.
neighbours.ruler: Ab Muammad Abd al-Wahid bin Yusef, governor

neighbours.name: The Atlas Mountains
neighbours.summary: To North Africans what the forest is to Europeans: the blank space where a story can always be found. It lies almost beyond the law, a refuge for exiled princes, resting bandits and heretical sects, with faerie towns, magical caves, ascetics' houses, diabolists' meeting places, wizards' towers and forgotten kings' tombs. It was perhaps the Titans' fortress against the Olympians, and may shelter the last of the coastal peoples who fled Rome, Greece or Arabia. The range seems endless, and past its sudden southern drop lies the Great Desert.

neighbours.name: The Merchant House
neighbours.summary: A merchant house turns to piracy on the side: a hand-picked, silent crew takes a ship now and then, kills or sells the witnesses far away, and sends prize or cargo on through foreign ports. Then a vessel vanishes with an important passenger, a redcap, noble or merchant prince, or with the characters' own supplies, and they are asked to find out what happened (p. 40).

neighbours.name: Robbing the Ifranj
neighbours.summary: Raiders stuff their holds with fighters for few supplies, which far Christian voyages do not allow, yet robbing the Ifranj wins them respect and perhaps formal standing if war comes. The characters may sail as raiders or as pirate hunters (p. 40).

neighbours.name: Making It Personal
neighbours.summary: The last scion of a destroyed noble house flees to sea, or is sold there, and leads pirates against those he blames. He spares pilgrims and has beautiful manners, and leaves the emir of Seville's interests alone, so the costly navy stays home. The characters may ally with him, aid his victims, or act for the true scion, now an apprentice or companion, who wants to know who uses his name (p. 40).

neighbours.name: Mercenary Pirates
neighbours.summary: No Muslim noble hires pirates, officially, but before a local war each side wants the other's trade cut, and servants quietly hire merchants, dhimmis, foreign Christians or magi. Characters offered the work know war is near, and can use the confusion to settle scores and gain resources (pp. 40-41).

neighbours.name: Imperial Legacies
neighbours.summary: Why did the Romans leave so many of these sites so suddenly at the end of the third century, when the Berbers had never driven them out in a thousand years? Roman ghosts might tell of Mercurian wizards who disturbed the Great Hunger; priests' scrolls and fragments of the road magic may lie in hidden refuges (p. 42).
neighbours.secrets: A large pack of bouda is moving in from the south to pick the region clean.

neighbours.name: A Pirate Crown
neighbours.summary: After 150 years the pirates of Anfa still hope to be free of their Almoravid suzerain, and quietly undermine the governor meanwhile. A Tytalus may take up their cause, or a rival may expose it to draw a foe into the open (p. 42).

neighbours.name: Punic Ghosts and Roman Ruins
neighbours.summary: Magi call up the dead at Chellah, where few will question digging, and Roman ghosts might know the way to the Hesperides. Then a curious youth or a grave robber tells the powers in Sale. Can the magi contain it (p. 44)?

neighbours.name: Tabula Non Rasa
neighbours.summary: A copper slate of Punic text turns up, perhaps Hanno's lost tablet from the sack of Carthage, with clues to avoid his hazards and find the Hesperides, the Tin Islands or some other famous place: a resource uncontested, for those who dare the unknown (p. 44).

neighbours.name: The Roads of Rome
neighbours.summary: A Bonisagus seeking the secrets of the Cult of Mercury asks the characters' help to study North Africa's Roman roads, some still whole in empty lands. Digging them up draws noblemen, whom he is quite unable to handle (p. 50).

neighbours.name: The Takers of Taxes
neighbours.summary: Rulers tax merchants at each border, and a greedy collector is a sign of a corrupt lord; decent men taunt, fool and harass such people, and the poor make heroes of those who do. Good for companions and grogs, and a way to meet allies and enemies who remember it when the covenant later seeks hard-to-find goods (p. 50).

neighbours.name: A Claim to the Throne
neighbours.summary: Imghrawn thinks a swath of the Maghreb his birthright and that, like Antaeus, he must raise a temple of his foes' skulls. He starts with a fortified ksour and oasis near the covenant, which supplies its dates and livestock. Rescue the people, or back him and draw the governor's men and tax collectors into a very strange war (p. 50).

neighbours.name: The Pavilion with Three Items
neighbours.summary: A captured thief offers a true tale for his freedom: in Marrakesh, in the garden of three brothers, stands a pavilion their dying father forbade them. It holds a sheepskin rug, a cap and a hashish pipe, all magical (p. 52).
neighbours.secrets:
The sheepskin carries whoever sits on it, and itself, in a blink to any place asked, even unseen or conditional ('wherever the man who stole my trousers has gone').

The cap makes the wearer and what he wears or holds invisible, but not mounts or objects like statues; he can still be heard, or smelled by dogs.

The pipe turns exhaled smoke to small gold ingots, without limit while there is hashish, but the smoker is out of his mind and under the storyguide's control, usually to his humiliation, and often with the other two items. That is why the merchant forbade the pavilion.

neighbours.name: The Monkey's Fist
neighbours.summary: Among treasure the characters find a sphere of golden cord, a 'monkey's fist', with the legend of Pithecousa written on it and a minor Hermetic enchantment. Those who know the Order may think of Verecunda, a Verditius of Favonius (The Sundered Eagle p. 83), expert in knots, whose familiar is a monkey (p. 47).
neighbours.secrets: Verecunda made it for the King of Monkeys in payment for her familiar. A treacherous servant stole it years ago and has become formidable. He needs it to return and challenge the King, and will pose as a helper to get it.

neighbours.name: A Familiar Ape
neighbours.summary: A magus who takes a monkey familiar from the island without the King's leave suffers Supernatural Nuisance as subjects come to fetch it back. If he asks, the King sets a test. Monkey mothers bear twins, love one and carry the hated one on the back, dropping the loved one to climb when chased, and the hated twin is often the Magic Animal. He must catch the mother and take the hated twin with no magic, harming no monkey (p. 47).

neighbours.name: False Embassy
neighbours.summary: The characters arrive for the Ceremony of the King's Urination, ideally with gifts, and meet the Embassy from Furthest Hind, exotic monkeys eager for their friendship (p. 47).
neighbours.secrets: They are shapechanged serpents sent by the King of Punt, the Egyptian name for Soqotra (Rival Magic ch. 5), to kill the King of Monkeys. Punt's mighty serpent king has further plans.

neighbours.name: The Descent of Man
neighbours.summary: The island's change works rather like the heartbeast, and a heartbeast form avoids it, so it may be an Ancestor Site of House Bjornaer (Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults p. 25). The Ritual of Twelve Years at the King's court might yield apprentices with exotic African heartbeasts, but the King will object, and the characters may be sent to win him over or evict him (p. 47).

neighbours.name: A New Ruler
neighbours.summary: A cousin of the ruler, in Marrakesh or a prisoner in Christian lands since Las Navas de Tolosa, asks the characters to clear his way: kill rival claimants unblamed, place their own appointees, and hold the empire together long enough for him to repay them (p. 51).

neighbours.name: Aiding a Governor
neighbours.summary: With no clear successor, magi can serve a governor without open war: spying, sabotage, improving his economy, striking at weak moments, and finish with friends in the new capital of North Africa (p. 51).

neighbours.name: Invited In
neighbours.summary: Desperate for their economy, the Almohads settle Christians and some Jews in Fes and seek treaties with Christian kings. A cousin of the ruler sends a redcap to say dhimmi magi would be welcome in Fes's foreign quarters. Skilled diplomats could win the right to settle elsewhere and money besides, more if they reclaim places like the Rif (pp. 51-52).

neighbours.name: Revenge Against the Order
neighbours.summary: House Flambeau hints it had a hand, perhaps with God's, in Las Navas de Tolosa, where up to 150,000 Muslims fell against some 2,000 Christians, mostly of fighting Orders it finds inconvenient. Whether or not it did, Hermetics in Morocco stand in the lands of men who want revenge; those who claim the Order find allies among the empire's gnawing enemies (p. 52).

neighbours.name: Rebellious Governor
neighbours.summary: If history holds the governor of Tunis rebels most successfully. The Hafsids must keep several things going their way, and magi backing them will be busy (p. 55).

stages.title: The Almohad Navy
stages.clues: Its sailors are also a great force of light infantry.
stages.ignored: No rebellion is possible while its captains stay loyal.
stages.stopped: Captains die or are lured away: ambush on land is easy but suspicious; defeat at sea is harder but easier to hide.

stages.title: Trade with Italy
stages.clues: Desert goods pay for armies; Tunis eats Sicilian wheat.
stages.ignored: A year's disruption ends the attempt: the people starve, riot and follow anyone who can feed them.
stages.stopped: Travel to the sources, clear supply, deal with the Italians; in history their embassies come soon after 1220.

stages.title: Conquer Tripoli
stages.clues: Weak navy, poor hinterland, more reliant on wheat than Tunis.
stages.stopped: A six month blockade may starve out its Almohad governor; holding it needs a trustworthy governor and diplomacy or war with the desert tribes.

neighbours.name: The Serpent of Bagradas River
neighbours.summary: Stories of the great serpent lead magi seeking a covenant site to the river mouth north of Tunis, where they may meet lesser serpents, the ghosts of Roman soldiers, or their reanimated bodies (p. 55).

neighbours.name: Lost Virgilian Magics
neighbours.summary: Notes point to Soussa, whose mosaics and auras hint at an unknown cabal of Virgilian sorcerers of Hadrumetum who hid texts and works in the catacombs from the Arabs. Someone else is searching too: sahirs, infernalists, renegades or the Augustan Brotherhood (p. 56).

neighbours.name: To Claim a Wife
neighbours.summary: Any man who survives a night with the jinn of the mosque south of Girba may take one of their wives. Tasks vary: strength, riddles, finding a misplaced thing, a story they have not heard. Failures serve them seven years. The wives, jinn or human slaves, stay beautiful even after they leave (p. 57).

neighbours.name: Cyclopskin Handiwork
neighbours.summary: Earthquakes shake Malta, and some blame the cyclopskin at war under the ground. Can the giants be convinced to stop before the cities fall (p. 58)?

neighbours.name: The Remains of the Day
neighbours.summary: The pharos of Apollonia holds a wrecked laboratory and a fresh corpse (p. 59).
neighbours.secrets:
The dead man is Diurnum Lumen of Flambeau, left behind from a Jerbiton-led Theban settlement abandoned under ten years ago. He was rebuilding the pharos to recover the Lineage of Abydaros, a lost African mystery cult of Apollo with powers from sunlight.

His killer may be Glaucus, a murderous Makhai (the Theban Muspelli of Rival Magic), who serves the sea Titan Okeanos and his monsters and has moved on. Magi who settle here may rebuild the experiments and invite his return.

neighbours.name: An Acquired Menagerie
neighbours.summary: Norman knights and a powerful Jerbiton magus track Muqadam, meaning to put him in the Tower of London's menagerie, where he would likely die of shame. Do the characters help him quietly and win his respect, or side with the Jerbiton (p. 61)?

neighbours.name: The Rogue Vassal
neighbours.summary: A Lion of Virtue, Syyd, is killing every man he can find at the edge of the Great Desert. Will the magi ask Muqadam to give him up, or find a way to take Syyd's arcane connection from him (p. 61)?
neighbours.secrets: A demon has preyed on Syyd's solitude and led him step by step to feel justified in killing.

neighbours.name: When Shallots Will Simply Not Suffice
neighbours.summary: A Gastronomer, hoping to host the Millenial Feast of 1248, secretly wants true silphium. He may be the head cook of Valnastium, a food-minded magus of Normandy or the hedge magician Gervais d'Avignon; all three may hire rival teams, or the same people (p. 63).

neighbours.name: End of the Line
neighbours.summary: Silphium could shake the feudal order: lords depend on serfs' children, the Church calls contraception sin, and meddling magi could end noble lines, with no sigil to trace. Tremere may act to stop its recovery, hoard it, or bargain with Mercere (p. 63).

neighbours.name: Uninvited Guest
neighbours.summary: A Bear of Virtue, driven out by newly arrived Tuareg, has made a den of a vital cache or vis site. Can the Tuareg or the Bear move? She is about to bear cubs (p. 64).

neighbours.name: Lost Legacy
neighbours.summary: A Bjornaer seeks a beast of Virtue to learn of pre-Hermetic shapeshifters through the shared Vandal past. Gothic lineages and hidden clans may roam the Maghreb, unwittingly awaiting reunion or confrontation with the Bjornaer (p. 64).

neighbours.name: The Great Desert
neighbours.summary:
Europeans imagine an ocean of sand no one can cross. In truth only a fifth to a quarter of it is sand, and those who know it find it hard and unsafe but passable, on horseback if need be. Water is the difficulty, not the going.

Six kinds of country make it up. Erg is the rolling dune sea, almost bare of plants, some 20 percent of the whole. Reg, the stony plains of sand and black, red or white gravel, is some 70 percent. Hamadas are the plateaus and mountains; chott the salt flats left by old or seasonal water. Wadis are deep standing pools fed by rain or springs, and oases the fixed places of food and water where Berbers, Tuareg, jinn and the odd stranger meet to trade and rest. Almost every other water is seasonal, lasting through winter and spring and boiling off by autumn.

It falls into the Fezzan, the Central Great Desert, the Tanezrouft in the west and the Ténéré in the south. Some say the Fezzan and the Ténéré run on into the Nubian Desert; most take that for the raving of men driven mad by jinn.

Myrtle Trees of Virtue grow in some hidden wadis. Sardinians make the liqueur Mirto from the crushed berries, murabitin use them to sharpen their reading of dreams, Jewish scholars hold myrtle the scent and sign of Eden, and some theurgists keep a sprig on the tongue to improve their casting.

Gaetula on the maps, and most of the continent. Westerners think it one sheet of sand, but that is true only of the ergs, or sand seas, which nobody lives in; most of it is the stony reg and the rock plateaus called hamada, with salt flats in the lee of mountains.

At its centre stand the Ahaggar (idurar n Ahaggar), with the eroded 'rock forests' of the Tassili n Ajjer on their north-east and the Adagh and the triangular Air massif to the south. Tuat, south-east of the Tademait, is a string of small oases along a dry wadi, an important road. Tanezrouft, the Land of Thirst, west of the Ahaggar and south of Tuat, has no oasis at all: dark sandstone hills and canyons of 250 to 500 paces between dune fields, the rock scoured into perfect concentric circles and ellipses.
neighbours.secrets:
Sun (BS&S p. 66): the Deprivation check for lack of water comes every 4 hours in the deserts, and exposed skin takes +1 non-combat damage (ArM5 pp. 180-181).

Dry quicksand in the ergs pulls a man under in two rounds, and he then suffocates. In the first round he may make a Strength or Quickness stress roll against Ease Factor 9 to get free; a botch traps his arms next round. After that it is up to his companions, though with free arms he may help in the second round, lowering their further Ease Factors by 3.

Brigands prey on caravans not clearly well guarded, as far as their need drives them. Sandstorms and dust-storms can smother or flay: natural, the work of sorcerers, elemental jinn, or witches in disguise. Jinn and demons send false oases; the victim learns of it when her first long drink turns out to be sand.

Myrtle of Virtue (p. 72): berries fermented in a silver urn underground for a season give a draught of +3 to all recovery rolls for a season. A flowering sprig gives its bearer Clear Thinker if the intended user sleeps with it under the pillow for a season, or by some Jewish traditions if it dries in the Holy of Holies, touched by each day's rising sun for a season. Soaked in seawater for a season in a place sacred to Aphrodite it stays supple and fresh and gives Venus' Blessing.

Why slaves rarely flee (p. 84): all three faiths hold that a runaway is a thief bound for Hell, tempted by evil spirits, though each forbids enslaving its own. Many are freed anyway: a mother of her master's child, warriors after a campaign, domestics by will or charity. A runaway in the Maghreb has nowhere to go where slaves do not already do the work, and some would rather be a trusted ghilman than free and poor. Maghrebi Muslims also take suffering as God's will, which flight cannot change.

Vis: a sprig of myrtle leaves with a flower or berry holds 2 pawns of Mentem. Its enrichment is in the Secrets.

Books: travellers can read up on the routes in Arabic works. Abu Abdullah al-Bakri's Book of Routes and Places (1068, drawn from two centuries of merchants' reports) is a summa on Area Lore: Maghreb, level 3, Quality 10, with a tractatus on Area Lore: Great Desert, Quality 10; it is held in merchants' and nobles' private libraries in the Maghreb and Al-Andalus. Ibn Hawqal's Kitab Surat al-'Ard, Face of the Earth, in the same libraries, is a summa on Area Lore: Maghreb, level 5, Quality 11, with tractatus on Area Lore: Provence, Iberia and Sicily, each Quality 11; its praise of Fraxinet makes some Hermetic scholars suspect he followed Jerbiton. Yusuf al-Warraq's On the Topography of North Africa is a tractatus on Area Lore: Maghreb, Quality 8, and al-Zuhri's Kitab al-Jaghrafiyya, Book of Geography, another, Quality 10.

neighbours.name: The Great Desert Regio Network
neighbours.summary: Many regiones under the deep desert join into one great network, known to Camels of Virtue and to the deep nomads: the Bedouin of the Empty Quarter and the Tuareg, who call it tinariwen, 'the deserts', for its many landscapes. Some mundane Tuareg and the mysterious Blue Men can find their way, which is how nomads strike suddenly and melt into the sands.

levels.name: Tinariwen
levels.see: Desert much like the mundane desert it touches.
levels.enter: Through small, unmarked Magic auras deep in the sands, shown only by a slight change in the great dunes and a shimmer in the air.
levels.notes: The book gives the higher regiones no aura strength. Guardian beasts and other wayfarers may be met; some paths end in dead ends or blank sand where thirst and heat bar going on or going back.

neighbours.secrets: A character with the (Desert) Regio Network Minor Virtue (Realms of Power: Magic p. 45; the catalog's entry is {land} Regio Network) can enter and leave at different mundane places. Some may reach other deserts this way: the Sahara, the Empty Quarter, the Nefud, the Kyzylkum and Karakum, the Taklimakan, and perhaps unknown deserts beyond Mythic Europe.

neighbours.name: The Ibadi of the Desert
neighbours.summary: An unusual Muslim sect, for whom leadership is open to any of the faithful and a bad or heretical leader may rightly be overthrown. Many fled to Wargala from Tahert when the Rustamid Imamate fell early in the 10th century; others live at Ghardaia and on Djerba.

neighbours.name: The Fezzan
neighbours.summary: Mostly sandy erg, with chott and salt hollows where salt-loving plants grow as at Siwa. The Idehan Ubari Erg and the Great Erg wall it from the Central Great Desert to the west, the Libyan Sand Sea from Egypt to the east, and the Al-Hamada al-Hamra, the Red Plateau, from the Mediterranean; in the south the Ahaggar and the Bilma Erg begin the Ténéré. It was the Garamantians' land, and they left only ruins, graves and a road with their name.

neighbours.name: The Haruj
neighbours.summary:
A vast dark field of volcanic cones and basalt in the south of the Fezzan, where several volcanoes sleep with hidden lakes in their calderas. The road from Awdjila to Murzuq skirts it; those forced to stop sometimes find wadis among the black rock.

A plateau of black rock rising from the sand of the Murzuq Desert, crowned with volcanic craters.

neighbours.name: Waw an-Namus
neighbours.summary: One of the Fezzan's sleeping volcanoes, in the south-east, known by the black ash coating its slopes and the land around.

neighbours.name: Al-Hamada al-Hamra
neighbours.summary: The Red Plateau, the buffer between the desert and the Mediterranean in the north.

neighbours.name: The Libyan Sand Sea
neighbours.summary: The Fezzan's eastern edge towards Egypt, crossed by the Garamantian Road from Siwa. The dangerous way to Cairo and Alexandria runs through the sands here.

neighbours.name: Al Kufra
neighbours.summary:
A lonely oasis under the Tibesti to the south-west and the Bilma Erg to the south. Most who reach it go on south-east into the Nubian desert, few south-west to Bilma, and some set out from it for distant Fada. Awdjila is 140 leagues north, Murzuq 180 leagues north-west.

Its Berbers live quietly and like their visitors brief. Three villages share the water: Al Jawf with rich gardens and date palms, the slave plantation of Ez-Zurgh, and Et-Tleilíb, keeping watch on the sands from the south-west corner, nearly four leagues from Al Jawf.

neighbours.name: The Field of Glass
neighbours.summary: East of Al Kufra in the Great Sand Sea, a stretch of desert strewn with green-white natural glass, in a Magic aura of 4.
neighbours.secrets: Vis: the clearest, brightest pieces, bared on windswept dune crests, hold Ignem or Auram vis, the best of them both. Very large pieces hold two or three pawns. Whether the aura outlasts the gathering of all the vis-bearing glass is an open question.

neighbours.name: The Mosque of Atiq
neighbours.summary: One of the oldest mosques in Africa, with odd conical domes, cool and pleasant within. Abdullah ibn Sa'ad ibn Abi as-Sarh, foster brother of the Caliph Uthman and once governor of Egypt, is buried at the oasis. The mosque gives all Awdjila a Divine aura of 4.

neighbours.name: Awdjila
neighbours.summary: A mostly Berber oasis and a crossroads of trails, where they speak Berber at their daily business. Caravans from the south and from Egypt take on dates and water here, and go on to Al Kufra or to Murzuq past the Haruj. Northward, outside some ruins of Cyrene, a village has grown as the Genoese trade more with the caravans. Cairo lies 200 leagues east-north-east and Alexandria about 180 north-east, both across the Sea of Sand.

neighbours.name: The Djofra Oasis
neighbours.summary: Three mostly Berber communities, each with palm groves of sweet dates and some figs and goats. Murzuq is a distant 90 leagues to the south.

neighbours.name: Sokna
neighbours.summary: A walled village of 7 gates and 33 bastions, with a poorly kept fortress, its kasbah, inside. Its houses are of cut stone and unbaked brick.

neighbours.name: Hon
neighbours.summary: A small market town 7 leagues north-east of Sokna.

neighbours.name: Waddan
neighbours.summary: Seven leagues south-east of Sokna, built up out of an old Roman town, with four mithraeums hidden under its streets. It sometimes holds a slave market that jinn attend, its stock brought from the south by caravans bound for Tripoli, Cairo or Murzuq; some rest here on the way to Ghat.

neighbours.name: Murzuq
neighbours.summary: An oasis town on the Garamantian Road and the Bilma Trail, a crossroads for Cyrene, Cairo, Ghat and the south. Ubari is thirty leagues north-west with the ruins of Garama between, and Ghat 75 leagues west.

neighbours.name: Ramlat Dawada
neighbours.summary: A swath of red sands just north of Murzuq with eleven very salty lakes. One teems with reddish prawns the nomads eat.

neighbours.name: The Changing Lake
neighbours.summary: A salt lake near Murzuq whose water turns from red to green to blue and now and then yellow.
neighbours.secrets: Vis: twice a year, as the season and the colour change, red sand blows over the lake, and some floats by the shore reeds as 2 pawns each of Imaginem and Muto vis. Locals sometimes gather it and work it into their pots and bricks.

neighbours.name: Ubari
neighbours.summary: Twenty lakes ringed with date palms and rushes under the dunes of the Ubari Erg, with ruined villages on the shores of several. The lake water is extremely salty but wells give fresh. Tuareg camp here to net small red shrimp, ground to paste and shaped into cakes. Sebha is 28 leagues off.

neighbours.name: Sebha
neighbours.summary: A stop 28 leagues from Ubari.

neighbours.name: The Cemetery of Hatya
neighbours.summary: A Garamantian cemetery rising out of the sands 5 leagues east of Ubari: the Royal Tombs of Ahramat al-Hattia, the royal part of some 100,000 tombs scattered across the old kingdom. Many are enchanted, marking the sorcerer-kings' borders and keeping finely preserved corpses ready to be raised for any emergency.

neighbours.name: The Forest of the Jobar
neighbours.summary: A copse of trees of dark stone shot through with grey crystal, rising from the sands. After terrible sandstorms some fall and split; now and then the erg bares a new one. The Tuareg shun it for fear of the Jobar, a great lizard that creeps through the dunes under cover of storms and takes children. Bones of its kind lie across the desert, and nomads steer by them.
neighbours.secrets:
The book does not say where it lies (p. 68). It prints the second Form as Aurum, read here as Auram.

Vis: split trees give fragments rich in Terram vis; one pawn in five is Herbam or Auram instead, but only in vis found in spring.

neighbours.name: Garama
neighbours.summary: The Garamantian capital, a ring of stunted palms around crumbling mud-brick and cut stone, left when the last sorcerer-king's palace was destroyed and its main foggaras fell in. Five centuries of caravans have stripped the surface; only those who can dig may find what the last Garamantians hid. The ruined Roman temple, set up after Balbus forced the kingdom into clientage, may once have drawn wizards wanting solitude and familiar surroundings in a still pagan land.

neighbours.name: The Garamantians
neighbours.summary:
A kingdom in the heart of the Fezzan from 400 BC to 600 AD, of eight cities, scores of villages and many forts under a line of one hundred kings. They raided south for slaves, drove off Rome until Balbus sacked several towns in 15 BC, and then lived as a nominal client of the Empire. Their sorcerer-kings took the feather as their sign, and their nobles hunted nomads for sport from horse-drawn chariots; the Roman Maternus wrote of going with a slave raid. Slaves guarded the borders, mined gems in the Tibesti, cut the foggaras, farmed barley, figs, grapes and wheat and herded shaggy long-horned oxen, while merchants sold salt, slaves and wheat to Rome. That trade made the first desert caravans.

Slaves served on after death: blackened, tireless corpses that needed no water tilled fields and dug mines until they fell apart. The last king went off in Arab chains in 668. Islam's Divine auras, among the slaves who worshipped, undid the rituals, and battle scattered the corpse-warriors to the wind. The slaves rose under their soldier caste. The surviving lords spitefully ordered their last corpse-miners to collapse the foggaras, and without water the people melted into the nomad tribes or left.

They wrote Punic in the Tifinagh alphabet, later taken up by the Berbers who absorbed their slaves and refugees; a little survives on rocks, ruins and buried urns. Some murabitin and Berber elders can teach the basics, but no one living in Africa has an effective score above 3. Summoned Garamantian ghosts speak the dead tongue, though nobles and merchants likely have some Latin too. They honoured Ammon above all, as Aman, whose temple and oracle stood at Siwah, now little but ruins and a small village.

details.wants: Nothing now: they are gone, though their dead may still work.

neighbours.secrets:
Their magic (pp. 70-71) was non-Hermetic, limited, and erratic near the Divine: preserving, animating, sensing through and commanding corpses, with a small side in sensing water. No text of its secrets left the kingdom, but some may lie in a hidden stronghold.

Their ritual for binding a horde of corpses without an Arcane Connection to each counts in Hermetic research as a Minor Magical Breakthrough. It yields a simple supernatural ritual adding a corpse to a horde bound to an object, often a crown or feathered headdress. Its wearer may use Voice and Group levels of effect for spells on or through the horde, at Arcane Connection distance and past a usual Group's numbers. The ritual has no Penetration, works only on mundane corpses and cannot last in a Divine aura. Recovered bound objects can be researched as a source of Garamantian Lore or Insight (Ancient Magic p. 8).

Hermetic Intellego far outdoes their water-sensing, but relics of it help to understand their methods or to translate Tifinagh.

neighbours.name: Zinchecra
neighbours.summary: Older than Garama, on a small plateau just north of it. Hardly anything remains, and the lake is salt flats now, but the spring still keeps a cut-stone fountain partly full all year.
neighbours.secrets: Buried in an urn in a small cave nearby is the last initiation script for Dowsing (ArM5 p. 64), in Tifinagh Punic. To self-initiate (Target Level 18; The Mysteries: Revised Edition p. 13) one must properly mummify and entomb 10 people in Garamantian tombs (+3), go to the cut-stone pool at the autumn equinox (+3), and bathe there by moonlight while ritually scarred, the equal of the Blatant Gift (+9). If Garamantian Lore + Presence + Initiation Script bonus exceeds 18, one gains Dowsing for drinking water. Finding and reading the script may be a whole story arc.

neighbours.name: Sarir Tibesti
neighbours.summary: Ancient mines along thin veins of tanos, the green-blue gem amazonite, hidden in the Tibesti Mountains on the Ténéré border. Corpse-miners may still be at work in the dark, honeycombing the rock and piling up uncut stones for masters who will never come. Tanos was once cut for signets and seals, and gives a +3 Shape and Material bonus in such devices.

neighbours.name: The Foggaras of the Fezzan
neighbours.summary: Hundreds of leagues of tunnels cut through the rock to draw water, thick around the oases from Ghat to Murzuq to Djofra. Sand fills nearly all of them, and most can be reached only by magical digging. Silent warriors may lie sealed within, waiting for a necromancer strong enough to command them.

neighbours.name: The Forgotten Foggara
neighbours.summary: As the rebellion began, a noble set corpse-miners to dig him a new foggara; slaves killed him before he told anyone. The workers dug a great reservoir under a rocky outcrop until water drowned their cave. The flow keeps a small wadi green. The noble's lost supply cache may be close by.
neighbours.secrets: Vis: after rare storms the overflow leaves 5 pawns of Aquam vis on the wadi's shore, in bone fragments of the lost workers.

neighbours.name: The Central Great Desert
neighbours.summary: Bounded by the Mediterranean and the Ahaggar, by the Ubari Desert to the east and the Grand Western Erg and Tademaït Plateau to the west: erg, rocky hamada and dry valleys, the driest part of the Great Desert, with little plant life even in the wadis.

neighbours.name: The Iter Praeter Caput Saxi
neighbours.summary: The Bab Ras al-Hammada, a thin line of Magic regio running hundreds of miles across the Fezzan, past the old Garamantian lands, to the fabled mountains of Agisymba. Pliny names it as the secret way of the Roman general Valerius Festus in the first century AD.

levels.name: The Road Past the Stone Heads
levels.see: A narrow desert track looping on itself, with a brackish well or waterhole every few miles.
levels.enter: At the northern entrance outside the ruins of Roman Lepcis or the southern one by Agisymba, each in a Magic aura of 2 and marked by an overgrown milestone with faint Mercurian magic. Elsewhere the road is too narrow to find without a Camel of Virtue.
levels.notes: Very secure, but useless as a covenant site.

links.note: Passes by the Central Great Desert

neighbours.name: Agisymba
neighbours.summary: A land far south of high mountains around a vast lake, home to giant beasts like the legendary monoceros and cameleopard, and rich in wild places with undiscovered vis. A small tribe of Plinian troglodytes lives hidden in its caves, remembering old Roman slave raids; they might make useful grogs.

neighbours.name: Djanet
neighbours.summary: A small Tuareg and Berber oasis in a valley on the western side of the Tassili n Ajjer, more a cluster of villages than a town, keeping a large date grove for trade with caravans on the Garamantian and Ghadames Roads. Ghat is about 25 leagues north-east, Ghadames 125 leagues north.

neighbours.name: The Arches of Djanet
neighbours.summary: More than a dozen natural rock arches within 7 leagues of Djanet, one shaped very like an elephant far bigger than any real one. A few rare texts by lost scholars of the Fay call them doors into a regio network; no one who tried has come back to say where they lead.

neighbours.name: Ain al-Faras
neighbours.summary: The oasis at the heart of Ghadames. The city's Divine aura of 3 does not reach many lacunae among its covered lanes.

neighbours.name: Ghadames
neighbours.summary: A stoutly walled city held by seven Berber clans, each with its district and its souk. Covered walkways join most of the buildings in a maze of lanes that shuts out the worst of the heat and hides bandits and cutthroats. The Third Legion garrisoned it for nearly 200 years; its crumbling fort stands on a hill to the south-west.

neighbours.name: The Ghardaia Oasis
neighbours.summary: Five fortified villages, or ksours, built to one plan: houses in rings around a mosque whose minaret is the watchtower, inside a high wall. Grain and weapons are stored in the mosques, but people spend the summer out among the date palms. Their close building around the mosques gives the villages a Divine aura of 3, and Ghardaia's own 4.

neighbours.name: The Mosque of Daïa
neighbours.summary: The mosque of Ghardaia village, holding relics of the female saint Daïa, who lived in a cave (ghar) in the valley.

neighbours.name: Ghardaia
neighbours.summary: Founded by Ibadi Muslims in the 11th century in honour of the saint Daïa.

neighbours.name: Melika
neighbours.summary: One of the five ksours of the Ghardaia Oasis.

neighbours.name: Beni Isguen
neighbours.summary: One of the five ksours of the Ghardaia Oasis.

neighbours.name: Bou Noura
neighbours.summary: One of the five ksours of the Ghardaia Oasis.

neighbours.name: El Atteuf
neighbours.summary: One of the five ksours of the Ghardaia Oasis.

neighbours.name: Ghat
neighbours.summary: 'The Last Oasis' to travellers on the Garamantian Road, on the eastern edge of the Tassili n Ajjer with the Idehan Ubari Erg north and the Bilma Erg south, and no real last, with Djanet 25 leagues away, though it lies off the regular road to Bilma. People stayed for the oasis, not for foggaras. The old town is dried mud-brick with covered walkways against the heat. A small fort on an outcrop to the south-west is the Garamantians' legacy, as is the cemetery of short grave pyramids north of town.

neighbours.name: Wargala
neighbours.summary: An Ibadi stronghold, with a large mosque on the town square and a wall of six gates. Date groves and fruit and vegetable gardens flourish around it and feed its souk, known for its shady arcade and for a busy slave market that the local jinn use.

neighbours.name: The Redoubts of the Tuareg
neighbours.summary:
The Tuareg hold the south-central reaches around the great mountain plateaus, though they turn up anywhere in the sands. In the Tanezrouft and the Ténéré a string of waterless Magic auras almost rings these mountains, leaving only the caravan route into the Haggar massif from the north, so the homelands can hardly be reached without the Great Desert Regio Network.

Painted dogs hunt in packs among the high peaks and raid the nomads' herds.

neighbours.name: The Ahaggar
neighbours.summary:
The Tuareg's spiritual home and refuge, a plateau of hard black rock split into pinnacles and towers, its valleys full of cooled lava, lilac in the setting sun. The central peaks are the Atakor, 'the place of stone'. Raptors nest here but the land only feeds the goats and sheep of the lesser Kel Ulli tribes; the Kel Ahaggar live mostly in the dark canyons around the edge.

The Egyptians believed the destructive force strongest in these mountains (see the Great Hunger), which may only be where a powerful faerie tied to it claimed to come from.
neighbours.secrets:
The remotest heights are pocked with Magic auras. In the sharpest clefts at their feet lie small Infernal auras, home to demons and Infernal jnun of the Aerial Powers and Furies, who send flash floods down the gueltas.

Vis: Tahat, Ilaman, Amjer, Tiouyen and Iherhe are the highest peaks, and the Tuareg say their spirits quarrelled over love. At the foot of Ilaman is the spring that opened when jealous Amjer struck his brother's shoulder; its water is a liquid form of Terram vis.

neighbours.name: Tamanghest
neighbours.summary: A rich oasis of ochre houses in the Ahaggar near the Tassili n Ajjer, with groves of lemons, dates, figs and almonds, millet, wheat and small goat herds. Its herders call themselves guardians of the Tassili's cypresses and have named every tree. It is an open secret among the tribes as a place to trade and rest; few outsiders come without the nomads' blessing.

neighbours.name: Abalessa
neighbours.summary: A haven almost 17 leagues west of Tamanghest, with the sealed tomb of Tin Hinan, said to have healing properties.

neighbours.name: The Tassili n Ajjer
neighbours.summary:
The northern massif, the 'Plateau of Rivers', just north of the Ahaggar: rocky upland cut by deep gorges and hidden gueltas, with hundreds of natural arches, stands of cypress, myrtle and wild olive, and dozens of petroglyphs. The tribes hold it sacred and the Wind Spirits often rest here. The plateau lies under a Magic aura of 2.

The ancient cypresses, tarout to the Tuareg, cluster in the eastern uplands, each over 2000 years old, gnarled, and with its own character. Many hold genius loci spirits protective of the Tuareg.

neighbours.name: Wadi Amazar
neighbours.summary: A stony wadi with the oldest grove, led by Tin-Balalan, 'the one with the pool at its feet'. Each tree is the body of a powerful genius loci, wiser than any man and a Magic guardian of its ground, like the elder trees of the German forests (Guardians of the Forest ch. 4; Realms of Power: Magic p. 106).
neighbours.secrets: Vis: Tuareg hedge magicians must beg a tree's spirit for timber. A fallen limb holds Vim vis, each tree's giving its own power once enriched: Tin-Balalan Puissant Leadership, Tin-Ambarak Puissant Ride, Tin-Gaded Wilderness Sense, Tin-Tamanzazt Lesser Immunity to Thirst. Wandering male inenden know the enrichment and must be bargained with or forced. Ancient cypress wood gives +3 to spirits and +3 to necromancy.

neighbours.name: The Aïr
neighbours.summary: Nine circular volcanic massifs overlooking the Ténéré, long a Tuareg stronghold, with acacia-shaded wadis that fill after the rains of early autumn. Their graven rock art includes a pair of long-necked creatures like Pliny's cameleopardalis. Each site marks a strong Magic aura, at least 4, aligned to Animal or Terram, valued by Tuareg hedge wizards, who oddly do not claim the carvings. The art draws packs of painted dogs, spotted jackal-like beasts that must be driven off before any rite.

neighbours.name: Idoukal-n-Taghès
neighbours.summary: The tallest peak of the Aïr, above the pilgrimage village of Abatol, holding a Magic regio.

levels.name: The Mediterranean garden
levels.see: A Mediterranean climate, with plants and herbs not found in the desert, among them common European Herbs of Virtue.
levels.notes: Herbam-aligned. The book gives no aura strength.

neighbours.name: The Adagh
neighbours.summary: A sandstone massif past the feared Tanezrouft, sometimes called the Adrar Ifoghas after the Kel Ifoghas who claim it. Unlike the other three its auras are mostly Faerie. Its rock art shows nomad life, and shifts from one visit to the next.
neighbours.secrets: The book prints no strength for its auras (p. 74).

neighbours.name: The Kel Asouf
neighbours.summary:
The People of the Empty Spaces, the true Faerie jnun of the desert, like the jinn of the Muslim north but wilder and darker. Some southern Tuareg tribes, the Kel Ifoghas, Iwellemmeden and Kel Geres, have many Faerie-blooded folk among them.

The lost tribes of the night. The northern Berbers think the Tuareg half supernatural for their strange ways, but the Tuareg have their own tales of invisible spirits in the desert's voids and dark. They fear and respect the Kel Asouf, partly for their links to eastern sahirs, and turn to amulets and charms from their tribal settuten. Gifted boys left in the south may be adopted by them.

details.rules: True jinn, which Sihr affects (p. 126); Faerie by p. 123.

neighbours.name: The Tanezrouft
neighbours.summary:
The western Great Desert, from the Atlantic to the Western Erg, the Tademaït and the Ahaggar, and the Bilma Erg; the Chech Erg presses the Atlas in the north. Few but caravans and the hardiest Tuareg come here. The wind sweeps away the tracks of those ahead, and stragglers get lost or fall to hyenas and jackals.

Sijilmasa, founded by Berbers in 757 on the road to Tangier, stands at its northern gate, struggling to live off the caravans of salt, gold and slaves. Old wealth from its great market in the western quarter raised its high ochre walls, stately temples and Sufi madrasas.

neighbours.name: The Mosques of Iwalatan
neighbours.summary: Several mosques that give Iwalatan a Divine aura of 3.

neighbours.name: Iwalatan
neighbours.summary: A wonder of cut stone, the southern end of the Iwalatan Road and the Taghaza Trail. The Massufa keep a few date groves with melons in their shade, and flocks of sheep, and after the long dry road its many wells taste all the sweeter. Timbuktu is 100 leagues east-south-east, and the salt mines of Taghaza 165 leagues north-north-east.
neighbours.secrets: The book disagrees on the road to Taghaza: 165 leagues north-north-east from here (p. 74), 125 leagues south-south-east from there (p. 75).

neighbours.name: Tasarahla
neighbours.summary: No more than a spot in the dunes where water seeps from the ground, marked by a middling stone and a patch of mud, with a few fire rings and low walls to shield tents. New arrivals must often clear the well and wait; the flow is slow but steady. Taghaza is about 53 leagues north, ten days away, and Iwalatan about 75 leagues south-south-west.

neighbours.name: The Salt Pits of Taghaza
neighbours.summary: A rich chott dug into pits, with not a tree in sight and an Infernal aura of 3.

neighbours.name: Taghaza
neighbours.summary:
Hardly an oasis: a barren mining town of the Massufa's all-male slaves, built of salt blocks and roofed with camel hide. Every threshold faces west, since evil jinn are said to be unable to enter from that side. Foreign merchants have a slightly better way-station on the east edge. The only food is camel, or dates and millet off the caravans; when these are late many slaves die. Flies swarm and the water is brackish. Yet the town is awash with gold and exotic goods from the south, traded with salt to northern caravans for slaves and manufactures.

The Chech Erg lies north, and the El Djouf makes the 165 leagues south to Timbuktu a trek for only the most determined caravans. Iwalatan is 125 leagues south-south-east and Sijilmasa some 20 days north.
neighbours.secrets: The book disagrees on the road to Iwalatan: 125 leagues south-south-east from here (p. 75), 165 leagues north-north-east from there (p. 74).

neighbours.name: Tuwat
neighbours.summary: A string of oases some 30 leagues long where the Tanezrouft meets the Central Great Desert, with hundreds of date palms watered by seasonal pools and foggaras down to deep fossil water. Four fortified ksours with thick walls and watchtowers stand here: Buda in the north and Reggane in the south keep the foggaras, and the other two tend the palms. The Tademaït's sandstone walls, up to 500 paces high, ring it south and east, and dunes slump in from the north and west. The sirocco blows hard and sometimes attacks caravans.

neighbours.name: Buda
neighbours.summary: A small ksour in the north of Tuwat whose people maintain the foggaras.

neighbours.name: Reggane
neighbours.summary: A small ksour in the south of Tuwat whose people maintain the foggaras.

neighbours.name: The Ténéré
neighbours.summary: The southern desert under the Aïr, with the Erg of Bilma at its heart and the Tibesti between it and the Libyan Desert. The Ennedi Hamada rises on its southern border, from which some claim to see the Nubian Desert or the haze of the Torrid Zone. Painted dogs try to steal from the nomads' goats and camels.

neighbours.name: Aouderas
neighbours.summary: A small oasis among the massifs of the Aïr, peopled by Tuareg and their slaves, who trade water, shelter and dates for supplies. Most live in a hilltop fortress that guards the well and the harvest from raiders and jinn who prefer blood to trade. Timia is 15 leagues north-east through treacherous canyons, and Bilma 120 leagues east-north-east over the Erg of Bilma.

neighbours.name: Bilma
neighbours.summary: The largest town before Siwa to the north or Nubia to the east, sheltered under the Kaouar Cliffs from the dunes, known for its gardens, salt mines and date groves. Caravans often turn back here for Egypt and Cyrenaica, or press on towards the fabled Sorcerer-King's lands. The oasis fortress of Djaba is 55 leagues north and Fachi due west.

neighbours.name: Fachi
neighbours.summary: A lonely citadel cut from volcanic rock in the Bilma Erg, living like Aouderas by salt, water and dates. A few sweet lakes make traders glad to deal before the 65 leagues east to Bilma or west to Timia. Its unspoiled state and lack of a mosque give it a Magic aura of 4.

neighbours.name: Fada
neighbours.summary: A small, very isolated Tuareg town 200 leagues east-south-east of Bilma, a day north-north-west of the Great Desert's greatest stone pool: a rain-fed wadi at the foot of water-carved cliffs that never dries, ringed with trees, with camels, crocodiles and stranger creatures. Only those bound for the Nubian Desert or across the Torrid Zone come here.

neighbours.name: Takedda
neighbours.summary: The Bilma Trail's last western outpost, a Tuareg oasis with copper mines and date plantations, rumoured to answer to a wizard named Sogolon Conde. West lie the 'Lands of Thirst' and the roads towards the purported Sorcerer-King of Sosso. It is 45 leagues east over the Bilma Erg to the Aïr. Those seeking gold come here, as Bilma has little.
neighbours.ruler: Tuareg, said to owe fealty to the wizard Sogolon Conde

neighbours.name: Timia
neighbours.summary: A valley paradise in Tuareg hands, famed for a huge deep stone well of dark water, a guelta that never empties and supports small orchards. The road from Aouderas to Bilma passes through, with 65 leagues of dunes to the next true rest at Fachi.

neighbours.name: The Erg of Bilma
neighbours.summary: The dune sea at the heart of the Ténéré, swaddling the Aïr. Rock salt is mined here in great quantities.

neighbours.name: The Kaouar
neighbours.summary: Cliffs and oases on the Bilma Trail, sheltering Bilma from the dunes.

neighbours.name: Djaba
neighbours.summary: An oasis fortress 55 leagues north of Bilma.

neighbours.name: The Iwalatan Road
neighbours.summary: The western route, from Marrakesh by way of Sijilmasa, through the pass held by the fortress of Tamdoult, across the Tanezrouft to fading Aoudaghost, then on to Iwalatan. Its caravans mostly bring back gold.

neighbours.name: The Taghaza Trail
neighbours.summary: From Sijilmasa twenty-five days south to Taghaza, ten more to the well at Tasarahla, and fifteen south to Iwalatan, though some bear south-south-east at Tasarahla. Gold and slaves go north, manufactures and salt come back. The great expeditions of thousands of camels leave at the start of the cool season in November, a smaller one in March, and rasher small parties at any time. Northbound caravans disperse from Sijilmasa to Fez, Tahert, Tangier, Tlemcen and Tunis.

neighbours.name: The Ghadames Road
neighbours.summary: Two forks in Ifriqiya, from Tunis and from Tripoli, meet at Wargala and go on to Ghadames, then south-east to Takedda or south-west into the Tanezrouft. Slaves, salt and gold go north, manufactures and slaves south. It keeps west of most of the Ahaggar, long and dangerous.

neighbours.name: The Garamantian Road
neighbours.summary: From Siwa over the Libyan Sand Sea to Zaouila and Ghat, then south to end at Tadekka. Northbound caravans often run on past Siwa to the souks of Cairo and Alexandria. As dangerous as the Ghadames Road, it keeps mostly east of the Ahaggar.

neighbours.name: The Bilma Trail
neighbours.summary: The shortest route, from Cyrene or Cairo through the Great Sand Sea to Murzuq, south between the Ahaggar and the Tibesti to the Kaouar oases and over the dunes to Bilma, where it turns east for Nubia or west for the Western Desert. Slaves, salt and ivory come north for horses, weapons and manufactures. Bilma is about 21 days from Takedda and the same from Murzuq.

neighbours.name: Tamdoult
neighbours.summary: A fortress guarding a pass on the Iwalatan Road.

neighbours.name: Aoudaghost
neighbours.summary: A fading city on the Iwalatan Road.

neighbours.name: Zaouila
neighbours.summary: A stop on the Garamantian Road past the Libyan Sand Sea.

neighbours.name: The Desert Caravans
neighbours.summary:
The crossing goes by stages of about 7 leagues (21 miles) and takes two to three months one way, on the backs of camels and slaves. Gold, slaves and salt go north; slaves, glass and horses go south, among much else. Northbound too are ivory, gum arabic, ostrich feathers, kola nuts, ebony and cloth, cotton cloth, hides, goatskins and leatherwork. Southbound are dates, figs, sugar, cowries, copper, ironwork, paper, books, tools, weapons, cotton, silk, textiles, ceramics and armaments, serving as currency with the nomads. Salt and copper from the desert are bought along the way. Wheeled vehicles cannot cross, since no road stays clear of sand, so bulk trade is rare. Barbary steeds, bred for slavers rounding up people where horses are unknown, cost ten to thirty slaves each.

Thousands of slaves cross each year, half-starved and carrying the goods, many expected to die. Moorish pirates take pagans from Rus, Christians from the Mediterranean and England, and the least scrupulous Muslims from Iberia and the Levant. Those from the south reaching the Maghreb are mostly women, at 3 to 9 Mythic Pounds, though a ruler may buy men for war, as Marrakesh's founder bought 2,000. Islamic law frees a concubine who bears a Muslim's child, and soldiers die or win freedom, so demand and prices stay high.

Berbers and Tuareg bring most of the caravans from the south, with hundreds of camels, into the markets in March and November; Muslim traders go the other way. The Genoese have traded along the coast since the mid-11th century, with enclaves at Safi, Sale, Tangier, Orano, Algiers, Bona, Tunis, Mahadia and Tripoli, chiefly for gold, timber, salt, cheese, wine, oil and grain, and take part in the slave trade too: many of their households keep two or three slaves. Many places forbid keeping Christian slaves, and an owner should free one who converts, which keeps demand from the north up.

Merchants bound for one city gather at its departure city, buy rested camels and choose a guide, on whom everything depends. He sets a day in the cool months, October to March. The merchant stays home, sending a trusted slave or young relative. Up to two thousand camels move as one, a stage a day, by night and morning, by a winding route that ends each day at water, though camels need it only every ten days, for a well may be dry, poisoned, buried, beset by bandits or not where he remembers.

A guide needs Area Lore to follow paths the sandstorms change, languages to deal with the tribes, Leadership to hold his men in trouble, the stars to steer by, and often dealings with creatures of the realms. He is paid in money or shares of cargo. Four days out a pair of runners goes ahead to warn the Sudanese, never one alone, for the demons of the desert play with single runners until they go mad or die of thirst; they earn pounds of gold for a few days' work. At a Maghrebi city everyone must buy, sell and change camels before the caravan leaves, and some cities see one a year or one in ten years, so the pressure is intense and crime by and against merchants pays.

Camels come in two breeds: big, slow pack camels, by far the commoner, and swift saddle camels used as combat mounts, faster than oxen and carrying more than horses. Caravans make 15 to 25 miles a day. The wealthy and pilgrims ride in small canopies, often for two, shielded from sun and sand, with room to talk, play chess or eat.

details.wants: Goods carried across and profit shared out.

neighbours.secrets: The Ride Ability covers camels. Many warriors ride a camel to battle and change to a horse to fight. Camel statistics are in the book's Bestiary Appendix (p. 136).

neighbours.name: The Bilad-es-Sudan
neighbours.summary:
The 'Land of the Blacks' south of the desert, fringed by the fertile Sahel, the 'shore', fed in the west by the Senegal and the Niger, with Sudanese, Berber and Arab people. Its people want no foreigners past the trade camps at the desert's edge, and in some places trade only at oases, sending agents into the desert to meet them. They say it is to hide the source of their gold, but there is no other way to it, and merchants would warn them of any invasion like the one that came once from the Tell.

Kombuh Saleh lies here.
neighbours.secrets:
Theories traded at dinner parties in the Tell (pp. 81-82): that the Sudanese are faeries; that their way of life would disgust the Arabs; that they are the servant caste of a people who shun Allah's servants, such as evil jinn; that the gold comes corruptly, perhaps as monsters' excrement; that the desert truly is the world's edge and the Sudan is in Faerie; that gold is as cheap as sand to them; or that their faerie rulers want the journey, not the gold, and every trade good ever brought sits in a pile outside Kombuh Saleh.

If history holds, the kingdoms here are small and war-tossed, between the fall of the Empire of Ghana in 1204 and the founding of the Empire of Mali about 1240.

neighbours.name: The Sorcerer-King of Sosso
neighbours.summary: Soumaoro Kanté, rumoured ruler beyond the trade routes and Caliph of Kanem, of a nominally Muslim kingdom, a shadow whose name Berbers and Tuareg only whisper, since he is said to hear it on the desert wind. Merchants' tales of him are written off as the madness of the long road, yet something at the end of the routes keeps demanding slaves, and the merchants will not say who buys them.

neighbours.name: The Silent Traders
neighbours.summary: Those who deal in gold guard its source. Northern caravan masters leave wares on an agreed stone and withdraw; the gold traders come out, leave what they think fair, signal and hide. The caravan takes the gold or signals it is too little, back and forth until one side leaves with gold or goods. Locals say two plants have roots of pure gold, a tale for the gullible.

details.wants: Their sources of gold kept secret.

neighbours.secrets: Who they are the book leaves open: faeries feeding on the exchange, demons breeding greed, tribesmen without speech, or emissaries of a lost kingdom such as Atlantis, Prester John or the Sorcerer-King of Sosso.

neighbours.name: The Two Great Spirits: The Red and the Black
neighbours.summary:
One way to read the Great Desert: Africa is the battlefield of two great Magical spirits, the Great Hunger and the Hope, too vast for magic to touch or to speak usefully with men. Each makes servants and tools, some of which may become familiars and draw magi into the war.

The Red's creatures poison wells and fill oases, helped by faeries who burn crops and towns; its greatest children are the spirits of the places it has consumed. Men whose heads, to Second Sight, are fennec foxes tend a seemingly endless horde of Set-beasts. Most Northwest African traditions favour the Red. The coast cities live by the Dominion, which helps the Black by protecting farmers; in pagan days they had powerful faeries.

The Black's lieutenants are mostly in Egypt. One who met the Romans calling herself Africa, a gigantic ghostly woman near Tunis, utters prophecies fated to come true, whether or not on the Faithful. Elsewhere it has the geniuses of great natural features, rain spirits, enigmatic horus-beasts, crafter traditions that call rain, and perhaps a sect of sorcerer Blemmyes once of the Temple at Philae, who would look human except to Second Sight.

Egyptians called the two the Black Land and the Red Land, and spirits and faeries repeat the colours: rival ants, chess pieces, feuding warlords. Red goes with desert, mountain, sand, chaos, foreigners, fire and the Set-beast; Black with river, oasis, soil, order, Africans, water and the Horus-beast.

stages.title: The Red grows
stages.ignored: Oases shrink, the Plateau loses its fertility and desert tribes push into the Tell, with the Almohads too weak to stop them, as when the Beni Hallali came from Persia and wrecked irrigation across the east.

stages.title: The Hope grows
stages.ignored: Rain increases and the desert gets easier to cross. More slaves are needed to farm, cities of strange cultures rise at new oases, forgotten faeries are remembered in resettled ruins, and nomads turn farmer, enriching the kingdom and making the Reconquista harder.

neighbours.secrets: Lieutenants of either side may initiate seekers into Mysteries that turn their side's power on the other; Red Initiations such as desiccation are in the book's next chapter.

neighbours.name: The Kingdom of the Ghouls
neighbours.summary:
The spirits at the desert's edge claim a vast kingdom of ghouls lies hidden in its gravel and sand. Ghouls mostly crave man's flesh but can be kind: girls rescued from ghoulish husbands have crept back, and a woman lives there still with seven ghoulish brothers, having fled a sultan to return to her monstrous husband. Its king never appears.

The old way to kill a ghoul: run home, for ghouls usually taunt their prey a few nights and may spare you a night for a finger put through the keyhole. Next day dig a grain pit behind your door, goad the ghoul to a frenzy, let it burst in and fall, then fill the pit with firewood and roast it. Ghouls kill each other the same way, and it works on lions too.
neighbours.secrets:
A choice for the troupe (the Faerie reading, p. 86). Use the cannibal spirit of Realms of Power: Faerie or The Cradle and the Crescent's tribe, or rework faeries into ghoulish knights, giants and beasts.

The ruler may be an ancient ghoul, an angel, a demon, a mortal tale-teller, the ghost of a Criamon Primus, nobody, or whatever spirit is nearest in the story.

The treasury is a cave that opens when asked in the name of a mysterious person. The stealthy, minding the ghouls' keen noses, may overhear the name from guards; it may be an Arcane Connection to the Ghoul King or the vault's maker.

neighbours.name: The Punishment of God
neighbours.summary: The Infernal reading: the world was a garden until man invented lying. God swore to drop one grain of sand from the sky for each lie, and men laughed at so small a thing.
neighbours.secrets: In this version the Great Desert has an Infernal aura of 2, higher where people hid in it to do crimes. Demons dance on its sands, parts are almost the Fiery Pit, Hell has gates in the mountains, and Infernal smiths forge weapons for the last war in the Hoggar.

neighbours.name: The Crack Between the Worlds
neighbours.summary: The high fantasy reading: the caravans come not from the far south but from other worlds, by portals deep in the desert.
neighbours.secrets:
Faerie markets: each caravan is a troupe of faeries bearing real, exhausted goods, trading for vital things or a part in mortal stories.

Wounded worlds: the Hope and the Hunger fight in other worlds too. Slavers from a Hunger-ruled world trade gold they cannot eat and captives they will not feed; or traders from a world drowned in fecundity, the Black's kind face a mask, come for life-giving salt with the gold that breeds under their earth.

Unknowable places: the caravans come from deep in the Magic Realm, as spirits or the Realm's way of clearing travellers' leavings. Magi who follow pass into the Twilight Void and never come back to tell.

neighbours.name: The Western Nile
neighbours.summary: Many Arabic geographers say the Nile rises in the Atlas, runs south over the Great Desert, joins the Nil-es-Sudan, follows something like the Senegal and the Niger, then turns east, splits around a vast island and rejoins. Across almost all the continent it turns north, taking water from the south, some say from the Mountains of the Moon past the unlivable Equator, and flows on through Nubia and Egypt.

levels.name: The faded river
levels.see: The Nile of the Blacks, full of magical spirits sheltering from the mundane world, and a battleground of the Red and the Black.
levels.notes: The book says a high Magic aura without a number. It lies far from the mortal world and is hard to reach.

neighbours.secrets:
The standard setting of this book: the Western Nile exists but has faded into a regio as the Red defeats the Black. Victories for the Hope draw it closer. A shattering injury to the Hunger, on the scale of the European Forest's splitting (Guardians of the Forest), might bring it back to the world.

A troupe may instead use real geography, where the Nile rises in central Africa and the Sahel lies beyond the desert. That suits characters built around crossing the desert, and gives it a more realistic tone; the Western Nile suits high fantasy and a permeable desert.

neighbours.name: The Black City
neighbours.summary: A city deep in the desert of a king in mourning, whose people wear black and paint their houses, mosque and wall black.

neighbours.name: The King in Mourning
neighbours.summary: The king of the Black City found his wife drugged him nightly to visit a lover. He tricked her into taking the drug herself, went to the lover in her clothes and beheaded him, and she died of shock at the sight of the head. He mourns until a true woman is found, and steers travellers towards talk of women, with no interest in ribaldry.

stages.title: A virtuous woman is named
stages.clues: Above all one with a terrible husband.
stages.ignored: He may send her a string of white pearls. Any woman who wears it turns into a dove and flies straight to his kingdom, where he takes it off and she is herself again.

stages.title: A new queen
stages.ignored: His people wash the town white in celebration.

neighbours.name: The City of the Silent Princess
