neighbours.summary: A desert city whose palace is ringed with 100 stakes, nearly all bearing a young man's head.

neighbours.name: The Silent Princess
neighbours.summary: The ruler's lovely daughter is mute. He has sworn no man may wed her unless he makes her speak, and beheads each who fails, no more than 100 in all, so she may never marry.
neighbours.secrets: She speaks if shocked into botching a Personality Trait roll, most easily by storytelling. Her servants know this has been tried and love stories fail; tales of outrage and vice rewarded may anger her into shouting.

neighbours.name: Zerzura
neighbours.summary: A secret oasis far to the west of the Nile, the refuge of the young men and women of Kush, sent there when an invader pushed south after their line lost Egypt's throne; he did not follow into so harsh a desert. Arab writers claim one visit: a city of plain Egyptian influence, guarded by a tribe of black giants, whose people worship a great bird. Its statue stands over the gate with the key in its beak. No Hermetic magus has heard the story yet, but Seekers will want it when they do.
neighbours.secrets: All its people sleep unaging under a king and queen; a thief may carry off what he can if he dodges the guards and does not stray near the couple, lest they wake. Why they sleep and what will wake them is unrecorded.

neighbours.name: The Long Voyage
neighbours.summary: A saga hook: a covenant of magi sets out from North Africa to find the Nile's headwaters and travels for years through strange kingdoms beyond the desert, to dissolve at last under the Lighthouse of Alexandria.

neighbours.name: Making the Nile Fit for Transport and Trade
neighbours.summary:
The Western Nile may be easy to navigate, the chief road of West Africa, or hard, with the covenant's work being to open it. Its headwaters are south of the Atlas: a city there might command the passes to the Maghreb, or the characters may found one, cutting passes and tunnels, bridging, killing predators and beating bandits and petty lords.

Like the Nile above Aswan it may have cataracts, to be removed by magic, portaged, canalled, or crossed with magical cranes, river sections flowing through the air, or tame elementals. Millet and sorghum are the great bulk trade; leatherwork, cotton, ebony, indigo, gum arabic, bronze and brass need less capital. Gold would likely move to the river. Would they let slaves pass on 'their' river?

neighbours.name: The City in the Atlas
neighbours.summary: A secluded green valley in the Atlas with a rich stone city, where gold is for tools, gems are trinkets, and the one piece of glass is worth all the rest.

neighbours.name: The Tin Lamp
neighbours.summary:
A sweet seller gone bankrupt crossed the Atlas to beg among strangers, carrying his last possession, a lamp of tin and red glass, and found a city no outsider had reached. The Pasha entertained him three days. Ashamed, he gave the lamp as all he owned, and the Pasha, who had never seen glass and could match the gift with nothing, loaded twelve camels with treasure. His family lives rich in their home city still.

The tale goes on that his wicked brother sold everything to trade there, and was robbed by bandits and perhaps killed; or reached the city with a glass gift of his own, and was given in return the Pasha's greatest treasure, the little tin lamp.
neighbours.secrets: The tale is told all over the Near East, so they may be faeries playing at wealth and poverty, or the valley may be real.

neighbours.name: The Modern Garamantes
neighbours.summary: With a Western Nile the Garamantian kingdom need never have fallen, its capital safe on the river's fertile land and the Fezzan ruins only a lost colony. They raid neighbours and rob merchants, their chariots sweeping out of the moonlit desert for slaves. Their great export is carbuncles or carnelian, whose Virtuous Form lets the holder see in the dark.

neighbours.name: Prester John on the River
neighbours.summary: In 1220 Prester John is thought to be in India; contact with the Mongols later moves him to Ethiopia or near it. A troupe wanting his legend and The Cradle and the Crescent's hooks with historical Mongols can set his kingdom on the Western Nile.

neighbours.name: The Kingdom of the Perfect Aphrodisiac
neighbours.summary: Arabic geographers tell of a Western Nile kingdom where a root grows, one dose letting a man have sex at will for the rest of the day. By law every plant is its king's, who has two hundred wives and will not sell into Muslim lands for fear of tempting men with only four. Old rulers who ask are refused or sent herbs for impotence. Its land tortoises are so big that a man can stand in their tunnels, and oxen teams pull them out for eating.

neighbours.name: The Root of the Two Hundred Wives
neighbours.summary: The characters may be asked to steal the herb. What if it holds Creo vis, and how are the grogs to be kept at their duties?

neighbours.name: The Kingdom of the Choosing Dragon
neighbours.summary: A Western Nile kingdom whose notables stand in a half circle before a treasure-decked cave. A dragon with a serpent's body, a camel's head and a lion's mane crawls out, touches one man's chin with its nose and turns back; he must run and pull out a handful of hairs from its mane or tail, and their number is the years of his reign.

neighbours.name: Shaving the Dragon
neighbours.summary: A character with the right magic items might pin the dragon down and shave it bare. Do the locals accept this king? Can the dragon answer?
neighbours.secrets: The prophecy works as the Death Prophecy Virtue, though a few kings do not actually die when their reign ends.

neighbours.name: The Vexillation of the Fata Morgana
neighbours.summary: Tremere diviners saw a Mongol invasion coming, and a vexillation went into the Fezzan disguised as a Genoese caravan to make an emergency redoubt in the Garamantian foggaras. They guard its place and purpose fanatically.

stages.title: A cache is found
stages.clues: The characters plunder a supply cache by chance, or stumble on the magi in the ruins.

stages.title: The secret at stake
stages.ignored: The Tremere may kill to protect it, in a Wizard War beyond Mythic Europe's borders that may not keep the Order's conventions.
stages.stopped: The two groups find a settlement.

neighbours.name: A Covenant in Agisymba?
neighbours.summary: Remote, rich in untapped magic and easily reached by the Iter Praeter Caput Saxi, Agisymba would suit isolationists, or those wanting a menagerie or a unique familiar.

neighbours.name: An Atakor Covenant?
neighbours.summary: Cut off by distance, desert and fierce tribes, the Tuareg bastion might draw wizards or a cooperative of sahirs of the Order of Suleiman tired of politics, at the price of utter isolation. Once subdued or allied, the proud Tuareg make fine covenfolk who know the shifting regiones, and the land is well guarded, with strong Magic auras and untouched resources.

neighbours.name: Wages of Sin
neighbours.summary: A devout magus uncovers a vast hoard of gold at Taghaza and must master his own greed, then ask whether taking away so easy a supply would hurt Hell's plans.
neighbours.secrets: The flies are a horde of False God demons. Where death and murder are common they feed on the sin, and whisk away gold from hovels and caravans whenever a weak fool needs tempting.

neighbours.name: Breaking the Bonds
neighbours.summary:
Taghaza's slaves walk free but the desert holds them, living on imported food and water. Magi might feed them by magic and upset the whole economy. Would they welcome a new master? The southern traders, needing the salt, may offer gold or turn to violence.

A second great salt mine, Taodeni, lies undiscovered further south, away from the trade route; settling it would also draw the region's power brokers.
neighbours.secrets: Anyone living at Taghaza or Taodeni takes -3 on Aging rolls for the conditions (ArM5 p. 170), plus any Warping from the aura.

neighbours.name: Where Does All That Salt Go?
neighbours.summary: Slabs of rock salt go south on camels in the yearly Azalai, and no miner or overseer knows where. In two or three months the camels return with new slaves, gold and ivory, and the northern Massufa traders have learnt not to ask. Guides cannot quite describe the dealings, grow distant, and in the end stop returning, replaced by look-alike kin with similar names. Some exotic goods are touched by Faerie or carry tainted vis.
neighbours.secrets:
The Azalai may end in Arcadia, where salt becomes goods and captives are changed and sent north as black slaves with altered memories. At least one merchant is a disguised faerie with Spirit Away (Realms of Power: Faerie pp. 23-24); guides are men Warped away or minor faeries.

Or demons run it to punish sinners, whose fragments of memory make Taghaza a mundane purgatory.

neighbours.name: The Mines of Despair
neighbours.summary: Taghaza's miners tell scraps of lives beyond the desert, sharing only the memory of being brought to the pits and of missing their families.
neighbours.secrets: Exposure to the site's Infernal occupants gives nearly all mundane miners Weak Willed through Warping, and most hold the equivalent of the Delusion Flaw: the memories are false, and neither mundane nor magical means show it. Some miners and overseers are incognizant dark faeries or demons who feed on the suffering and warp the memories of the miners and female slaves.

neighbours.name: The Stolen Prize
neighbours.summary: The Pale Fox of Virtue snatches a bow, satchel or waterskin and offers a bargain: if a lone character catches it, it will show the group a vis site, a short cut through a regio, or a buried caravan the wind has bared. It relishes wordplay and accepts clever readings of the rules if the words stand: only one must catch it, but others may chase.

neighbours.name: Men of War
neighbours.summary: The rumoured Sorcerer-King of Sosso has an endless hunger for slaves for his wars against rivals and the deep desert's jinn.
neighbours.secrets: Some claim he can use traded salt and gold as Arcane Connections, and see and hear through the slaves he sends into Mythic Europe.

neighbours.name: Lost...
neighbours.summary: Moorish pirates seize covenfolk travelling on business.

stages.title: The trail south
stages.clues: Arcane Connections point to the Maghreb, but something masks the prisoners' exact whereabouts.
stages.stopped: The characters find them in the coast markets before they are sold.

stages.title: Across the sands
stages.ignored: After any misstep they must plunge into the desert after their friends.

neighbours.name: ...And Found
neighbours.summary: Disciplined, well-trained pagan grogs from the south offer the magi their service, and Frosty Breath of the Spoken Lie finds them honest. They need no church or mosque, but in civilization they hide or slip away at bad moments.

stages.title: The owner's claim
stages.ignored: The matter goes before a magistrate.

neighbours.secrets: They are a slave-soldier cadre who killed guards in their escape. Their owner comes to reclaim his property before a local magistrate.

neighbours.name: The Archetypical Road
neighbours.summary: The desert crossing is a road story, ripe for faeries to steal vitality from: guides, beasts and bandits all fit, and all survive against the odds. Do the fay enjoy the slaves' suffering, the travellers' misery, the merchants' greed, or all three?

neighbours.name: The Time-Lost
neighbours.summary: If the Sudan is strange and faerie, its slaves may come from a kingdom fallen into Faerie, from isles near India, or from Europe before the Flood. Faeries hoarding people from disasters may change supply as stocks run down: a thousand on sale, speaking classical Latin and claiming to be from Pompeii.

neighbours.name: Fantastic Slaves
neighbours.summary: The southern slaves may not be human: faeries, constructs from strange factories, Plinian races, spirits bound in solid forms, or the dead forced to labour.

neighbours.name: The Bitter Fruit
neighbours.summary: A chieftain's son among neighbouring Berbers has been stung by a Deathstalker Scorpion of Virtue, and dozens of them guard the only nearby Alkhad gourds in a hidden wadi. Numbers doom a charge, and those passing under a ward find the gourds hidden: they must deceive the deceivers.

stages.title: The gourds won
stages.stopped: The tribe may serve as grogs for a time, reveal a local jinn's hidden external vis, or show an unknown spring.

neighbours.name: Kaf Ajnoun
neighbours.summary:
The Hall of Spirits, a high and citadel-shaped mountain standing out of the sands of the Fezzan, near the Tasili n Ajjer. The people round about keep away: it is fiercely hot, no wadi runs near, and its slopes betray the foot.

The Tuareg say the lights and drums of the feasts on its summit carry for leagues. Jinn come there to meet the Winds and to deal in slaves, trinkets and vis.

levels.name: The Palace of the Winds
levels.see: A sumptuous palace on the summit.
levels.notes: Lesser zephyr spirits wait on the Winds here. The book gives the mountain's aura and no separate one for this regio.

neighbours.name: The Council of Winds
neighbours.summary:
Most of the old spirits of the Maghreb faded when Islam came. The desert winds did not: they wander, are tied to no one sacred place, and hold the region their own whatever its people believe. Seven genii loci and daimons sit in council: the Chergui, the Gregale, the Haboob, the Harmattan, the Khamsin, the Simoon and the Sirocco.

All of them roam, to the Levant and the East, and now and then to their peers in Iberia, Provence and the North, gathering the world's news. When Africa is the matter they meet at Kaf Ajnoun. They have lately argued over the Crusade at Damietta and what to do if it spreads west; before that, the Maghreb's pirates, the Romans and Garamantians, and the many caravans of the Great Desert.

details.wants: To keep the Great Desert dangerous and wild: they favour the deeds and the people that serve this.

neighbours.name: The Cult of the Sun and Moon
neighbours.summary:
In antiquity the Sun and Moon were worshipped with fanatical devotion from small shrines all over the Tell, and with animal sacrifice; the historians record it again and again as central to Ancient Libyan life. In a few places the sun was Sol Invictus, but in most she was the goddess Tafuyt, and the Moon was the god Ayyur. St. Augustine and Samuel the Confessor both tell of pagans trying to make them sacrifice to the Sun Goddess.

The legacy is in how Berbers sort magic: any power not of the Divine is the sun's if a man works it and the moon's if a woman does.

The sun here is no nurse but a harsh mistress, the tool of hardship. Awettuf the Ant taught sun magic, so it is believed, to protect against the world's evil: an impersonal, scholarly art that turns harm aside and bends natural forces to human good, and has charge of healing, creation and summoning. Sun magicians are the imhergi (singular amherg). Sahirs and elementalists have their own name, asehhar, the Tamazight form of sahir, and count as sun magicians even when female. Berbers would call much of Hermetic magic sun magic.

Moon magic is passionate and visceral, often destructive, or turning destruction to good use. Ayyur, god of the moon and of sacrifices, taught it to the settuten, priestesses of the First Mother of the World, who made the world and all the evil that plagues it.

details.rules: Berber magicians very often have the Cyclic Magic Virtue or Flaw, tied to the fitting body (p. 92). Sahirs: The Cradle and the Crescent ch. 3; elementalists: Hedge Magic Revised Edition ch. 2.

neighbours.name: The Imhergi and Ngagef
neighbours.summary:
Most imhergi are learned tattoo magicians, much like Cunning Folk. Among Berber women the ngagef (singular neggafa) are cosmeticians who specialise in the same sun magic although they are women.

They draw no spoken charms. They paint passing tattoos called tawzayt, or mark like signs on the ground or chalk them on buildings; an amherg's lasting work is a permanent tattoo, an ahadjam, or an inscription, which wakes when uncovered and fades when its charges or its time run out.

details.rules: Tradition Imhergi and Ngagef (pp. 93-94). The traditional symbols and Design & Inscription Bonuses are on p. 95; the fifteen symbols are the Beak, Lion's Paw, Fingers, Barley, Partridge Eyes, Gameboard, Frog, Seeds, Eye, Saw, Snake, Afous (the hamsa, Africa's commonest protective amulet), Sun, Moon and Ship.

neighbours.name: The Cult of the Dead
neighbours.summary:
Among the Berbers the dead stay part of the living people. Elders and marabouts speak with them through dreams, and so a whole cult keeps up the tombs and reads the dreams the spirits send, asking those beyond the grave what they see coming. The dead keep the reach they had alive: a dead ruler watches over his entire people. Though it isn't strictly needed, an ancestor is best consulted in his own tomb.

For this the pyramid tomb complexes hold sleeping niches called dream houses, set in a courtyard that is square but for an extension in the middle of its east side. In the larger ones, that extension holds a small copy of the main pyramid.

details.rules: Sleeping in a dream house gives +3 to Dream Interpretation rolls on the dreams had there (p. 92; the Ability is in Realms of Power: The Divine p. 137 and pp. 128-130 here).

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Juba II
neighbours.summary: The tomb of the former king of Mauretania. Dream interpreters still go there.

neighbours.name: The Royal Tombs South of Tahert
neighbours.summary: The largest of the dream-house tomb complexes, on two hills in Mauretania south of Tahert. Berber kings, high priests and famous ancestors lie there. The Imazighen regularly send their best dream interpreters to divine what threatens the region and the people. Many other ghosts haunt the hills too.

neighbours.name: The Tomb of Tin Hinan
neighbours.summary:
Tin Hinan, Queen of the Berber and mother of the Tuareg, rests at Abalessa in the Ahaggar, in Tilfilalt, ten days south of Fes. The tomb, set into the mountainside, is all that is left of her many-chambered palace on its hill. The Ahaggar matter deeply to the settuten, being the centre of the Great Desert and perhaps a haunt of Lazz, the Great Hunger.

The queen lies in state on a leather-covered bed, seven gold bracelets on her right arm and eight silver on her left. The Tuareg tribes take turns at the honour of guarding the tomb and defend it fiercely from outsiders, yet they stop no settut, wherever she comes from. Those who rest in the entryway with a token of Corpus or Creo vis often rise healed.

The inscriptions, for one who reads the Libyan script and language, are summae on each settut Supernatural Ability and on Divination, Level and Quality between 6 and 12 by subject (pp. 92, 97). She is consulted by the Divination Ability, and necromancy on her body gives +10 on events touching the Imazighen as a whole (p. 102). The grand convocation of the settuten meets here (p. 106).
neighbours.secrets: The healing sleep is the work of Tin Hinan's ghost; few guess their good fortune comes from her.

neighbours.name: The Brides of Ayyur
neighbours.summary:
The settuten (singular settut) are the witches of the Berbers; any woman who works magic is called one, but the name belongs first to this tradition of sorceresses, whose poetic title, Tisliten n Ayyur, weds them to the Moon. Since the old gods declined they have kept the old religion, priestesses of every Berber god, devotees of Yemma-t n Dunnit, the First Mother of the World. Most have The Gift and must live apart from their tribes, often in an old tomb or a marabout's. The few men among them live and are treated as women in everything.

A settut wears an indigo shawl stitched with moons and other signs, and blue on her lips and round her eyes; on business, whether with a client, her peers or a ceremony, she stains her forehead with yellow ochre and saffron. She does not marry, which mildly scandalises the Berbers, and takes herbs against pregnancy in imitation of her sterile goddess.

They heal, set bones, keep the midwife's and apothecary's trades and teach women to read. The tala, the women's court, sometimes seeks their advice, never forgetting that their goddess gives evil counsel. Even in Muslim districts they bless births and bury the dead, and watch closely for Gifted children at these rites: a boy is usually 'cured' by a year of Disjunction, a girl may be taken as an apprentice when she is old enough. Some, mostly the unGifted, turn to prostitution as a quick road to wealth.

A tribe tolerates its settut while she serves it; only the particularly pious risk angering her, and a wronged settut is a true curse. To them sahirs, the asehharen, are Arabs and blood enemies. They will band together to hunt one out of Berber lands, dismissing his spirits and disjuncting his magic before setting a war band on him, though they seldom mean to kill. With this power, it is said, they set the Umayyad summoners at war with their servile jinn.

details.decides: The tineqiqqiten (singular tineqiqqit), seeresses with the Divination Virtue, are their only leaders and call the local convocations, which meet irregularly.
details.rules:
Tradition Settuten (Berber); the Settut, Dust Devil and Settut Divination Virtues (pp. 95-106). Amulets and their Potency pp. 96-98, Durations and the moon p. 98, the Abilities pp. 99-103, dispelling with the jedwel pp. 103-104, the Tamzawit Curse pp. 104-105. Male settut must take Gender Nonconforming (p. 96, by the errata).

A local convocation swaps news and knowledge, hears divinations, reports sightings of asehharen, and votes to blacklist a person or town or lift a ban: the blacklisted get no help from any settut and are fair game for curses. Everyone Disjuncts her own Gift on arriving, the tineqiqqiten last, after they have Opened new members' Gifts and Initiated the unGifted; the stronger give amulets to those who cannot do it themselves.

The grand convocation meets at the Tomb of Tin Hinan every nineteen years, when the full moon returns to Cassiopeia on the shortest day. The book leaves its date to the storyguide. All the tineqiqqiten must attend; first they divine the fortunes of the settuten together until they agree, and the strongest or fiercest usually wins, The Gift being still on them. Exotic sorceresses and now and then supernatural guests attend too.
details.offers: Healing, advice, exorcism, midwifery and the old rites.

neighbours.name: The Tuareg Settuten
neighbours.summary:
The Tuareg have settuten of their own. Both peoples own the same origin for their powers, but neither counts the other as of its tradition, and they rarely work together. They go by no poetic name.

Usually one settut rides with each band, carrying it over the vast spaces and making lightning raids on caravans and villages; many go disguised as men in the litham veil. When bands meet they may trade their settut, and she has little say. It spares her the resentment of The Gift, for no one has time to tire of her, though it also keeps anyone from growing used to her. A wronged settut being so dangerous, she is seldom treated as a possession.

Their rare seeresses are the appointed guardians of Tin Hinan's shrine at Abalessa and speak for the southern settuten.

Tuareg parents have no Disjunction to quench a Gifted boy. Found early, he is raised a girl and made a settut, sold north as a slave, or left in the southern deserts for the jnun of the Kel Asouf or for death. Some of these are taken in by the Blue Men, the outcast inenden, or a wandering sahir or Hermetic magus.

Some men long in the deep desert, and some Blue Men, have Dislocation by Mystery or as a gift of the spirits. They carve its amulets from cypress or metal with ancient Libyan runes, and keep it hidden from settuten and comrades for fear of being called witches.

details.rules:
Tradition Settuten (Tuareg) (p. 106): Dislocation in place of Disjunction, Dismay in place of Dissidence, a waral lizard in place of the dust-devil under the curse, Skinchanger (waral lizard) in place of Dust Devil, usually adept at Geomancy. They cannot suppress their Gift. Those who live as men may take Gender Nonconforming (pp. 105-106, by the errata). A man with Dislocation gets no magical defences unless raised a true settut (p. 105).

No local convocations: bands share what they know when they meet. At the grand convocation they keep aloof, sneer, speak only to the tineqiqqiten and only in their own Tamazight, and must accept Disjunction or stay out; raiders mostly stay away, for fear of being called asehharen.

neighbours.name: The Daughters of Four Fathers
neighbours.summary:
A small, close family of shapeshifting women who say they all descend from one mother. Four friends on a long journey, the story goes, were missing the company of women. The carpenter, on first watch, carved a perfect woman from wood; the tailor, on second, dressed her in beautiful clothes; the magician, on third, gave her life. They always stop before saying what the thief did.

Each can take a dove's shape at will and sends messages by a single feather, which flies free, writes as a quill and returns. In human form each is supernaturally beautiful, wise, widely read and watchful. Children of a wildly successful thief, they were raised like the daughters of a rich merchant or minor noble. They flock together, and almost always live in groups.

In the city where they are active they hide spare feather pins in places like the baths; a few swallow an engraved stone feather, which lodges in the dove's crop and comes up at need.

details.rules: Every Daughter has Skinchanger (dove) in a Major form, Feather Messenger (Minor), Wealthy and Close Family Ties (Minor), on p. 107: a prepared feather, or any picture of one, serves as the cloak, her clothes and gear become feathers, and in dove form she has a common dove's statistics with +3 Soak. Some are Well-Traveled, and some chroniclers give them Venus's Blessing. Their learning leads some to think them faeries who made up their own stories.

neighbours.name: The Inducers
neighbours.summary: The scholars of the Maghreb count three kinds of magician, and these are the least: they cannot change the world, only make a victim's mind believe it has changed. This is not illusion as magi know it, for no species are touched. The diamond necklace an inducer conjures is seen by the victim alone, and not even by the inducer.

details.rules: The Induction Virtue, pp. 107-108, with the box on Entrancement and Induction, p. 106.

neighbours.name: The Potteresses
neighbours.summary:
Several lineages of magical potteresses work in Africa; these are the weaker ones. Many keep customs over the clay: some sacrifice chickens or rice before gathering it, others will not gather on a Monday or Friday. Most press their clay over forms, and among some tribes those forms must come from men whose first wives have died. A form from a man whose wife lives will curse a potteress, and may kill her.

They gather every year for sacrifices of animals or cowrie shells, for dancing and the handing down of lore, and to bring young women into adulthood, often by genital excision. There the eldest show their power: they slap the earth and water rises for the dancers to wash in, lead trees about on bridles of string, gather mounds of earth to make the dancing ground, rule the weather and breathe fire. Their magic often seems to come from the mouth, not the hands.

details.rules: Maker of Water Vessels and Maker of Textured Vessels (p. 108). Each vessel costs a Long Term Fatigue level; one without the gifts, training and blood who tries it suffers Enfeebled for life. The senior potters are an oral tradition of Elementalists (Hedge Magic Revised Edition pp. 17-33).

neighbours.name: The Leather-Workers
neighbours.summary: Leather is the male twin of the female art of pottery in Desert Africa: the same tradition in another stuff. The worker's highest calling is saddlery. Saddles often help the rider, bridles the horse's stamina and resistance to pests, halters and hobbles the groom. North African tack has far more tassels than European, and bridles often have a headband crossing above the eyes, which keeps off flies and is often enchanted to protect or strengthen horse or rider.

details.rules: The potteresses' two Virtues in leather; each Virtue covers clay or leather, not both (p. 109).

neighbours.name: The Rippers
neighbours.summary:
Minor magicians, thickest round Tunis but reported as far as the Muslim settlements of Iberia and Sicily. A ripper can tear things open with his mind, but not people, so most of them work the big markets as standover men: every cloth merchant or livestock dealer pays a little, regularly, so that his cloth stays whole and his beasts keep their bellies.

Rippers can pass the talent to their children. Scholars think variously that they are one bloodline, that the family knows an Initiatory Ordeal, that they are a murabit's acolytes, or that there are many kinds who each come by it differently.

details.rules: Ripper, Fabric Ripper and Leather Ripper (pp. 109-110).

neighbours.name: The Geomancers
neighbours.summary:
Geomancy, ilm al-raml, the science of the sand, reads rows of seemingly random marks scratched in earth. One Muslim legend has the angel Jibril teach it to Idris before Islam. Another credits an apocryphal easterner, Tumtum al-Hindi, whose book passed through the pre-Islamic prophets to Khalaf al-Barbar of Medina, an early convert.

It stays popular with the Tuareg, the half-literate Arabic and Berber hedge magicians of the Maghreb, and some Andalusian Ex-Miscellanea lines. Most magi think it cruder than astrology, and the scholarly hedge traditions look down on it.

Some inenden carve cypress dice marked with its figures, and an alchemist in Syria is said to have built a many-dialled brass instrument that casts them.

details.rules:
The Geomancy Ability and its Virtues (Geomancy, Lesser Geomancy, Skilled Geomancer, Astrological Geomancy), pp. 110-112; stylus bonuses p. 111. Astrological Geomancy is unknown in Africa and Mythic Europe.

Books, p. 111. Kitab al-Raml, thought a translation of Tumtum al-Hindi's book: summa, Level 4, Quality 10; poor Arabic copies and mistranslations Quality 5 to 8 are common, and occasional good Berber, Persian or Greek texts Quality 9. Experimentarius, a flawed Latin verse translation by Bernard Silvestris, in northern libraries since the 12th century: tractatus, Quality 8. A copy of its Arabic original: tractatus, Quality 9, from a Maghrebi bookseller or an Andalusian library.

neighbours.name: The Inenden
neighbours.summary:
A low caste of pariah craftsmen outside the Tuareg's drum groups, speaking their own dialect of Tamazight, Tenet. They are feared as magicians belonging to neither Sun nor Moon. None has The Gift, yet many have its effect on others. Their role looks like the bouda's of Morocco, but they cannot change shape.

The men work metal or carve wood, the famous Tuareg saddles among it; the women make ornate jewellery of metal and glass, with magic in it. Their superior pieces lend a small bonus to one roll and can be sold to anyone; excellent pieces, rarer, help several rolls but only the man they were made for.

details.rules:
Tradition Inenden; Inenden Crafter, Touched by (Realm), Mythic (Craft), Crafter's Eye (the catalog's Eye of Hephaestus) on pp. 112-114. Outcast; many have Offensive to Animals or Magical Air. Wondrous items pp. 114-116; rare Gifted inenden p. 112.

Common wondrous items of Africa (p. 114): the Ettebel of the Chief (a chief's drum, Craft Level 14), Odili of Soothing (a sorghum-wood flute that holds an animal still, 15), Saddle of the Temperate Camel (17), Jar of Potable Water (takes the salt from water, 15), Bukar of Clear Sight (a black turban, 17), Boots of the Tahr (+3 to climb, 13), and the Hyena Pelt (a mantle and hood that make the wearer a hyena until sunrise or sunset, 17; Muto Corpus (Animal) base 10, +1 Touch, +2 Sun, requisite free, by the errata).

neighbours.name: The Blue Men of the Desert
neighbours.summary:
Some Tuareg of the deep desert are changed over time by its strong Magic auras and by forever wearing enchanted litham veils, until they become Magic Humans. Nominally of the great spirit called the Black, these wanderers stand guard against the worse things that rise from the deepest sands or cross where the boundaries between the mundane and the Supernatural run thin.

Those fully changed are bigger and more magical than their human kin. There also seem to be lesser Blue Men, born to it in the deep desert, Magic-kin with no Might and no monstrous look.

details.rules:
The fully changed have Transformed by Magic and commonly Large or Giant Blood; built by Realms of Power: Magic ch. 4 (p. 116). Magic-kin suit grogs and companions, or an Ex Miscellanea magus, or a Mythic Companion as Spirit Votary of the Black.

Inherited Virtues: Dislocation, Geomancy, Greater Immunity (Deprivation), Lesser Geomancy, Lesser Immunity (Thirst), Personal Power: Aura of Rightful Authority, Desert Regio Network, Skinchanger (waral lizard), Ways of the Desert, Voice of the Desert. Required Flaw: Vow (always wear the litham). Inherited Flaws: Anchored to the Desert, Delusion (Tuareg superiority), Disfigured (blue dyed skin), Dutybound, Feral Scent, Obsessed (camels or racial purity), Overconfident, Oversensitive (appearance), Poor Concentration, Proud, Social Handicap (poor hygiene), Short Attention Span, Wanderlust, Weak Senses (Cold Sensitivity).

neighbours.name: The Desiccated Men
neighbours.summary:
Far into the Tanezrouft, the Land of Thirst, wander the darker kin of the Blue Men. They are Tuareg who, dying of thirst and heat, were bound by a pact to the desert Daimon called the Hunger or the Red, and brought back to a semblance of life as its servants. They have lost much of their humanity. Free and proud no longer, they name themselves Ag Lazz or ibn al-Ju' to show whom they serve.

Their magic runs on thirst and the drying of water; some can also command heat, raise sandstorms or call up swarms of desert creatures.

details.rules: Variants of the Drowned Men (Realms of Power: Magic pp. 96-97): Transformed Human and the Major Story Flaw Servant of the Desert (p. 115). They seem aligned to Aquam in a negative sense.

neighbours.name: The Folk Witch Bouda
neighbours.summary:
Some human bouda of Morocco claim a legendary clan or tribe, and their magic is thought to come down from their parents. They are mostly men, though their way of changing sex confuses the count, and most have The Gift. Besides ruling their hyena shape and their minds of others, they work smith's or woodcarver's magic, typically Muto Terram or Muto Herbam.

As they warp they turn slowly into inhuman faerie bouda, as a gruagach turns troll.

details.rules: Tradition Bouda (folk witches), pp. 118-119: Folk Witch, Gender Shift, Theriomorph and Touched by Faerie Realm; Judged Unfairly, Short-Ranged Curses and Primitive Tradition; Sex Shift, as the book first names it, is the catalog's Gender Shift. Warping replaces the Witch's Moon. Ordeal Flaws run to the hyena's unsavoury qualities: Feral Scent, Disfigured, Hunchback, Tainted by Evil, Repellent.

neighbours.name: The Jnun of Africa
neighbours.summary:
Few supernatural beings matter more here. People think in terms of jnun, not of realms, which confuses any magus trying to learn about them. Jnun, jnoun and jinn are near enough one word in different mouths: jnun more the further west you go, jnoun in the old Carthaginian lands, jinn in Egypt and from Arab merchants of the east.

Alone in the Sahara, it is said, you can hear the whispers of thousands of invisible jinn. The wild jinn are spirits of an oasis, a mountain or a stretch of desert, true genii loci of the Magic realm, and cannot go far from their land without a bargain or coercion. Others are faeries who ape the Berber, Bedouin and Tuareg peoples beside them, and others are Infernal.

Tunisian and Libyan 'jinn' are harder to master than eastern ones because many of them are not jinn at all.

details.rules: Which jnun Sihr commands: rules.africa, pp. 123-125. All true jinn have the Free Virtue Jinn, nearly all Ways of the (Land) and Greater Malediction: Bound by Bargains, and Magic ones elemental powers. Multiple animal shapes, Shapeshifter sizes and hybrid shapes pp. 123-124; building them, The Cradle and the Crescent ch. 4.

neighbours.name: The Afarta
neighbours.summary:
The winged messengers and nobles of the jnun (singular afrit), spirits of the air kin to the leriah but outranking other jnoun, as mighty as the strongest marid of the East. Many lesser afarta take the shape of long-haired winged serpents and carry messages for the sultan of the jinn under their chief, Eblis.

The greater afarta are the jnun's nobility, terrible and monstrous, many-headed serpents or beast-headed giants. Many afarta possess humans, and the possessed is called a majnun, a madman. When the Order of Suleiman talks of the untamable jinn of the Maghrib and Libya, it usually means these. Solomon's lost Seal, they say, is the one thing that would master them easily.

details.rules: Lesser afarta are Infernal dragons (p. 125), not true jinn and unlike the eastern 'afrit despite the name: Sihr does not touch them, and sahirs cannot summon them. The greater vary in Realm, most being Magic variants of the Aerial Powers, and can lend subjects Recalcitrance (Realms of Power: The Infernal p. 42). The strongest are Magic Daimons, manifest as Aspects, not easily controlled by non-theurgical Hermetic magic. None is a true jinn.

neighbours.name: The Seventh Depth
neighbours.summary: A vast Faerie regio off the southern Mediterranean coast, where Sidi Moussa, sultan of the jnoun of the sea, holds court.

neighbours.name: The Baharia
neighbours.summary: The jnoun al-Bahar, found only in Africa and thickest along the coasts round the Tunisian peninsula, though they are said to live in all oceans. This strictly ranked Faerie tribe looks like mermen and tritons, a man's body to the waist and a fish's below. They are blamed for storms and tempests, and superstitious locals still offer them sacrifices and rites whatever Islam teaches.

details.rules: Mermen and tritons are in Realms of Power: Faerie pp. 90-91. Not true jinn: Sihr does not touch them (p. 125), though they may share jinn's Traditional Wards, including the authority of Islam, and other magic can summon them.

neighbours.name: The Awlad al-Hut
neighbours.summary: A secret brotherhood of Tunisian fishermen, drawn from those called the Ouata, who cling to totemic beliefs older than Islam in the face of the orthodoxy of Mahdia. Fishermen of the society are initiated into a non-Hermetic Mystery Cult.

details.rules: Mostly unGifted. Some leaders may have hedge magic, as Mythic Alchemists or Water Elementalists, seemingly of Faerie and not Magic (Hedge Magic Revised Edition; p. 124).

neighbours.name: The Siadna
neighbours.summary: The Masters Underground: the Walad al-Ahmar, sons of the Red, and the Walad al-Akhdar, sons of the Black. They live chiefly among people, invisible or as dogs, donkeys, camels, serpents, chickens, fish and above all cats, and keep secret lairs and palaces underground, playing the roles of Europe's common faeries.

details.rules: Closest of the faeries to eastern jinn: vulnerable to the traditional wards and the sahirs' binding, built as Pious jinn (The Cradle and the Crescent ch. 4; p. 126).

neighbours.name: Al-Maghrebi
neighbours.summary: The evil Moroccan magician runs through the Thousand Nights and One Night like a dark thread, ruining trusting youths who become wise heroes by escaping him. These Faerie wizards mostly bear non-Arabic, usually Berber, names. In some western tellings a like figure of magian birth and Persian looks takes the villain's part: these seemingly Zoroastrian faeries are the al-Majusi.

neighbours.name: The Amadagh
neighbours.summary: To the Berbers any wasteland, even a forested one, is an amadagh, the outskirts of the Otherworld, part underworld and land of the dead. All is reversed there: rivers run uphill, trees lift their roots into the air, and sheep are black, with black milk. It is barren by definition and full of dire things, and there the lowhush are found.

neighbours.name: The Lowhush
neighbours.summary: Lowhush (singular lwash) is the Berber word for monsters: it covers dangerous mundane beasts, Magic spirits and monstrous faeries alike. The jnun count too, though their forms and stories owe more to Arab and Bedouin ideas than to the old Berber beliefs.

details.rules: For statistics, see the Faerie Bestiary of Realms of Power: Faerie ch. 4 and The Cradle and the Crescent ch. 4 (p. 126).

neighbours.name: The Murabitin
neighbours.summary:
Murabitin (singular murabit), or igurramen in Tamazight, are at once scholars, dream interpreters, religious hermits and makers of protective amulets. They mostly live in zawiyas, houses built near tombs, tending a saint's shrine and honouring him by study and prayer. Above all they are the religious authority of the Berbers round them, debating Qur'an and law and settling disputes.

A murabit names no price for an amulet, but he may remark how hard it was to make, and the wearer gives something fitting, goods or livestock; now and then he asks a favour or a task instead.

A brotherhood, a tariqa or Path, sometimes forms round a murabit and his line. Its members, talibs or students, swear obedience to the line as heirs of its founder's divine grace, and some believe their joined faith lets murabitin heal and grant salvation. A few zawiyas stand by pre-Islamic tombs, where dream interpretation reaches the ancestors and the scraps of memory they hold; it marks the murabitin as heirs of Berber antiquity and protectors of its shrines.

The art usually passes from father to son, though a likely candidate may be adopted. They seem akin to the Jewish Ba'al Shem, as neither would admit, Jews having once lived in numbers among the Maghreb's Berbers. The Order thinks them hedge wizards unworthy of membership.

details.rules: Tradition Murabitin; Mystic Tradition: Favored Abilities Blessing, Ceremony, Craft Amulet, Dream Interpretation, Understanding; Murabit, Pious and Vow. The Murabit, Talib, Craft Amulets and Dream Interpretation Virtues and both Abilities, pp. 127-130.

neighbours.name: The Sufis of the Maghreb
neighbours.summary:
Sufis take the Qur'an as speaking straight to the heart, and know the Divine as a personal, all-consuming love. Their name comes from suf, the wool of their plain clothes. They hold that their way comes from the Qur'an, breaks no law of Islam, and is needed for its fulfilment. They count Mansur al-Hallaj and Junayd Baghdadi of the early 10th century as their effective founders; Abu Nasr al-Sarraj and Abu Hamid Muhammad al-Ghazali put the theory in order, and the mystic poet Ibn-Arabi of Damascus is now the most active thinker.

They helped fix Islam among the Berbers. Brotherhoods reached the Maghreb in the 12th and 13th centuries, though far stronger in the Levant, and young groups are forming in Marrakech and Fes. Tariqas gather in a convent or a saint's tomb round a senior Sufi, a shaykh, or a guide, a murshid, with his muridin; most see one another as peers. A murid becomes a shaykh by receiving the khirqa, the cloak of the silsilah, the chain back to the Prophet through which wisdom flows.

Often thought heretics, they are more and more seen as models of piety. Some rulers build zawiyas, khanqahs (convents) and ribats (hospices) for them, partly to keep them under watch. Many murabitin are Sufis and the ignorant mix them up, but the two traditions are distinct. The most pious, the zahids, are said to work miracles, karamas, flying, healing with a touch and conjuring food and clothing by prayer. The most learned seem to bend the world a little: they find what they need, and events fall out their way, which they call the will of God.

Renowned Sufis of the Maghreb, all dead: Abu Madyan, a popular mystic from Iberia whom many Almohads feared, who died in 1198 on his way to the Caliph at Marrakesh and lies at Tlemcen, nearly its patron saint. Ali Hirzihim, whom Abu Madyan took as his spiritual leader, who spread al-Ghazali's works and taught at the Qarawiyin in Fes, taught by an uncle who was al-Ghazali's pupil, and took his khirqa from Ibn al-Arabi. Al-Dakkak of Sijilmasa, who studied beside Abu Madyan in Fes, gave him the master's khirqa, and lies outside Bab al-Gisa in Fes. Al-Ghazali, the Persian Sufi who set Sufism within mainstream Islam, to some the most important Muslim after Muhammad, who died at Tus in 1111. Ibn al-Arabi of Seville, a great judge of Islamic law, who weighed the belief that knowledge comes only by purifying the soul, and died at Fes in 1143.

details.rules:
Zahids: Realms of Power: The Divine p. 116 (p. 131 here).

The Khirka of Abu Madyan (p. 129): a patched grey woollen cloak, handed from master to student, radiating calm. Faith Score 5, 5 Faith Points, Divine Might 50, with the Saint powers Celestial Immunity, Grant Serenity, Resist Temptation and The Incombustible Shroud (Realms of Power: The Divine p. 88).

Books, in Arabic (p. 129). Abu Madyan: Bidayat al Mouridin, Ouns al Wahid, Tahfat al Arib and his Diwan, each a Theology tractatus, Quality 9, in private libraries of the Maghreb and al-Andalus, sometimes the Levant. Ibn Masarrah: Kitab al-i'tibar, Kitab khawass al-huruf and Tawhid al-muqinin, each a Theology tractatus, Quality 10, there too, rarely the Levant; several works they cite are lost, so his system can hardly be rebuilt. Al-Ghazali: The Revival of Religious Sciences, summa, Theology: Islam, Level 5, Quality 8; Incoherence of the Philosophers, The Deliverer From Error and The Jerusalem Tract, Theology tractatus, Quality 8; in the Maghreb, al-Andalus and all the eastern Muslim world.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Carthage
neighbours.summary: Outside Tunis, on the site of the city, the Punic and Roman works are abandoned and looted for their cut stone, and little can be recognised. Carthage was utterly destroyed in 146 BC, its enemies writing all that survives of it. Tunis is what remains of its greatness.
neighbours.secrets:
The ruins belong to the Infernal realm, the legacy of the gods of Carthage (p. 132).

The book prints the city's destruction as 164 BC on p. 132, likely a misprint: p. 15 gives 146 BC, used here.

A great mass of melted bronze lies buried here, the remains of a tophet destroyed in the razing, and with it Ba'al Ammon's urns of vis-rich ash.

Every Punic colony had to build a temple to Tanit and Ba'al Ammon, its shrines beside a tophet: a great bronze god or goddess with upstretched arms and a fire within. Petitioners laid bound offerings on the sloping hands to fall into the mouth and burn. The priests buried the ashes in urns dedicated to Tanit, and the demon drew on the pits as vast stores of vis.

neighbours.name: The Priesthood of Carthage
neighbours.summary:
Long dead. The priests of Carthage drew their tradition from the Cabieri, a circle of ancient mystics and smiths with a sanctuary on Samothrace. They ranked second only to the kings and queens, bargained with the gods for a fee, carried back the gods' demands, saw that petitioners paid, and schooled the young in the faith. Later priests hid their founder's discoveries in myth and allegory so that Greeks and Romans should not steal them.

That founder was Sanchuniathon, priest of Ba'al Ammon and sorcerer of Berytus, whom Plutarch thought truthful. He mastered the mysteries of Taautus of the Cabieri, the Egyptians' Thoyth and the Alexandrians' Thoth, whom the Greeks called Hermes; he studied the secret writings of Levantine Punic priests, and joined the two. Philo of Byblos put his work into Attic Greek, and no copy now survives.

Their worship stood on celebration, sacrifice and serpents. They raised standing stones, stelae, carved with the gods' signs, to win favour or give thanks, most of them Tanit's, and pillars inscribed with their myths. They burned the 'first fruits' in great bronze altars, the firstborn of prominent citizens among them, though several treaties demanded it stop; as the legions broke the defenses the nobles burned 300 high-born children. Serpents they honoured as images of rejuvenation and immortality with festivals, sexual rites and sacrifice, drawn from Taautus's mysteries.

They taught that their gods had been men, kings raised to godhood by ancestor worship, and that the greatest priests and kings might rise likewise. No account of how survives.

details.rules:
The Priesthood's ruins have no printed aura; Tunis is described with the coasts.

Serpent amulets of shed snakeskin give long life: +3 to aging rolls and Tainted with Evil while worn (p. 134). Some pillars may carry True Names, and their remnants may give Seekers insight into lost magic (p. 132).

Books. Praeparatio Evangelica by Eusebius, in Latin (p. 132): summa, Area Lore: Ancient Carthage, Level 2, Quality 5, and Theology, Level 3, Quality 5, in private libraries in the Levant and Egypt and in Constantinople; it was meant to discredit paganism and became the last map to Punic magic. One copy is papyrus scrolls on iron rods capped with brass bull's heads, in a dark cedar box with brass fittings, in a fine narrow hand in a Roman dialect. Bibliotheca Historica Book III by Diodorus Siculus, in Latin (p. 130): summa, Area Lore: Ancient Carthage, Level 2, Quality 5, same libraries; it tells of the 300 children. De Superstitiones by Plutarch, in Latin (p. 130): tractatus, Area Lore: Ancient Carthage, Quality 5, in private libraries and Constantinople; on the flutes and drums that drowned the sacrifices' cries.

neighbours.secrets:
Their realm is the Infernal. The apotheosis was a lie. The gods were a single demon who enjoyed the work, granting just enough to encourage more sin and bloodshed, and charging for things it would gladly have done anyway.

Their rite was a now-lost Profane Sacrifice, joining Sacrifice and Profaning the Holy (Realms of Power: The Infernal pp. 95-96): burning an offering makes a pawn of Vim vis infesta for each +2 the offering would give, 5 pawns for an innocent human.

A storyguide may instead make them Faerie hedge wizards of Faerie Bargaining (p. 130; Realms of Power: Faerie p. 131), the child sacrifices giving vitality. Later they raised slave children to offer in place of their own; such faeries, finding the trick, could withdraw their protection.

neighbours.name: The Broken Gift
neighbours.summary: A boy meant to be a magus's apprentice is carried off by veiled women to be subjected to Disjunction. Can the magus reach him before his Gift is quenched? Can he bargain with the settuten, or is magical war the only choice? (p. 104)

neighbours.name: Sun Versus Moon
neighbours.summary:
A covenant that offends the local settuten may be blacklisted and targeted. The Aegis probably saves its buildings from Dissolution, but not its water or crops, and Dissidence could ruin the covenfolk's ties with the community (p. 104).

Some will want to destroy these hedge wizards, and find themselves facing many foes and the Berbers besides. Others will seek peace, a hard road with The Gift souring every meeting.

neighbours.name: Forewarned Is Forearmed
neighbours.summary: As a prelude, perhaps, to an Arab push into Berber land, sahirs plot to murder the tineqiqqiten at the grand convocation. Without them no settut can Open The Gift, and some or all of the Initiation Scripts may be lost. Premonition and omen have warned the seeresses, who are seeking allies, but will not say at once why (p. 104).

neighbours.name: Predators and Prey Alike
neighbours.summary: A bouda pack hunting the countryside has come to like the taste of covenfolk. Will the magi find the killers and destroy them, or bind them to service? What if they get inside the covenant and hunt from there? And if they do serve, will their masters feed them slaves or make true scavengers of them? (p. 116)

neighbours.name: Dream a Dream of Days Past
neighbours.summary: The characters seek out a local murabit to find a spirit, a lost site or some fragment of antiquity through the ancestors he can call. The dreaming ghosts remember as far back as Rome, not always reliably. Could his gift lead to the Ancient Magic of Canaanite Necromancy, or to Insight into an initiation of Dream Magic? How will they persuade so pious a man to share? A magus might become his adopted son by saving his firstborn from a bargain with a sahir and the appetites of an insatiable slaver jinn (p. 128).

neighbours.name: A Lost Key
neighbours.summary: Locals bring the magi a low pedestal, a cippus, dedicated to Melkart of Tyre as a votive, carved in Greek and strange signs. It bears the True Name of Melkart, and a native Goetic infernalist wants it: he hides among the visiting peasants, working round every precaution to steal it (p. 131).
neighbours.secrets: The Cippus of Melqart, in Classic Greek and Punic: a tractatus of Dead Language: Punic, Quality 5, studied for a season with Dead Language: Punic or Classic Greek of 4 or more. It is a key to Phoenician.

neighbours.name: Undiscovered Heritage
neighbours.summary: A magus finds a cache of ancient Greek manuscripts credited to the Cabieri, in the libraries of Constantinople or in ruins of the Theban Tribunal. They hint at a tie between the Punic magic of Carthage and the rites of Thoth-Hermes, and name secret cult sites in the mountains west of Carthage (p. 131).
neighbours.secrets: Seekers who follow the trail may find the false faerie Ba'al Ammon lingering there, or easily called. He offers ancient magic, and the risk of unwitting corruption.

neighbours.name: Health and Long Life
neighbours.summary: As a gift, from ruins, or from the bazaars of the Tell, the magi come by a life-extending amulet of the Punic priests. Is it an Arcane Connection to Ba'al Ammon, a relic of Carthage, or a trap laid by Gifted sahirs of the Caliphate? Is the Aging bonus worth the risk? Would taking it apart for Insight yield a minor Breakthrough in longevity? (p. 131)

neighbours.name: Wages of Carthage
neighbours.summary: A Gifted sahir against the magi seems to have endless Vim vis, and a stream of supernatural assassins harries them whenever they leave the covenant. Beat him, and his tainted trove remains: will they take it, and what will they do with it? How will they keep another sahir from doing the same? (p. 131)

neighbours.secrets: He has found Ba'al Ammon's cache of vis infesta outside Tunis.

neighbours.name: To Resurrect the Brazen Tophet
neighbours.summary: In the ruins of Carthage a magus finds a huge lump of melted bronze that seems to hold several pawns of vis. Dug out and reformed, it would work again as a Tophet of Sacrifice, turning offerings into Vim vis. Such a prize might lead greedy magi deeper and deeper into depravity; and if word reaches vis-poor Tribunals or amoral, vis-hungry magi, its owners will be challenged on many fronts (p. 131).

description.biography:
Printed as a starting companion who needs 2 more Minor Virtues to balance, and may take one more if he takes another Minor Flaw. His Knight Virtue is printed as Amghar (Knight). Desert Regio Network, Disfigured (indigo skin) and Short Attention Span come from Warping (BS&S p. 33).

Combat: Fist Init +0, Atk +3, Def +2, Dam +1. Kick (mounted) Init -1, Atk +7, Def +5, Dam +4. Takoba & Aghar Init +2, Atk +11, Def +10, Dam +7. Takoba & Aghar (mounted) Init +2, Atk +14, Def +13, Dam +7. Allagh (lance, mounted) Init +2, Atk +13, Def +8, Dam +6. Soak +14 (Stamina, Tough, full chain). Encumbrance 3 (9). Veil powers: Brave the Sandstorm, ReAu 25, Init 0, Personal, Sun, 2 uses a day, repels the breeze that carries the dust. Ward Against the Kel Asuf, ReVi 15, Init 0, Personal, Sun, 2 uses a day, Penetration +10, repels minor Faerie spirits of the deserts.

characters.summary: A Targui amajegh, a noble of the Ahaggar who leads raiders on camels, known locally as merciless, with a veil worn so long that his skin has gone indigo.

description.biography:
Natural Characteristics before Ablating: Com 0, Sta +1, Qik 0. Corrupted Abilities comes from Warping and marks Leadership and Single Weapon (+3 for sinful uses, -3 for virtuous). Rules for Summoning and Ablating are in Realms of Power: The Infernal pp. 114-117.

Combat: Greatsword Init +4, Atk +12, Def +10, Dam +11. Longsword & Round Shield Init +5, Atk +11, Def +10, Dam +8. Gauntlet Init +2, Atk +7, Def +8, Dam +4. Soak +8. Encumbrance 1 (3). Wounds -1 (1-6), -3 (7-12), -5 (13-18), Incapacitated (19-24), Dead (25+); Size is printed 0, though Large and these ranges are those of Size +1.

Infernal Vitality, 0 points, Init +4, Corpus: wounding with the great sword reduces his overall Wound Penalty by as much (a Medium Wound by 3), never past zero, while his opponent lives. Penetration base 0, plus his own Penetration; blood makes an easy Arcane Connection. Equivalent to a level 25 effect.

Equipment: partial chain, infernal heirloom in the shape of a great sword.

characters.summary: A young Hassane of the Banu Khalida seeking fame as a warrior: nearly seven feet tall, ebony-skinned and shaven, his face painted with red ochre for battle, in a chain shirt under a black djebellah. He cannot leave a jar, door, shutter or chest open.
characters.secrets: He preys on the ghosts of those he beats, Ablating experience, Confidence, Characteristics or healing from them, fifteen victories so far, gaining Warping and Infernal Reputation, and tainting his Abilities. The remnants hang at the edge of his sight, which is why he closes every place a spirit might hide. A demon is bound in his great sword.

characters.name: Abu Mohammed Salih (Al-Mighri)
characters.summary: A Sufi mystic of 67, beloved of Asfi's elders, with a ribat in the town and the beginnings of the Magiriyyun order. If history holds he has 14 years to live, teaching ascetics and writing the Bidayat al Mourid, on Tassawuf and on Sufi saints such as his teacher Abu Madyan.

characters.name: Kerrew
characters.summary: A pious sorcerer who lives in Comino's caves and has a magic cloak that lets him fly, on which he sometimes goes to Malta for long stays.

characters.name: Zeynab
characters.summary: Youngest daughter of the headman of the village by Cyrene, the only person who knows the nymph Kura still lives. She stumbled into the regio last spring and now visits often.

characters.name: Merin ag Gwafa

tradition_effects.parameters: R: Personal, D: Sun, 2 uses per day
tradition_effects.notes: ReAu, Init 0, enchanted into his indigo litham veil. It keeps sandstorms off the wearer by turning aside the breeze that carries the dust.

description.biography:
BS&S p. 113. A Companion, balanced as a starting character, his minor craft magic aligned to Magic. Faith 1 (1), from the relic he carries. The book's Inenden social status is not in the Virtue catalog. His Disfigured (indigo skin) and Short Attention Span come of Warping from always wearing the magical veil. Fear is of the Kel Asuf; his Vow is to wear the litham always; his Herbalism acts as Medicine (Art & Academe pp. 55-56).

Fist: Init -2, Attack +2, Defense -2, Damage +2. Soak +2. Fatigue OK, 0, -1, -3, -5, Unconscious. Encumbrance 0 (0).

Equipment: litham veil, woodcarving and blacksmith tools, various amulets. Of those only two work: a minor relic (1 Faith point and Magic Resistance 10) and an imerghi Vulnero Magicam charm with 2 charges left, against Faerie creatures of Might under 15.

To make him a Mythic Companion, choose 11 more points of Virtue, such as Geomancy, Mythic Herbalism, Leather Ripper, Premonitions or Touched by (Realm); or remake him as a Cunning-Man or Elementalist at magus level with Hedge Magic Revised Edition.

characters.summary:
A Tuareg inenden saddle-maker who wanders the Ahaggar, his pariah birth barring him from the lasting protection of any drum group, though the nobles he serves prize his work. Mortally afraid of the desert spirits, he trades much of what he makes for charms against magic, most of which do nothing. He is worn in the face, in a tattered light veil and a dirty white robe, and hung all over with small metal amulets and glass.

His saddles are made for one rider and give +3 to riding or a Ride score of 8 on camels, or carry small Animal enchantments: they calm an animal, or let it go longer without water, or speed it across shifting sand.
characters.secrets: Only two of his amulets do anything: a minor relic and an imerghi Vulnero Magicam charm.

creatures.name: Satyrus, an Ape
creatures.how_many: the monkeys of Pithecousa; mundane kin in North Africa's mountains

powers.name: Ape the Beast
powers.description: Takes on a minor natural ability or mundane Quality of an animal he sees, such as a frog's swimming, a cat's night vision, horns, spines or a bear's pelt, but no major change like wings. One at a time; a second replaces the first. It lasts indefinitely, but he loses a Might point each sunrise and sunset while he keeps it, regained in three hours or less in a Magic aura. MuAn 25 (Base 4, +2 Sun, +1 Part, +1 Constant effect, +1 can change ability possessed); Personal Power (25 levels, -2 Might cost).

powers.name: Mimic the Man
powers.description: Copies any sound exactly, even human speech, without understanding it. MuIm 3 (Base 1, +1 Conc, +1 Complexity); Personal Power (3 levels, -1 Might cost, +1 Init).

creatures.appearance: A tailless monkey of yellowish, gray or brown fur, paler beneath, with a darker face.
creatures.notes:
Reputations: none.

A mundane monkey: remove Magic Animal, Might, Magical Qualities and Inferiorities (with the Essential Traits and Powers) and vis, and lower Quickness by one. The satyrus (Simia in Latin) is the commonest kind and the only tailless one, and is found mundane through North Africa's mountains. The island may hold other exotic monkeys, such as tailless black-furred giants or tiny creatures with immense eyes.

Cercopithecus: the smallest, a thief with a shaggy red-brown coat, long tail, white legs and underparts, a brighter red cap and black lines from face to ear. Also in Mauritania's scrubland, with gray-furred black-faced kin near the Torrid Zone. Size -4 (Str -8, Qik +4), add Minor Virtue (Light Touch), Minor Flaw (Carefree) and Fast Runner.

Callithrix: black, with a long white beard, a shawl of white fur on the back and a white tail tuft, and no thumb. From the Horn of Africa, sometimes an Egyptian's pet. Size -3 (Str -6, Qik +3), add Minor Virtue (Perfect Balance) and Minor Flaw (Palsied Hands).

Sphinx: docile, shaggy and long-tailed; males have a lion's mane and a red-striped, blue-muzzled, yellow-bearded face. From the Empire of Ghana, brought north by travellers. Add Minor Virtue (Inspirational) and Minor Flaw (Noncombatant).

Hamadryas (or cynocephalus, not to be confused with the Magic Humans of that name): a fierce olive-brown, dog-faced monkey; males have a silver-gray cape and mane. From the eastern deserts and highlands. Add Minor Virtue (Berserk) and Minor Flaw (Oversensitive to Threats), drop Timid, and make Brave +2.
creatures.source: Between Sand and Sea: Mythic Africa p. 46

creatures.name: Muqadam, the Barbary Lion of Virtue

powers.name: Know Thy Subject's State
powers.description: With a moment's concentration he learns the physical state of any Beast of Virtue whose token he holds. InAn 35 (Base 3, +4 Arc, +4 Boundary); Ritual Power x2. Might spent so is recovered only by resting in a Magic aura of 4 or higher.

powers.name: Routing Bellow
powers.description: A roar that makes men and beasts who hear it flee in fear. ReAn(Me) 30 (Base 5, +1 Diam, +3 Sound, +1 Mentem requisite); Greater Power (30 levels, -3 Might cost, +5xp Penetration).

powers.name: Circle of Beast Warding
powers.description: A ring traced in the earth that no mundane beast of Size +4 or less may cross; he thinks it unsporting for hunting. ReAn 20 (Base 2, +1 Touch, +2 Ring, +3 Size); Lesser Power (20 levels, +5xp Penetration).

powers.name: Cowing Snarl
powers.description: A man or beast of his size or less, caught by his gaze, kneels in fear. ReAn 25 (Base 4, +1 Eye, +1 Diam, +2 Size, +1 Mentem requisite); Lesser Power (25 levels), Improved Powers x3 (-5 Might cost, +10 Initiative).

powers.name: Trackless Step
powers.description: His sweeping tail erases his tracks as he walks. ReTe 10 (Base 4, +1 Touch, +1 Conc); Lesser Power (10 levels, +15xp Concentration).

powers.name: Hunter's Pounce
powers.description: Leaps up to 50 paces. ReAn 25 (Base 15, +2 Size); Personal Power (25 levels).

powers.name: Sleep with Eyes Open
powers.description: He sleeps with open eyes and is hard to surprise. ReAn 20 (Base 4, +2 Sun, +2 Size); Personal Power (20 levels, -1 Might cost).

creatures.appearance: A great tawny lion near the size of a moose or aurochs, with huge paws, carefully sharpened dark claws and a mane hung with small objects. His tail swishes when he is irritated, and lying down his left rear foot twitches. His flanks are scarred and a small notch marks his right ear.
creatures.notes:
Natural weapons: Large claws Init 0, Atk +5, Def +3, Dam +4; Large teeth Init 0, Atk +4, Def +1, Dam +3. Hide Protection +2. Flaw details: Fury (lion captors), Weakness (surrendering foes).

The greatest of the Barbary lions, who exists to hunt and rule the beasts of the Maghreb. His roaming court holds lesser Lions of Virtue (Realms of Power: Magic p. 60), Bears, Jackals and Leopards of Virtue, with Foxes and Griffon Vultures as heralds and spies, and Gazelles and Antelope as messengers. The tokens in his mane are Arcane Connections to his vassals, tied there by his valet, Srba, a Barbary Ape of Virtue. He favours the Vultures over the Foxes and the Antelope over the Gazelles, counts the Leopards his peers, dislikes the Jackals' attitude but values their work, and finds the Bears enigmatic and erratic.

He distrusts humans, remembering Rome's capture of Barbary lions for the arena, and hunts small parties, scattering them and taking their mounts; only if attacked does he strike people, often enough that the tribes avoid parts of the Great Desert in spring and autumn. Since two of his cubs were taken, anyone seen holding a captive lion in the sands forfeits his life. Otherwise he behaves as Pentule, the Lion of Virtue (Realms of Power: Magic p. 60).
creatures.source: Between Sand and Sea: Mythic Africa pp. 60-61

creatures.name: Azru, the Atlas Bear of Virtue

powers.name: Terrible Roar
powers.description: A roar that freezes men and beasts who hear it, trembling with fear. ReAn(Me) 30 (Base 5, +1 Diam, +3 Sound, +1 Mentem requisite); Greater Power (30 levels, -3 Might cost, +5xp Penetration).

powers.name: Thunderous Swipe
powers.description: A blow that throws anything up to his own size 5 paces; Dex against Ease Factor 12 to stay standing. Thrown straight up or into something hard, the target takes falling damage (+1 per 2 feet, +7 at most). It may join a claw attack. ReAn 25 (Base 10, +1 Touch, +1 Size, +1 Corpus requisite); Lesser Power (25 levels), Improved Powers (-5 Might cost).

creatures.appearance: A large shaggy bear of up to fifty stone (700 pounds), over seven feet tall upright, with a coat from light brown or yellowish to black, most often medium brown, big claws and a deep, echoing roar.
creatures.notes:
Natural weapons: Large Claws Init 0, Atk +5, Def +3, Dam +4; Teeth Init 0, Atk +3, Def +1, Dam +1. Hide and fur Protection +3. Virtue and Flaw details: Ferocity (when injured), Weakness (sweet foods); Extra Natural Weapons (bite); Improved Damage and Improved Initiative (claws).

Once hunted for the arena, Africa's only native bear ranges from Marrakesh to Tripoli in its mountains and their surrounds: mundane ones brownish black with a reddish-orange belly, no white on the short muzzle, stout and strong-clawed, hunting wadi and brush and always seeking a beehive.

Enrichment: wrap the Bear's claws in its hide round a dry river rock from a wadi in its hunting grounds and leave them 20 days in the sun. The fetish grants Tough.
creatures.source: Between Sand and Sea: Mythic Africa p. 64

creatures.name: Imghrawn, Scion of Antaeus

powers.name: Mien of Man or Massif
powers.description: He looks and sounds like a Size 0 man. MuIm 25 (Base 2, +4 size, +2 Sun, +1 Moving Image); Improved Powers: -3 Might cost.

powers.name: Friend of the Desert
powers.description: He ignores heat and fire damage of +15 or less. ReIg (Base 4, +2 for +15 or less, +2 Sun, +1 size; the book gives no total); Improved Powers: -2 Might cost; Slow Power.

creatures.equipment: Acacia wood cudgel, sack of salt, gold, trinkets
creatures.appearance: Nearly three times a man's height (14 ft, 2775 lbs), fearsome and strangely handsome, thick and curly of beard, strong of nose, with bright calculating black eyes. He wears Berber robes, with skulls in swaths of indigo at his waist, and carries a huge acacia cudgel studded with green-white desert glass. A miserable camel bears his hoard, and now and then he leads a chain of slaves, usually to trade for baubles, sometimes to eat.
creatures.notes: Reputations: none. Flaw details: Fury (disrespecting his bloodline), Weakness (must meet a declared challenge); Improved Damage (Fist) x2; Personal Power (Friend of the Desert, Mien of Man or Massif).

creatures.appearance: A shrivelled, leathery corpse blackened by the sun, in tattered rags, with pale, milky, pupil-less eyes and a slow, stuttering gait.
creatures.notes:
Lies still unless carrying out its last orders, which it repeats until it cannot or until a more important order applies. A season's study makes one a source of Garamantian Lore or Insight. No vis.

powers.name: Give Chase
powers.description: Its gaze fills a victim with the wish to chase it until sunrise or sunset. ReMe 15 (Base 4, +1 Eye, +2 Sun): Lesser Power (15 levels, -2 Might cost).

powers.name: Gone to Ground
powers.description: Teleports to a place within 500 paces to which it has an Arcane Connection. ReAn 20 (Base 20): Personal Power (20 levels, -1 Might cost). Not while observed.

powers.name: Unsporting Stalker
powers.description: Blends into the terrain, +3 to vision-based Stealth checks. MuIm 3 (Base 1, +1 Diam, +1 moving images): Personal Power (5 levels, -1 Might cost, +15xp Concentration). The book prints Duration Conc but prices +1 Diam.

creatures.appearance: Pony-sized, long in the body with a narrow head and muzzle, big ears and short limbs; sandy fur, ivory at the belly, the tail darkening to a sooty tip.
creatures.notes:
Natural Weapons, Teeth: Init 0, Atk +3, Def +1, Dam +1. Printed Flaw Restricted Magic (it cannot use Gone to Ground while observed) is recorded as its Minor Flaw; the catalog has no Flaw of that name. Wounds: -1 (1-6), -3 (7-12), -5 (13-18), Incapacitated (19-24), Dead (25+).

Pale Foxes live in small family groups, rest in burrows up to 10 paces deep through the midday heat, and go out at twilight, needing no water. They love a good trick or a long chase, leaving tracks and glimpses to draw it out, and taunt hunters and steal their kills.

Enrichment: its tail lining a cloak hood or boots of the finest gazelle hide, made only by moonlight, gives Puissant Guile (the cloak) or Puissant Stealth (the boots). A tail makes one item.

creatures.name: Axudad, the Deathstalker Scorpion of Virtue
creatures.how_many: Dozens guard the hidden wadi of The Bitter Fruit

powers.name: Venomous Sting
powers.description: If its Attack Advantage beats the victim's armor Protection (not Soak), the victim suffers an exceptionally debilitating poison (Stamina roll against Ease Factor 6, Incapacitating), wounded or not.

powers.name: Drive Berserk
powers.description: Its touch drives the target to attack everything nearby for a Diameter. CrMe 10 (Base 4, +1 Touch, +1 Diameter): Lesser Power (10 levels, -1 Might cost, 5xp Concentration, +5xp Penetration).

powers.name: Lie in Wait
powers.description: Sitting still, it looks like a plain rock or small dune. MuIm 10 (Base 5, +1 Conc): Personal Power (10 levels, -1 Might cost, +10xp Concentration).

creatures.appearance: A dull black or slate grey creature with crab-like chitinous legs, glossy obsidian eyes, oversized pincers and a barbed tail arched over its back; as big as a healthy dog or a six-year-old child.
creatures.notes:
Natural Weapons: pincers Init +0, Atk +3, Def +3, Dam +4; tail sting Init +4, Atk +2, Def -6, Dam +1. The book prints Grapple Defense as +* and Sting Damage as -3* with no key, so Grapple Defense is 0 here. Wounds: -1 (1-3), -3 (4-6), -5 (7-9), Incapacitated (10-12), Dead (13+).

Cruel and belligerent, it hunts warm creatures sleeping by fires or on sunny rocks, and lurks under the sand to sting what steps over it.

Enrichment: its stinger set on a willow handle, anointed with Alkhad gourd sap and left a month plunged in a dune, carried as a token, gives Greater Immunity to Venom. The Tuareg claim the creeping Alkhad or Tadjalt plant and its inedible gourds cure scorpion venom; the cut gourd's milky sap is said to purge poison.
creatures.source: Between Sand and Sea: Mythic Africa pp. 81-82

creatures.name: Demon of Thirst and Despair
creatures.how_many: A kind; they haunt the desert
creatures.weakness: Protected Group: it can prey only on solo travellers.

powers.name: Coagulation
powers.description: Takes a material form in one round, most often a wave of grinding stones, and may discorporate almost at once. Its rocky body can hide trails and landmarks.

powers.name: Elemental Control of Water
powers.description: Variable cost: any Creo, Muto or Rego Aquam effect at 1 Might a magnitude, minor effects of level no higher than its Might. It taunts those dying of thirst.

powers.name: Envisioning
powers.description: Subtly alters dreams to make them more ominous and depressing.

powers.name: Obsession
powers.description: When a human commits a venial sin and it spends Might, then at the next crisis of worthiness the storyguide rolls a simple die +3 and the player a simple die + a suitable Personality Trait - adjustments for harsh surroundings. If the demon's total is higher, the character gains Doubt +1; acting on it puts him in a state of sin, and the demon then coagulates and kills him.

creatures.appearance: Often an elemental of grinding stones, or a moving pillar of salt, rarely a human shape, which it never shows to those strong enough to fight it.
creatures.notes:
Rules from Realms of Power: The Infernal. Abilities include specialization in the Attack and Defense totals. Wounds: -1 (1-6), -3 (7-12), -5 (13-18), Incapacitated (19-24), Dead (25+).

It misleads travellers until hardship and fear of death cost them their faith, then kills them before they can repent, often turning its body into a grave and tempting the victim to throw himself in; the few with human form make pools and drown them. It is why caravan runners go in pairs.
creatures.source: Between Sand and Sea: Mythic Africa p. 83

creatures.name: Aisha Qandisha

powers.name: Allure
powers.description: +3 on all rolls to impress others. Base 3, +1 Touch, +2 Sun.

powers.name: Grant Major Flaw (Wildness)
powers.description: Ritual, no Hermetic equivalent. Her lover grows helpless before all faeries, and suffers a different random Minor Personality Flaw each scene, stilled briefly by ecstatic experience such as dance, music or wandering dry riverbeds in hope of meeting faeries again.

powers.name: Grant Minor Flaw (Impotence)
powers.description: Ritual, no Hermetic equivalent. Her lover cannot have sex with others.

powers.name: Guide
powers.description: Leads a character into danger like the Common Sense Virtue, but serving her ends. ReMe Base 5, +2 Voice, +1 Conc, +2 Group.

powers.name: Hound
powers.description: Tells her the direction and distance of her human quarry. InCo Base 3, +4 Arc, +1 Conc.

powers.name: Invisibility
powers.description: A personal Veil of Invisibility (ArM5 p. 146). Base 4, +2 Sun, +1 moving image. The book prints '1 point, Init 0, Mentem' before these figures.

powers.name: Pine Away
powers.description: A major disease, Ease Factor 15, causing a Light Wound, treatable with Faerie Lore or Medicine; the victim loses the will and the vitality to live. Base 30 (5 + 25 virulence), +2 Voice.

powers.name: Silent Motion
powers.description: Constant: she moves without a sound. Base 3, +2 Sun, +1 constant. The book prints '1 point, Init 0, Mentem' before '1 point, constant, Imaginem'.

powers.name: Steal Judgment
powers.description: The target believes almost any lie she tells; an Intelligence roll against Ease Factor 6 resists, easier for truly incredible lies. Base 4, +1 Eye, +2 Sun. The book prints '1 point, Init 0, Mentem' before these figures.

creatures.equipment: Any trappings of a woman of wealth and dubious virtue.
creatures.appearance: A beautiful woman with the legs of a goat, though her Presence and Allure stop this hindering her.
creatures.notes:
Not a player character. A famous jinn from Morocco, an ancient creature of sterility and temptation who walks dry riverbeds seducing men. She profits from the Hunger's barrenness without quite serving it. She prefers not to fight, seducing attackers or vanishing and sending enthralled men against them.

Stamina is printed as Tireless. The block lists her Abilities as Pretenses, 'many, but notably' these. Greater Powers x3 cover Guide, Hound, Pine Away, Steal Judgment, Invisibility and Silent Motion; Ritual Powers x4 the two Grants. Her vis has no printed Art. Wounds: -1 (1-4), -3 (5-8), -5 (9-12), Incapacitated (13-16), Dead (17+).

creatures.name: Sirocco, the Howling Thirst of the Maghreb

powers.name: Presence
powers.description: A Constant effect. With a few moments' concentration he learns anything that happens within the bounds of the Great Desert.

powers.name: Donning the Corporeal Veil

powers.name: Eidolon

powers.name: Master of Sandstorms

powers.name: Master of Thirst

vis.where: in the dust on his clothes or in his cyclone

creatures.appearance: A Tuareg warrior, robed and veiled, a falchion at his side and sand swirling round his feet; or a whirling cyclone of dust and sand.
creatures.notes:
The hot, dust-laden wind out of the south-east, which often reaches hurricane speed. In Africa it prefers its Arabic name, the Ghibli, and grudgingly owns that Europeans know Sirocco better. It appears most often as a veiled Tuareg raider, and always as some sort of warrior, short-tempered and with a biting falchion.

Proud and Wind are its Essential Traits; its Homing Instinct is for Kaf Ajnoun. Its Qualities are printed as Focus Power: Auram x2, Greater Power (Donning the Corporeal Veil, Eidolon, Presence), Major Virtue (Magical Master), Improved Abilities x4, Improved Might x5, Improved Powers (Focus Power, Master of Thirst) and Lesser Power (Master of Thirst). The block gives three Greater Powers for the three named.
